Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Get more news Live on Share Add NBC News to Google Nov. 13, 2026, 4:09 PM EST / Updated Nov. 13, 2026, 9:35 PM EST By Corky Siemaszko , Tom Costello , Joy Y. Wang and Marlene Lenthang U.S. air traffic was brought to a standstill Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for departing flights that lasted more than five hours. The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET, after more than 5,000 flights were canceled and airports across the country became packed with stranded, irritated passengers. The sudden and stunning alert was issued at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the FAA said. It offered no other information beyond stating that “all departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.” Follow along for live coverage. Hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, in a White House news conference Friday evening, blamed the outage on an outdated air traffic control system in which the routers “got overloaded with data.” What caused the ground stop Duffy explained that once the routers became overloaded, it led to “instability for our radar and our communications in our centers, in our TRACONS throughout the country.” TRACON stands for Terminal Radar Approach Control and is an air traffic control center. “The TRACONS and the centers, we started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and our communication with airplanes,” Duffy said. That instability was detected at 3:36 p.m., he said. Duffy said the FAA did not lose all telecom or radar capabilities but because of the instability, the ground stop was issued as a cautionary measure. It’ll take time for the airspace to recover from the ground stop as crews and planes are out of place and staffers may have reached on-duty shift limitations. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no sign of a cyberattack and the public was never in danger. “FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage. At the time of the ground stop, there were over 3,500 airplanes in the air, Duffy said. When the FAA issued the alert, 4,042 flights headed for U.S. destinations were airborne, according to Flightradar24 , a Swedish service that displays real-time aircraft flight tracking information. Secy. Mullin says FAA ground stop was caused by 'telecommunication outage' 01:51 Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system using analog equipment, which has led to several issues over the past few years. Mullin said earlier Friday that President Donald Trump was briefed on the ground stop. Mullin said that why authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest that. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said. Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X . Packed airports Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations. Chicago O'Hare International Airport, filled with waiting passengers. Jacek Boczarski / Anadolu via Getty “Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.” But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, was at capacity, and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, meaning there was no place for the planes to park, a source with knowledge told NBC News. With planes stranded on runways, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said. FOR SUBSCRIBERS From potato farm to data farm: Inside the Chinese city powering the country’s AI ambitions Slide 1 of 1 Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti called the outage “extraordinary.” Guzzetti emphasized that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing. He added that the situation is turning from a safety issue to a massive logistics problem. Airports are becoming crowded with planes trying to land as the aircraft currently on the ground aren’t able to depart. Planes on the ground may have to move and park on taxiways, Guzzetti said. There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are the ones affected by the outage. Some airports beginning to run out of space for planes amid nationwide ground stop 02:48 At Newark Liberty International Airport, personnel in the control tower said the situation is “a whole mess right now,” according to LiveATC. “We’re running out of space” and “there’s significant gate issues” were comments also heard on the live audio feed. “I’m as much in the dark as everyone else. I’m not getting any information from anybody,” one controller at Newark said, according to the feed. Shortly before the FAA issued its alert, both major airports in Chicago — O’Hare and Midway International Airport — were listed on a ground stop alert due to an “equipment outage,” NBC Chicago reported. Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded. “At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’” Werne, a consultant who helps manufacturers and other industries adapt AI technology, said he is a frequent flyer and this was a first for him. He said there was “a mixture of emotions” from his fellow passengers on hearing the announcement. “Then I started hearing from other friends who were on planes, including one in Chicago who was stuck on a runway,” Werne said. “Right now, our plane is heading back to the terminal, so at least we’re going to be able to deplane.” United Airlines issued a statement acknowledging the ground stop. “United flights that are already airborne will continue,” the statement said. “New domestic flights will not depart while the FAA ground stop remains in place.” Planes are parked at Harry Reid International Airport during a nationwide ground stop, in Las Vegas. John Locher / AP Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare Ground stops across the nation are a rarity in U.S. history. After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports. In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights for a few hours, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers. This is a developing story. title: Reverse engineering my Coway air purifier to ditch the cloud
body_text: Reverse Engineering My Coway Air Purifier to Ditch the Cloud | Scott's Blog Scott J. Goldman Posts RSS Reverse Engineering My Coway Air Purifier to Ditch the Cloud November 11, 2026 16 min read Nice enough air purifier, but I don’t love the app. The year is 2017. A string of annual wildfires rocks the West Coast. The sky looks like this in the daytime: My home, like many in the Bay Area, has no insulation and isn’t really air sealed. To avoid choking on soot, a lot of people started buying air purifiers like this one : The venerable Coway Airmega It’s an overpriced box fan with a HEPA filter and an air quality sensor. It has some controls for the fan speed, and it can also automatically ramp up if the air quality is bad. It’s ugly, but they’re so ubiquitous around here that I feel like no one even notices them anymore. Also, FWIW, the device works. It really does improve air quality. This device became a staple item in our household when my wife eventually started cranking up the fan at night for white noise (a dual purpose!). Over time, I have become accustomed to it and now also require it to sleep. The Good Night button # Our home also has smart lighting, and it’s all integrated with Apple Home. At night, I always press the “Good Night” button, which shuts off all the lights. I really wanted to tie the fan into that. I’d press Good Night, the lights would shut off, and the fan would crank up to my wife’s preferred white noise volume. The old Airmega didn’t have Wi-Fi, so there was no easy way to integrate it with Apple Home. When it eventually broke, I bought the now-discontinued Coway Airmega IconS (for non-discontinued Wi-Fi models, check out the Airmega 250S or Airmega MightyS ). It’s still just a box fan with a HEPA filter, but it’s considerably more expensive, aims to look like a piece of fancy mid-century furniture, and most importantly, can be controlled over Wi-Fi (sort of). The Coway Airmega IconS The existing Home Assistant integration # Coway’s iPhone app is an absolutely classic IoT affair. It takes forever to load, and it asks me to change my password nearly every time I launch it. Thankfully, a brave soul reverse-engineered the app and wrote an integration for Home Assistant . The integration more or less pretends to be the phone app. It polls the Coway cloud service for status updates and sends commands through it to control the fan. Home Assistant bridges that to Apple Home and… voilà! Coway IoCare cloud Coway's servers, somewhere on the internet commands ↑ status ↓ status ↑ commands ↓ My house Home Assistant IoCare integration Air purifier Airmega IconS, on Wi-Fi Apple Home the Good Night button Why ditch the cloud? # The downside of this approach is that you’re still at the mercy (or lack thereof) of the Coway cloud service. It seems like at least once or twice a year, it breaks. Here are some of the reasons I have seen it break: Coway didn’t like the integration hammering their servers and banned it. After a protracted argument with the community, they eventually settled on allowing it. Coway rewrote their phone app and rebranded it from IoCare to IoCare+, so the integration had to be rewritten as well. Coway made minor changes to the layout of the HTML that the integration scrapes, which broke it. Coway’s servers were periodically offline, which prevented any remote control of the device. Coway banned my account at one point for running an old version of the integration. I couldn’t control the fan remotely for weeks while I waited for their support team to reverse the ban. On top of this, it seems unlikely that Coway will maintain this service forever. I suspect that eventually, like all IoT manufacturers, they’ll either charge for this service or discontinue it. My fan model is already discontinued (though there are other Wi-Fi enabled models, so… who knows). A way in # I admit, I have been lazy. For years, I put off trying to figure out a way to ditch the Coway cloud, because if the device was really locked down, it would be pretty tough. Presumably, when the fan starts up, it connects to coway.com (or whatever) and checks that the server’s SSL certificate is valid. Most likely, I wouldn’t be able to make a fake certificate that passes that check, so the fan wouldn’t connect to my server. Also, setting up a man-in-the-middle (MitM) environment is just a pain in the neck. The fan would have to connect to an isolated Wi-Fi network that routes all its traffic through my own server on the way out to the internet. To do that, you have to configure a bunch of routing and firewall rules to redirect traffic. None of this is impossible (I’ve done it before), but it’s a hassle to set up, and it’s always finicky to get right. And once you have it set up, that’s just step one. All that said, two major things have changed. First, there was a recent security incident (October 2026) where someone discovered that eMudhra, one of the trusted internet certificate authorities, had used a very weak parameter for some of its private keys. Ian Carroll @iangcarroll For the next few days or weeks, anyone now has a root CA thanks to eMudhra. Time to have some fun with MiTMing unwilling devices! 10:15 AM · Oct 20, 2026 So, if the device is unpatched AND it has hardcoded root certificates AND it doesn’t pin the cloud service’s certificate, then… maybe that’s a way in. Admittedly, that’s a lot of ifs, but assuming the device doesn’t have any major security mistakes in its design, this could be the foothold needed to take control of it. The second thing is simply AI. An LLM can set up everything you need for a MitM environment, so you can get straight to sleuthing out how the fan works. It can do this unattended, in minutes. Once you can sit between the fan and the internet, you can see how it communicates, which should help us understand how to get the fan to talk to us instead of the cloud. Our man in the middle # Initially, I tried to set it up like this: Air purifier Airmega IconS Wi-Fi Raspberry Pi Wi-Fi access point the Pi in AP mode, its own isolated network all traffic redirected mitmproxy decrypts and logs the traffic My home router the regular home network Coway IoCare cloud out on the internet This actually didn’t work, because a Raspberry Pi uses a smallish PCB trace antenna that doesn’t get a ton of signal strength. With the Pi in the room with my router, the signal was too weak to reach the fan. I guess I could’ve moved the fan into the room with the router, but why do that when I can solve this with a convoluted technical solution? The Raspberry Pi uses its Wi-Fi radio to run its own access point for the fan to connect to. It can’t easily do that while also connecting over Wi-Fi to the home network. So, I moved the Pi into the room with the fan and plugged its Ethernet port into my laptop, which bridges it to the home network over Wi-Fi: Air purifier Airmega IconS Wi-Fi, same room Raspberry Pi Wi-Fi access point the Pi in AP mode, its own isolated network all traffic redirected mitmproxy decrypts and logs the traffic Ethernet My laptop Internet Sharing, bridging Wi-Fi to Ethernet Wi-Fi My home router the regular home network Coway IoCare cloud out on the internet Next, we need to configure the Pi. I’m not really making a value judgment here on whether this is a fair thing to block, but Claude will not oblige the request, not even for… uhh… testing purposes. Luckily, ChatGPT has no such compunctions. After a few rounds of that, here are the nftables rules it ended up with: scottjg@pi:~ $ sudo nft -a list ruleset table inet mitmproxy_ap { # handle 8 set client_interfaces { # handle 4 type ifname elements = { "wlan0" } } chain prerouting { # handle 1 type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; meta nfproto ipv4 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 80, 443 } counter packets 2 bytes 120 redirect to :8080 # handle 6 } chain input { # handle 2 type filter hook input priority filter - 10; policy accept; iifname != "lo" iifname != @client_interfaces tcp dport 8080 counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with tcp reset # handle 7 iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 9 bytes 2397 drop # handle 8 iifname @client_interfaces ct state established,related accept # handle 9 iifname @client_interfaces udp dport { 53, 67 } accept # handle 11 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 53, 8080 } accept # handle 13 iifname @client_interfaces ip protocol icmp accept # handle 14 iifname @client_interfaces counter packets 23 bytes 4697 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 15 } chain forward { # handle 3 type filter hook forward priority filter - 10; policy accept; iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 16 oifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 17 iifname @client_interfaces udp dport 443 counter packets 1 bytes 57 reject # handle 18 iifname @client_interfaces oifname != "eth0" counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 19 } } table ip nm-shared-wlan0 { # handle 12 chain nat_postrouting { # handle 1 type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 ip daddr != 10.42.0.0/24 masquerade # handle 2 } chain filter_forward { # handle 3 type filter hook forward priority filter; policy accept; ip daddr 10.42.0.0/24 oifname "wlan0" ct state { established, related } accept # handle 5 ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 iifname "wlan0" accept # handle 6 iifname "wlan0" oifname "wlan0" accept # handle 7 iifname "wlan0" reject # handle 8 oifname "wlan0" reject # handle 9 } } Basically, the masquerade rule translates the traffic from the isolated Wi-Fi network out through our home internet, and the redirect rule forwards HTTP/HTTPS to a running instance of mitmproxy . Also on the Pi, mitmproxy runs with its web interface, mitmweb , using a command line like this: mitmweb \ --mode transparent --showhost \ --listen-host 0.0.0.0 --listen-port 8080 \ --web-host 127.0.0.1 --web-port 8081 \ --set web_open_browser=false \ --emudhra-old Yes, off the shelf, mitmproxy has a built-in option ( --emudhra-old ) to automatically use the eMudhra root CA to intercept traffic. Snooping on the fan # Next, I used the iPhone app to set up the fan on our Pi-MITM-Test Wi-Fi network. Partway through, the app reported that setup failed. Let’s glance at the mitmproxy web interface: So, we know there was some kind of connection issue, since the app said the fan failed to connect. But it clearly got onto our isolated Wi-Fi, because it made a request . The request is very suspicious. It looks like the fan is downloading the root certificate for Amazon’s certificate authority over plain HTTP. This interface only shows connections that got far enough to make an actual HTTP request. If, for example, the fan doesn’t accept the eMudhra cert we’re using to impersonate the real servers, its HTTPS connections will fail before that point and never show up in the list. Hypothesis: The device downloads this public certificate over HTTP so it has something to validate its later (currently unseen) HTTPS connections against. It doesn’t have any root certificates built in at all. mitmproxy has a plugin mode where you can modify specific requests. We can use it to swap in mitmproxy ’s own generated CA certificate in place of this public one. If our hypothesis is correct, the fan will trust that CA, and we can intercept the rest of its traffic. """Serve this lab's public RSA CA only to the authorized Coway test device.""" from pathlib import Path from mitmproxy import ctx, http def response (flow: http . HTTPFlow) -> None : if ( flow . client_conn . peername[ 0 ] == "10.42.0.93" # device IP and flow . request . scheme == "http" and flow . request . method == "GET" and flow . request . pretty_host == "rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com" and flow . request . path . split( "?" , 1 )[ 0 ] == "/AmazonRootCA1.pem" and flow . response is not None and flow . response . status_code == 200 ): certificate = Path( "/var/lib/mitmproxy-ap/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem" ) . read_bytes() flow . response = http . Response . make( 200 , certificate, { "Content-Type" : "application/x-pem-file" , "Cache-Control" : "no-store" , }, ) flow . metadata[ "coway_test_ca_served" ] = True ctx . log . info( "Served lab RSA CA to the Coway's HTTP CA bootstrap request" ) Sure enough, the device now fully connects, and we can see some new requests: Hypothesis confirmed We can intercept the traffic between the fan and the server, which means we could probably build our own server to replace the Coway IoCare cloud. It also turns out we don’t need the eMudhra hack at all. The fan downloads its root CA cert over plain HTTP. It was always MitM-able. The one thing missing is that none of these requests have anything to do with changing the fan speed or anything else you can do in the app. That’s easy to figure out, though. If you run tcpdump on the Pi while clicking buttons in the app, you can see encrypted traffic on port 8883, the standard port for MQTT over TLS. MQTT is a message bus protocol commonly used in IoT devices. Going back to the POST in the request list above, here’s what that API call returned: { "header": { "success": true, "result": "S1000", "message": "SUCCESS" }, "payload": { "macAddr": "<redacted>", "certToken": "<redacted>", "host": "a29vouc2qruduj-ats.iot.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com", "port": 8883, "serial": "<redacted>", "certSvrUrl": "https://cert.iotp.coway.com/iot/v1/cert/r0", "caUrl": "http://rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com/AmazonRootCA1.pem", "privateUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-private.pem.key", "certUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-certificate.pem.crt", "svcCode": "002AIR007", "countryCd": "US" } } So, if we control the response to this call, we control which keys the fan uses to connect to the MQTT server, and also where that MQTT server is. For now, we can write another mitmproxy plugin that injects our own key into this response, and then use that to proxy the MQTT traffic. The plugin code gets kinda long, so I didn’t include it here, but AI generates it fairly quickly. mitmproxy doesn’t decode MQTT, but it can still show us the raw stream: The data looks like a mix of binary and ASCII gibberish, but it’s a standard MQTT protocol stream. When I adjust the fan speed in the app, you can see a new message come from the Coway server to the device. Usually, I’d load this into a traffic dissector and make a table of what gibberish comes in when I press each button in the app, but now… and after a few minutes… There’s enough here now to build our own web server that hands the fan its certificates and configuration during setup, plus our own MQTT server to send it commands. That completely cuts the Coway cloud out of the picture during normal operation, but we’re still using the Coway app to set the device up. We also still need a fairly annoying MitM environment to get the fan to connect to us instead of Coway. Bluetooth setup process # When you use the Coway app to set up the fan, it searches for the device via Bluetooth. I was hoping we could figure out a way to configure the device ourselves, without the app. Plus, if we’re lucky, we might find something else useful along the way. I have reverse-engineered Bluetooth devices before . My old strategy was to get the Android version of the app, decompile it , and then just pore over the code. It’s not always as straightforward as it sounds. Developers often obfuscate their apps, which makes the decompiled code harder to read. Some bytecode also doesn’t decompile cleanly back to source code, which means you end up having to read the raw bytecode. Still, in my opinion, this is usually easier than dealing with iPhone apps. Android apps are usually written in Java (or Kotlin), and it’s just easier to reverse-engineer Java apps than apps compiled from Swift or Objective-C. This time, I tried a new strategy, which was to use the built-in Android Bluetooth debug logs. Then, I connected the phone over USB and asked the AI to drive the phone via adb , look at the Bluetooth logs, and reconstruct the protocol. The AI took a while to churn through this task. Eventually, it identified that the message carrying the Wi-Fi configuration was encrypted. Since we would ultimately need to figure out what algorithm was used for the encryption, we would probably have to look at the decompiled app. Sure enough, the next thing it did was pull the Coway app off the phone, decompile it. Then, it started matching up the source code with the Bluetooth logs. After all that, we can see the provisioning works like this: Read the fan’s identity over Bluetooth from characteristic FFA0 (a “characteristic” is a Bluetooth endpoint you can read or write). This gives you some basic information about the device, including its MAC address. Write an encryption key (20 random lowercase ASCII letters) to characteristic FFA2 : "P001" + protobuf { command: 1, key: Base64(random_letters) } Construct the AES key by concatenating the key from step 2 with the 12 uppercase ASCII characters of the MAC address. Build the configuration payload, which looks like this: { "cmd": 2, "ssid": "Example Wi-Fi", "pwd": "example-wifi-password", "bssid": "AABBCCDDEEFF", "type": 1, "macAddr": "112233445566", "caUrl": "http://192.0.2.1:8080/ca.pem", "certSvrUrl": "https://192.0.2.1:9443/iot/v1/cert/r0", "certToken": "example-enrollment-token", "serial": "EXAMPLE000000000001" } That gets wrapped in protobuf, padded with PKCS#7, and encrypted using the AES key from step 3. Then it gets prefixed with the string “P002” and sent to FFA2 as well. Needless to say, figuring this out end to end from the decompiled Android app would have been very time consuming to do by hand. It’d be at least hours of work (likely days). AI really comes in clutch here. It took the AI about 20 minutes. The good part, though, is that all the data you need to decrypt that payload is in the Bluetooth logs we captured from the phone, so we can check that our reimplementation is correct just from those. From there, the AI made quick work of reimplementing the whole setup flow in a little Python script. I was watching the progress pretty carefully while this was going on. The AI never actually showed me the full payload, but I could see it in the intermediate output of the scripts it was writing. And that’s when I noticed something. Two of the URLs from our capture are set right in this payload ( caUrl and certSvrUrl ). The first tells the fan where to download the root CA cert over plain HTTP, and the second tells it where to POST over HTTPS to get its MQTT configuration. Since we’re the ones sending this payload now, we can point those URLs anywhere we want. Most importantly, that means we don’t have to do any MitM anymore. We just have to run our own server and plug in its URLs when we set up the fan. Home Assistant integration # Based on the findings in this article, I was able to build a Home Assistant custom integration for the fan . My Home Assistant server doesn’t have Bluetooth, and it’s pretty far away from my fan, so I opted to do the provisioning with Web Bluetooth. That way you can bring your laptop next to the fan and provision it to talk to Home Assistant directly. After that, the device talks directly over Wi-Fi to Home Assistant. And, more importantly, it gets bridged from Home Assistant to my Apple Home. All in a day’s work. Now, I can finally click Good Night. title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026 (1960)
After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
body_text: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models — Haddy Alchaer Haddy Alchaer World models · JEPA · Planning After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models By Haddy Alchaer · November 2026 Solving long-horizon tasks without any extra training 0 / 24 on target · step 0 Vanilla LeWM can be augmented to solve long-horizon physics tasks on out-of-distribution goals. This method uses transformations on a memory graph to generate on-the-fly subgoals without any additional training. Shown here are some of the hardest tasks it solved. There's a big debate in AI right now about what a world model should be. Most of the attention goes to generative world models, which predict the future by generating it, usually in pixels. Many scientists, including Yann LeCun, argue that this is wasted effort. Most of the pixels don't matter for deciding what to do, and many of them can't be predicted at all. [1] The proposed alternative is JEPA, the joint-embedding predictive architecture. It has three parts: an encoder, a predictor and a planner. The encoder turns each frame of observation into a learned embedding, a compact vector that describes the scene. The predictor takes that embedding plus an action and predicts the embedding of the next frame. The planner then tries hundreds of action sequences inside the predictor and picks the one whose predicted end state lands closest to the embedding of the goal. The whole loop runs in embedding space, so the model only has to learn the parts of the scene that are important for deciding actions. The three parts of a JEPA world model. This year a team including LeCun released LeWM [2] , a JEPA world model whose main benchmark is Push-T [3] , a simulation where a robot pushes a gray T-shaped block across a table until the T sits in the green target position shown in a goal image. I've spent the last few months running 600 experiments on it. A goal image from Push-T The planner is given an image like this one and has to make the scene match it. The gray T is the block, the blue disc is the robot's pusher, and the green T is the goal position painted on the table. One detail in this image turned out to affect the success rate more than replacing the predictor with simulated physics. The first thing I wanted to know was how much LeWM is held back by its predictions, so I started by swapping out the predictor for the simulator's perfect physics, while keeping everything else the same. I then gave both versions long-horizon tasks, with the goal 75 steps away, along with the same subgoals: frames from an expert demonstration, one every 25 steps. Vanilla LeWM succeeded 78% of the time. The version with true physics succeeded 77%. Along the kinds of paths it was trained on, LeWM's predictions are already as good as perfect physics for planning. Success on 250 long-horizon tasks 78 % Vanilla LeWM learned predictor ≈ 77 % LeWM real physics the simulator itself That means the next gains for a JEPA world model come from how the trained architecture is used, and that's where most of my 600 experiments went. Without retraining the model once, I found four new planning methods. The first two together took LeWM's success rate on long-horizon tasks from 22% to 85%, about the same as a planner that is handed the ideal subgoals from an expert demonstration. The other two methods extend LeWM to harder goals, and one of them, a single change to how the goal is scored, raised the success rate by 60 points, three times as much as swapping in perfect physics did. 1. Plan through subgoals 25 steps apart Used exactly as published, LeWM succeeds on 22% of long-horizon tasks, where the goal is 75 steps away. [2] When the goal is 25 steps away, it reaches it 89.7% of the time, within a point of the exact-physics version at 90.5%. So the model is accurate over 25 steps and struggles over 75. The usual explanation is that small prediction errors compound over a long plan, which would call for a better model. I tested that against the alternative on the same 250 long-horizon tasks. 250 long-horizon tasks, goal 75 steps away LeWM, all 75 steps at once as published 22% Exact physics, all 75 steps at once the simulator itself 42% +20 LeWM given a new subgoal every 25 steps same model, shorter hops 80% +58 0 25 50 75 100% Exact physics added 20 points. Splitting the task into 25-step segments, each the length LeWM already handles almost perfectly, added nearly 60. LeWM's useful planning horizon is about 25 steps, so it was clear that the way to go further is to chain segments of that length together. LeWM's planning horizon is about 25 steps Plan all 75 steps at once ... one search, far goal 22% A subgoal every 25 steps ... three short searches 80% Chaining 25-step searches through subgoals keeps every search inside the range where LeWM is accurate. This is hierarchical planning: a high level picks subgoals and a low level reaches them. It's widely considered one of the main open problems for world models, and on Push-T it's worth three times as much as swapping in perfect physics. Extra search doesn't substitute for it. Running the planner four times and keeping the lowest-cost plan took four times the compute and added less than one point, because the four runs almost always succeeded or failed together. The subgoals in this experiment came from an expert demonstration, which a deployed robot won't have. The second method removes that dependence. 2. A latent memory graph with a cost on every jump LeWM was trained on expert demonstrations of the task, and its encoder can embed every frame of them, giving about 460,000 embedded states that I connected into a graph. Each state links to the states that follow it in its own demonstration, and to states in other demonstrations that are close in embedding space. To solve a long-horizon task, the planner searches this graph for a path from the current state to the goal and uses the states along that path as subgoals. This only works if distance in embedding space means something physical, and it does. Take one subgoal the robot can reach within 25 steps and one it can't, and LeWM's embedding distance ranks the reachable one as closer 87% of the time. So the embedding space doubles as a map of what the robot can reach. The first version had a flaw. A jump between nearby states in two different demonstrations cost the same as a real step, so the search strung jumps together into paths the block could never follow (318 of 1,015 plans tried to use six or more jumps). The fix was adding a cost on every jump between demonstrations in the graph. Using nothing but LeWM's own embeddings of past demonstrations, success on the same 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away) went from 62% to 85%, which is the same score received by the planner using expert subgoals. Can't get much better than that, right? Planning through a memory of demonstrations start goal Jumps are free · 8 jumps · 62% Each jump has a cost · 1 jump · 85% Each thin path is one demonstration. With free jumps, the shortest route hops between demonstrations into a path the block can't physically follow. With a cost per jump, it stays on them. The standard Push-T test is easier than it looks The caveat is that the standard test takes a demonstration, starts the robot partway through it, and sets the goal a fixed number of steps further along the same demonstration. That's a reasonable design, but in Push-T every demonstration ends with the block in the same place. So every test goal sits on a path that demonstrations already travel, heading for the spot they all end at. For 84% of the standard test's goals, the memory graph already held a nearly identical state from another demonstration. demonstrations, all ending in about the same place goals in the standard test goals from other demonstrations The standard test picks its goals along these streams. The harder test asks for goals like the orange ones, which no single demonstration leads to. The usual sample is also small. On the official 50 episodes, LeWM succeeded 68% of the time with the goal 50 steps away. On 250 fresh episodes drawn the same way, it succeeded only 44%. Changing nothing but the planner's random seed flipped 38 of 250 episodes between success and failure. That's where I decided to build a harder test, where each task takes its start from one demonstration and its goal from another, so the robot has to travel between states that no single demonstration connects. It only counts as a success if the block stays on target for the last 10 steps. Under these rules the memory-graph planner succeeds 75% of the time on standard tasks and 45% on the new ones. The third and fourth methods I found work on that gap. 3. Fill gaps in memory with transformed memories A memory graph is only as good as its coverage. When I deleted every stored state near the goal, success fell from 93% to 32%. Push-T has a useful symmetry here. The physics of pushing a block doesn't change if you shift, rotate or mirror the whole table. So when the graph has no states near a goal, it can take demonstration segments from elsewhere, transform them to fit the gap, and plan through those. With these transformed segments, success came back to 85%. They also stretch a small memory a long way (a graph built from 1% of the demonstrations plus transformed copies did about as well as one built from 10%). Filling a gap in memory with transformed demonstrations a demonstration segment from elsewhere the same segment, shifted, rotated or mirrored Block reached its target, 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away) 93% full memory 32% states near the goal deleted 85% gap filled with rotated and mirrored copies On the harder test, transformed segments raise success from 45% to 56%, and they help most where demonstrations are thinnest. When the goal lies in the direction the demonstrations flow, the memory-graph planner already succeeds 69% of the time. When it lies the opposite way, plain memory gets 27% and transformed memory gets 46%. Harder test, by where the goal lies about 83 tasks per row Goal lies with the flow of the demonstrations 69% Goal lies across it 39% 54% Goal lies against it 27% 46% 0 25 50 75 100% success rate plain memory with transformed segments 4. The cost was “wrong” I also built an interactive demo where I could place the block anywhere and pick any goal. A goal has to be an image, and an image of the scene has to show the pusher somewhere, so I placed the pusher just behind the goal. In one run, the robot pushed the block to within 14 pixels of the target, close enough to count as solved. Then it pushed the block away from the goal, and kept moving the pusher toward where the pusher was in the goal image. The goals in the harder test are frames from expert demonstrations, so each one also shows where the expert’s pusher happened to be at that moment. A planner that compares its prediction with the whole goal image is trying to put the pusher there too. To measure how much this matters, I took the model out of the question. I ran the exact-physics planner twice on the same 50 tasks from the harder test, and the only difference was whether its cost included the pusher’s position as well as the block’s. Block held on target, same 50 tasks exact-physics planner Block and pusher 9 / 50 Block only 39 / 50 success with either cost 30  succeed only without the pusher 0  succeed only with the pusher included Thirty tasks went from failure to success when the pusher was left out, and none went the other way. A split like that happens by chance about twice in a billion. The physics here is from the actual simulator, not predicted, so the 4x in success comes from how the goal was created . The planner that scored the pusher did exactly what it was asked. On the 30 tasks that flipped, it got the pusher to within half a pixel of where the goal image put it, and lost the block on the way. Placing both the T and the pusher in the exact goal position is a much harder problem to solve. Pusher included vs. not Cost compares the block and the pusher Cost compares the block only target for the block where the goal image put the pusher Replay But LeWM can’t simply be told to ignore the pusher. It scores a plan by the distance between two embeddings, and its embedding of a goal image holds the block and the pusher together, with no part labeled “pusher”. So, as a test, I measured how far a planner gets by searching over the pusher instead. It compares each prediction against 16 versions of the goal image, all with the block in the same place and the pusher moved to positions taken from stored demonstrations, and keeps the closest match. That doubled LeWM’s success on the harder test, from 11% to 23%, without retraining. Sixteen versions of one goal A predicted end state 16 copies of the goal with the pusher moved, and the closest one sets the cost This applies to any robot because a goal should just be a set of end states, not a copy of an image. “Put the cup on the shelf” is solved wherever the robot’s arm ends up, but a goal image picks one arm position and makes the planner match it. A good goal accepts every end state that solves the task, and still includes what the task needs from the robot, like coming to rest at the end. The good news is that large sets of demonstrations already contain many real frames of the same object in the same place, each with the robot somewhere different. Scoring a plan against the closest of those goals allows for a larger set of valid end states to plan for. What comes next None of these four discoveries change the model's weights. They apply to LeWM as published, and they should carry over to larger JEPA world models that plan the same way, at no extra training cost. The biggest open problem remaining is generalizing to tasks that don't have perfect demonstrations. On the harder Push-T test, the best planner holds the block on target 56% of the time, and most of the remaining failures are goals that run against the direction of the data. Closing that gap needs a higher level that can propose its own subgoals beyond the demonstrations, and do it better than today's learned hierarchies like H-JEPA [4] , which so far match or slightly beat flat LeWM on Push-T. Hierarchical subgoal planner on top of LeWM demonstrations in memory subgoals taken from memory a goal beyond the data Going in, I assumed LeWM's predictions would be the bottleneck, but a JEPA small enough to train in a few hours already predicts about as well as the simulator itself, and there are several gains that can be achieved simply by changing the way it plans. What it can't do yet is choose its own subgoals where no demonstration has been. That's what I'm currently working on, and if you want to see more, I'll post about it first on X, @haddyalchaer . References [1] Y. LeCun, A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence . OpenReview, 2022. [2] L. Maes, Q. Le Lidec, D. Scieur, Y. LeCun, and R. Balestriero, LeWorldModel: Stable End-to-End Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture from Pixels . arXiv:2603.19312, 2026. [3] C. Chi et al., Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion . RSS, 2023. [4] W. Zhang, B. Terver, M. Rabbat, Y. LeCun, and R. Balestriero, H-JEPA: End-to-End Learning of Hierarchical World Models for Visual Planning . arXiv:2610.06805, 2026. © 2026 Haddy Alchaer

Phil Brink · Monday, November 09, 2026 NVIDIA's headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Authorities are investigating the reported theft of $11.4 million in NVIDIA computer hardware during a shipment from Oakland to Texas. (Photo: NVIDIA) Six pallets of NVIDIA computer hardware worth a reported $11.4 million disappeared during a shipment from California to Texas. A truck collected the merchandise in Oakland on Aug. 29 for delivery to Fort Worth. Investigators reportedly tracked the vehicle through several extended stops before losing its trail in Southern California. The Oakland Police Department confirmed an ongoing grand theft investigation following a complaint filed Sept. 13, 2026. The disappearance comes amid reports of nearly $111 million in stolen data center freight involving other high-value technology shipments. According to The Mercury News , the vehicle displayed a food transportation company’s logo during the scheduled pickup. The driver subsequently traveled south, making several stops lasting multiple hours. Investigators eventually lost track of the truck in San Bernardino County. A separate $12 million cargo theft investigation involved suspects who allegedly exploited established trucking identities to obtain freight. Authorities have not linked the two investigations. Oakland police confirm investigation The Oakland Police Department provided FreightWaves with the following statement: “The Oakland Police Department (OPD) is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026. The investigation is ongoing, and anyone with information is asked to contact the OPD General Crimes Unit at (510) 238-3728.” The Sept. 13 complaint date does not establish when the theft occurred. Police have not confirmed the reported $11.4 million valuation or identified the specific merchandise. Authorities also have not identified the cargo’s owner, shipper, motor carrier or driver. Investigators have not publicly explained the vehicle’s extended stops or established whether criminals impersonated a transportation provider. Police have not announced arrests or confirmed any recovery of the merchandise. FreightWaves contacted NVIDIA for comment and followed up, but the company has not responded. Previous thefts involving NVIDIA products The Oakland investigation follows other significant thefts involving NVIDIA merchandise in Northern California. During 2025, Fremont and Union City police investigated burglaries involving more than $7.5 million in NVIDIA products. Those incidents targeted valuable computer hardware at separate locations. Authorities have not established any connection between those investigations and the latest disappearance. In a separate September incident, thieves stole two PlusAI trailers, including one displaying NVIDIA branding , from a Fremont, California, warehouse. The trailers contained approximately 40,000 pounds of sand rather than NVIDIA hardware. Police recovered both trailers in nearby Newark. Investigators have not established any connection between that theft and the Oakland case. Why it matters The reported disappearance of $11.4 million in NVIDIA hardware underscores the financial stakes of transporting high-value freight. Regardless of how this shipment disappeared, carrier verification, shipment visibility and communication remain critical throughout transportation. body_text: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths | Mathematics | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Close dialogue 1 / 3 Next image Previous image Toggle caption Print subscriptions Newsletters Sign in US US edition UK edition Australia edition Europe edition International edition The Guardian - Back to home The Guardian News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Show more Hide expanded menu News View all News US news US politics Midterms 2026 World news Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness Opinion View all Opinion The Guardian view Columnists Letters Opinion videos Cartoons Sport View all Sport Soccer NFL Tennis MLB MLS NBA WNBA NHL F1 Golf Culture View all Culture Film Books Music Art & design TV & radio Stage Classical Games Design a better world Lifestyle View all Lifestyle The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money Search input google-search Search Support us Print subscriptions Newsletters Download the app Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us The Guardian app Video Podcasts Pictures Inside the Guardian Guardian Weekly Crosswords Wordiply Corrections Tips Search input google-search Search Digital Archive Guardian Licensing Live events About Us World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development Gödel’s work inspired Alan Turing and paved the way for the digital age. Photograph: Alfred Eisenstaedt/The LIFE Picture Collection/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Gödel’s work inspired Alan Turing and paved the way for the digital age. Photograph: Alfred Eisenstaedt/The LIFE Picture Collection/Shutterstock Mathematics ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems Alex Bellos Fri 13 Nov 2026 11.38 EST Last modified on Fri 13 Nov 2026 13.38 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems , published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age. After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science. Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it. Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about. The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought. View image in fullscreen Albert Einstein presenting Kurt Gödel (second from right) with an award at Princeton University, where the two became friends. Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann Archive “I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.” Did you solve it? Gödel’s incompleteness theorem Read more Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation. In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978. Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team. In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature. “In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts. “The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen A microfilm image of an example of Gödel’s shorthand from one of his notebooks. Photograph: Institute for Advanced Study Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice. Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes. The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern. “What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.” Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.” In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! [incorrect] or schlecht! [bad].” Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.” Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.” Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.” Explore more on these topics Mathematics AI (artificial intelligence) Finland Europe Austria news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development News Opinion Sport Culture Lifestyle Original reporting and incisive analysis, direct from the Guardian every morning Sign up for our email About us Help Complaints & corrections Contact us Tip us off SecureDrop Privacy policy Cookie policy Tax strategy Terms & conditions All topics All writers Newsletters Digital newspaper archive Bluesky Facebook Instagram LinkedIn Threads TikTok YouTube Advertise with us Guardian Labs Work with us Accessibility settings Back to top © 2026 Guardian News & Media Limited or its affiliated companies. body_text: Announcing Rust 1.100.0 | Rust Blog Rust Blog Rust Install Learn Tools Governance Community 🖌 Light Dark System Announcing Rust 1.100.0 Nov. 12, 2026 · The Rust Release Team The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup , you can get 1.100.0 with: $ rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0 . If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel ( rustup default beta ) or the nightly channel ( rustup default nightly ). Please report any bugs you might come across! What's in 1.100.0 stable Never type Allocator API DropGuard API Conjuring zero-sized types Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo min-publish-age Stabilized APIs Never type After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable ! This also completes the project goal for this work. The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return , break , and std::process::exit , also have the type ! . Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if : fn mrrrow ( option : Option < u32 > ) { let value = match option { // `x` has type `u32` Some ( x ) => x , // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`, // allowing the `match` to pass type checking. None => return , } ; // ... } While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions ( -> ! ), this release allows naming the never type anywhere: fn infallible_unwrap < T > ( res : Result < T , ! > ) -> T { // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before let Ok ( v ) = res ; v } Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using ! . This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization). Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible , we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024 . This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable. We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it. Allocator API This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api , enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box . These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait. This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal . A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon! DropGuard : run a closure on every exit path The Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return , ? , or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket . Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard : a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped. DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable. DropGuard also implements a dismiss associated function [1] which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure: use std :: mem :: DropGuard ; use std :: num :: ParseIntError ; /// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`. /// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged. fn parse_all ( nums : & mut Vec < u32 > , strings : & [ & str ] ) -> Result < ( ) , ParseIntError > { let len = nums . len ( ) ; let mut nums = DropGuard :: new ( nums , move | nums | { nums . truncate ( len ) ; // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure } ) ; for s in strings { nums . push ( s . parse ( ) ? ) ; // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back } DropGuard :: dismiss ( nums ) ; // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard Ok ( ( ) ) } Conjuring zero-sized types As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this. This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: std::mem::conjure_zst . Instead of transmuting () , MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() , or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing. Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's Python<'py> is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition. Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every bin in a package when only some may use it. Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g. warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber` --> Cargo.toml:23:1 | 23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ | = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber` A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running cargo check --bin foo won't show warnings for unused [dependencies] because another bin may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused dev-dependencies because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built. This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the [lints.cargo] table in Cargo.toml , completing this project goal . See also the other lints that have been introduced . Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the build-dir and then uplifts final artifacts to the target-dir . At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like --features , can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the build-dir . These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a build-dir across git worktrees. The build-dir now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory. This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal , unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking. We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases. Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns. You can opt in via .cargo/config.toml : [ registry ] global-min-publish-age = " 3 days " When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back: $ cargo update Updating crates.io index Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago) Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago) When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update: $ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE = a l l o w cargo update clap - -precise 4.6.9 Updating crates.io index Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days) The newer version will be recorded in Cargo.lock and kept from then on until a later cargo update re-resolves it. A few things to keep in mind: This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back. cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with cargo install foo@1.2.3 if needed. Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would. Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal , including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases. Stabilized APIs impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for Vec<T, A> impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for &[T] impl PartialEq<Cow<'_, [U]>> for &mut [T] std::alloc::Allocator std::alloc::Global std::alloc::System impl Allocator for Global impl Allocator for System impl<A: Allocator> Allocator for &A impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Box<T, A> impl<A: Allocator> Allocator for &mut A impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Arc<T, A> impl<T: Allocator, A: Allocator> Allocator for Rc<T, A> Box::new_in Box::from_raw_in Box::from_non_null_in Box::into_raw_with_allocator Box::into_non_null_with_allocator Box::allocator Vec::new_in Vec::with_capacity_in Vec::from_raw_parts_in Vec::from_parts_in Vec::into_raw_parts_with_allocator Vec::into_parts_with_allocator Vec::allocator Child::main_thread_handle impl Default for std::sync::Once bool::toggle Box::take Box::map Rc::map Arc::map impl AsRef<T> for ! impl AsMut<T> for ! core::mem::DropGuard core::mem::conjure_zst UnsafeCell::replace UnsafeCell::as_ref_unchecked UnsafeCell::as_mut_unchecked str::trim_prefix str::trim_suffix [T]::trim_prefix [T]::trim_suffix Path::trim_prefix Vec::from_fn os::windows::process::CommandExt::show_window Other changes Check out everything that changed in Rust , Cargo , and Clippy . Contributors to 1.100.0 Many people came together to create Rust 1.100.0. We couldn't have done it without all of you. Thanks! it has deliberately been chosen not to be a method to avoid name collisions with the DerefMut -enabled method resolution on the inner type. ↩ Get help!
