Turn SVG artwork into stitches, fine-tune it in the editor, and export PES, DST, EXP, JEF, or VP3 for broad compatibility with embroidery machines—or send designs directly to a Brother Skitch (PP1) over Bluetooth . Draw in Illustrator, draw in ZigZag, or let an agent draw. The Rust engine and zigzag command-line tool power the same workflow outside the editor. See ZigZag in action zigzag-demo.mp4 Stitching on a Brother Skitch (PP1) Download the video (MP4, 1080p) · Original post on X . Download for Mac Download ZigZag.dmg For Apple Silicon and Intel Macs, macOS 11 or later. Open the DMG, then drag ZigZag into Applications. The release is signed and notarized by Apple. No Rust installation is needed. Or with Homebrew : brew install --cask simpsoka/zigzag/zigzag To update a Homebrew installation: brew upgrade --cask --greedy simpsoka/zigzag/zigzag Starting with version 0.1.3, ZigZag also offers an in-app updater: it tells you when there's a newer release and installs it when you say (ZigZag › Check for Updates…). Download for Windows Download ZigZag for Windows — the ZigZag-<version>-x86_64-windows.zip asset on the latest release. For 64-bit Windows 10 (version 1709 or later) and Windows 11. Unzip it and double-click ZigZag.exe . Windows SmartScreen warns on apps without a Microsoft-trusted signature the first time they run; click More info → Run anyway . No Rust installation is needed. Download for Linux Download ZigZag for Linux — the ZigZag-<version>-x86_64-linux.tar.gz asset on the latest release. For x86-64 Linux desktops with glibc 2.35 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12+), X11 or Wayland, and OpenGL. Extract the archive and run ./zigzag-studio inside the extracted folder. It also includes the zigzag CLI and zigzag-mcp bridge; no Rust installation is needed. See the included README.txt for runtime dependencies and Bluetooth setup. Release notes and checksums · Changelog · Publishing a release zigzag/ src/svg.rs SVG import (usvg): fill and stroke parts, transforms, text src/document/ editable document; settings saved back into SVG ids, layout edits as SVG transforms, lettering src/params.rs stitch settings tokens + fabric presets src/stitch/fill.rs tatami fill (scanline sections, staggered rows) src/stitch/satin.rs satin columns: two rails, auto-satin, underlays, short stitches, lean src/stitch/columns.rs shapes that branch or have holes, cut into satin columns src/stitch/stroke.rs running / triple-run stitch src/boolean.rs polygon booleans and offsets (i_overlay) src/design.rs planner: overlap removal, cap order, routing, trims src/route.rs travel out of sight: a way through fills and under what covers src/checks.rs digitizing checks (sizes, widths, lettering, hoop) src/machine/profile.rs machine profiles: hoops and file format, built in (profiles.json) or your own src/formats/ PES (+PEC), DST, EXP, JEF, VP3, Skitch PEN writers; PES/PEC/DST/EXP/JEF readers; preview; worksheet src/machine/ Skitch Bluetooth protocol (+ btleplug client, `ble` feature) src/studio/ editor (egui on OpenGL via glow) + MCP server (`gui` feature) src/mcp_bridge.rs stdio ↔ HTTP bridge for MCP clients that launch a command Build cargo build --release # CLI + MCP bridge, no system deps cargo build --release --features gui,ble # + the studio editor and Skitch upload Linux needs the usual X11/Wayland and OpenGL dev libraries for gui . libdbus is vendored for ble . Stitch types Type What it does Works on Fill (tatami) Staggered rows, any angle, with underlay (edge walk + rows) and pull compensation Filled shapes Satin Zigzag column between two rails, with center/contour/zigzag underlay, pull compensation and short stitches on tight curves; plain, S-stitch or zig-zag top stitching; stitches square across or leaning ( lean=8 ); several threads across the column (multicolor satin) Strokes (any width); Ink/Stitch-style two-rail paths with rungs; filled shapes : rings use inner/outer outline, bars and crescents split at their tips, letters and other shapes that branch or have a counter are cut into columns where the branches part (a P into its stem and bowl, a T into bar and stem), or border follows the outline Run Running stitch, single or triple (bean) Strokes and outlines Contour Rows that follow the outline inward, or one spiral out from the center (Ink/Stitch's circular fill) Filled shapes Blanket E-stitch: a line with prongs into the shape Edges, appliqué Appliqué Placement line → stop → tack-down → stop → satin cover Filled shapes Manual Every path point is a needle point Imported machine files, pen tool Meander One wandering line through the shape, quilting style: light and soft Filled shapes Ripple Open running-stitch rows following the outline, or one spiral Filled shapes Cross-stitch A grid of X's, sewn as rows of half-crosses out and back Filled shapes Tartan Woven stripes in several threads (a mirrored sett you edit in the panel), each thread its own color block Filled shapes Satins wider than 7 mm are auto-split (shorter, staggered stitches) and use auto spacing (narrow columns more open, wide ones denser). Planner features: Remove overlaps: fill hidden under later objects isn't sewn (keeps 0.5 mm of overlap). Cap order: center-out, bottom-up, grouped by color, still respecting layering. Routing: travel stitches stay out of sight: straight across where a straight line stays inside the fill, otherwise round the inside of its outline (Ink/Stitch's underpath), otherwise any way through the fill (round its holes, through its necks), under a satin that's about to be sewn, or under whatever is sewn later on top. An object's last piece is sewn toward the end the next object can be reached from. So satin lettering sewn stroke by stroke needs cuts only between letters when each stroke is followed by one that covers the way to it (a T's stem before its bar; an E's bars before its stem). A fill in separate parts is sewn part by part, each part's underlay and top together. So a fill with cut-outs, or a dither in scattered blocks under another color, is sewn with few or no cuts. Trims only where none of that works (up to 50 mm of travel). Sewing control per object: a start and an end point (where the thread comes in and leaves, so the next object is close), trim after, stop after (to lay foam or trim appliqué). What's left to cut is the document's Connect bar: drag it to sew across gaps up to N mm (between objects, or the parts of one) with running stitches instead of cuts. Those stitches show, so the panel counts the cuts saved as you drag and the canvas lights up what would be sewn. Fabric presets: standard, thin cotton cap, structured cap, knit. Checks: narrow fills, wide/narrow satins, small lettering, tiny gaps, fully covered objects, hoop fit. Group colors: reorder to cut thread changes without breaking layering. Mac app On a Mac with Rust and the Xcode command line tools ( xcode-select --install ): packaging/macos/make-app.sh --install # builds ZigZag.app and copies it to /Applications packaging/macos/make-app.sh --dmg # also makes dist/ZigZag-<version>.dmg to share packaging/macos/make-app.sh --universal # one app for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs packaging/macos/make-app.sh --release # the DMG to publish: universal, signed, notarized --release signs with your Developer ID and has Apple notarize the app and the DMG, so it opens on any Mac without warnings. Once, beforehand: add a Developer ID Application certificate (Xcode › Settings › Accounts › Manage Certificates › +), make an app-specific password at account.apple.com, and save the notarization credentials in your keychain: xcrun notarytool store-credentials zigzag-notary --apple-id YOUR_APPLE_ID --team-id YOUR_TEAM_ID The app bundles the studio, the zigzag command-line tool and the MCP bridge. To use the command line from anywhere: ln -s /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag /usr/local/bin/zigzag . For Claude Desktop, point the MCP config at /Applications/ZigZag.app/Contents/MacOS/zigzag-mcp . Without --release the app is signed ad hoc, not notarized. It opens normally on the Mac that built it. On another Mac, macOS blocks it the first time: open System Settings › Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway (on macOS 14 and earlier, right-click the app and choose Open instead). macOS asks for Bluetooth permission the first time you send to the Skitch. Studio The approved embroidered icons live in packaging/macos/AppIcon.png (light) and packaging/macos/AppIcon-dark.png (dark). The Mac build regenerates both multi-resolution .icns files; run bash packaging/macos/make-icons.sh to regenerate them separately. Finder and the unopened app use the light icon. While the studio is running, its Dock icon follows the app's light/dark theme, including the ZIGZAG_THEME=light|dark override. zigzag-studio [design.svg | logo.png] [--mcp-port 7878 | --no-mcp | --mcp-stdio] Laid out like Illustrator, styled like a Mac app: Tools down the left edge: Select (V), Direct Selection (A), Hand (H), Pen (P): click for corners, drag for curves (Option breaks the handles, Shift keeps 45°, Space moves the point being placed); while drawing, Option lends it the Anchor Point tool (drag a segment to bend it, a handle to move it alone, click a smooth point for a corner) and ⌘ lends Direct Selection (drag a point or handle, then keep drawing), and on a selected path Option-drag bends a segment too. Illustrator's Pen group is behind it: Add Anchor Point (+) clicks a point onto an outline without changing its shape, Delete Anchor Point (-) clicks one out (Option swaps the two while held), and Anchor Point (Shift+C) converts points between smooth and corner and drags one handle alone. Press and hold the Pen (or right-click it) for the group's flyout, Option-click it to step through the group, or tear the group off into a toolbar of its own with the strip at the flyout's edge; the Shape tools work the same way. Brush (B), with VectorCraft's path clean-up tools in its group: Smooth (drag along a path to take the wobble out: fewer points, smoother curves; Smoothness in the bar above), Path Eraser (drag across a path to cut that part away) and Join (scrub between two open ends to join them, or an open path's two ends to close it). Shapes (M rectangle, L ellipse, \ line; hold or right-click for polygon and star), Fill Angle (G), Measure (I), Text (T). Below them, the selection's thread swatch: click it for the thread color picker. Curves, the Illustrator way: the Pen clicks corners and click-drags curves (Option while dragging breaks the handle for a sharp turn; Shift keeps points and handles at 45°; hold Space to move the point you're placing). Click the last point to make it a corner, or drag from it to start the next curve in a new direction. Click the first point to close a shape; Enter, Esc, ⌘-click or another tool ends a line and keeps it. With a path selected, the Pen continues it from an open end, adds a point on its outline, deletes a point you click, and Option-click turns a point corner ↔ smooth (Option-drag pulls out new handles). While drawing, click another open path's end to join the two into one. The cursor shows what a click will do. Direct Selection drags points and handles of any shape from your SVG (circles and rects become paths); dragging a curve bends it under the pointer (Option-drag bends a straight one; a plain drag moves it); Delete removes points, arrows nudge them. Smart guides while drawing (View › Smart Guides, ⌘U): Pen points, shape corners and dragged points land on other objects' anchors and centers, where two outlines cross, on an outline, on 45° rays from the last point (level and upright handles too), or in line with any of those, with a magenta label saying which ("anchor", "intersect", "path", "align"…). With Shift, a point keeps its 45° angle and slides into line with the nearest target. Round corners: in Direct Selection a small circle sits inside each sharp corner; drag it in to round the corners (the selected points', or all of them), each only as far as its sides allow. Object › Path › Round Corners… does the same with a radius and Round, Inverted or Chamfer, previewed live. Brush (B), after Illustrator's Paintbrush: paint a line freehand and it comes out smooth, sewn as a satin column at the width you set (or as a running stitch). Smoothness takes out the hand's wobble; sharp turns stay sharp; end where you began to close the line. The cursor is a circle as wide as the satin. Shapes, the Illustrator way: Rectangle (M), Ellipse (L), Polygon, Star and Line (\). Drag from a corner; Option draws from the center, Shift makes a square or circle, keeps a polygon or star upright and a line at 45°. While dragging a polygon or star, ↑/↓ add or remove sides or points. Click without dragging to type an exact size. The bar at the top of the canvas switches shapes and sets corner radius, sides, points and the star's inner radius. Closed shapes come in as fills, lines as runs, in the current thread. Path tools: Object › Pathfinder (Unite, Minus Front, Intersect, Exclude; also buttons in the Transform panel when two or more objects are selected) and Object › Path (Offset Path…, Outline Stroke, Simplify…, Round Corners…, Clean Up…). Simplify… is VectorCraft's slider, from fewest points to closest to the original, previewed live, with Auto-Simplify picking the level for the selection's size. Clean Up… removes stray points, objects too small to sew (under 1 mm by default) and extra points (points on top of each other, points in the middle of straight lines), showing how many of each it found first. Results come back as smooth curves with their real corners (least-squares curve fitting), not as many-sided polygons. Logos from images (Image Trace): open, drop or place a PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP or TIFF and the Trace Image window traces it into flat-color shapes, previewed on your hat's color. Choose how many colors (or Auto), the width, detail and the smallest speck to keep; remove the white background; snap every color to your Brother, Janome or own palette's threads; and sew thin lines as single lines. Flat logos trace exactly (edges placed to a fraction of a pixel, corners restored, circles and straight lines exact); photos are posterized. The command line traces too: zigzag convert logo.png -o logo.pes . Contextual task bar: under the selection, the next things you'd do: its stitch type, its thread, Edit Points, Round Corners, Simplify, Unite (two or more), Duplicate. View › Contextual Task Bar (or its ••• menu) hides it. Ask an agent: the Agent panel (full height in the left dock; the sparkle at the bottom of the tool strip opens and closes it, and ⌘K or Window › Ask Agent… opens it with the prompt ready) runs Claude Code or Codex in the background, connected to this studio's MCP server, so you watch it build the design. It can only use the design tools (no shell, no file edits). The transcript shows what it said and each step, with a spinner on the one running (the one place it's shown; collapse the panel and its header shows the step and the time instead). On the canvas, the objects it's working on get a moving outline, a shimmer and a label saying what it's doing (Drawing, Placing, Restyling…), for any agent connected over MCP, not just the panel's. The panel is named for the agent (Claude Code or Codex; switch in its ≡ menu); + in its header starts a new chat, Stop ends a run. Uses the claude or codex command you've already signed in to. Like any panel it can float, join another as a tab or dock right; sharing a dock it sits at the bottom, under a divider you drag to give it more room. Thread colors and palettes: the picker shows the nearest Brother/Janome thread, a palette to click (Brother, Janome or your own), and a small custom color field. Make palettes from scratch, from the design, or from a thread kit you own (the palette's ≡ menu › New Palette from Thread Kit: Brother's 12, 40 and 22 color sets, or 40 + 22 for all 61; then Match All keeps a design to the threads in your box), add the selection's thread with +, right-click to remove; they're remembered between launches. Threads panel: the design's threads in sewing order (each color block numbered, with its stitches, and "stop" where the same thread comes twice running) or By Color (each thread once, with how many objects use it). Click a row to select what it sews; click a swatch to change that block's thread, or in By Color that thread everywhere. Group Colors and the count of color changes and trims are under the list. The panel's ≡ menu has Match All to the chosen palette, and Show Palette puts a palette to click under the list (off by default, since the thread picker has the same palettes). Panels, the Illustrator way: the Agent has the left dock to itself; Objects, Stitch, Transform, Lettering, Threads and Document are on the right. The design's issues are in the status bar (bottom right): a warning sign with a count, or a check when all's well; click it (or Window › Issues) for the list, each linked to its object. Drag a panel by its header to reorder it, move it to the other dock, or drop it on the canvas to float it (each panel's ≡ menu also has Dock Left / Dock Right / Float). Drop a panel on another panel's header and they share it as tabs; drag a tab out (or use Separate in the ≡ menu) to part them, drag the header to move the group. » at the top of a dock collapses it to a strip of icons for a bigger canvas: click an icon and the panel flies out beside the strip (drag an icon to move that panel). Click a header to collapse a panel; Window › Reset Panels puts everything back. The layout is remembered. Rename an object: double-click its name in the Objects list, as in Illustrator's Layers; Enter keeps the name, Escape doesn't. A single click only selects. Tabs, one per document (as in VectorCraft and Illustrator): Open, drop or New opens a file in a tab of its own over the canvas (the empty document you start with makes way for the first one); a file that's already open just comes forward. Each tab keeps its own undo history, selection, zoom and stitches. Click a tab to switch, ⌃Tab / ⌃⇧Tab (or Window › Next / Previous Document) to step through them, drag one to reorder, middle-click or its × (or File › Close, ⌘W) to close it; + opens a new document and » lists every tab when they don't all fit. A dot in place of the × marks unsaved changes, and closing such a tab asks whether to save it first. Right-click a tab for Close Other Tabs and Copy Path. Quitting doesn't ask: every tab comes back next time, each with its unsaved changes. Lock and hide: every row of the Objects list has an eye and a lock (Illustrator's Layers columns; Option-click for every other object, and Object › Lock ⌘2, Unlock All, Hide ⌘3, Show All). A hidden object isn't shown or sewn; a locked one can't be selected or moved, so a background stays put while you work on what's over it. Drag the Selection tool over empty canvas for a selection box; two-finger scroll, Space-drag or the Hand tool moves the canvas. Updates itself: ZigZag looks at its latest release on GitHub when it opens, and the toolbar shows an Update button when there's a newer one. On a Mac, Install and Relaunch downloads it, checks it against the release's checksum and Apple's code signature (it has to be signed by the same developer as the copy that's running), swaps it in and reopens with your documents as they were. ZigZag › Check for Updates… looks on demand; Settings › General turns the automatic look off. Windows and Linux are told and taken to the download. Travel stays out of sight: the thread gets from one part of an object to the next under stitches still to come or under what's sewn on top; a fill's sections are sewn in the order that allows it. Where there's no such way the thread is cut, or (Document panel › Travel › Sew over fill) sewn over the fill already there, which saves cuts and shows. The checks say when travel crosses stitches already sewn. Menu bar (File, Edit, Object, Type, View, Window, Help) with the usual ⌘ shortcuts. Help › Report an Issue… opens a new issue on GitHub in your browser, started with which ZigZag you have and what it's running on. It's the real macOS menu bar on a Mac, drawn in the window elsewhere. Cursors drawn for each tool: the Pen's nib (with what a click will do), crosshairs for the Shape, Measure and Fill Angle tools, Direct Selection's hollow arrow, and a curved arrow at rotate corners. Right-click menus on the canvas and the Objects list, styled like the tool flyouts: the stitch types with their icons, then the usual commands with their shortcuts. Stays quick on big designs: stitches are planned once per change, reusing every object that didn't change (overlap removal too: moving one object redoes only the objects it overlaps); a design that takes more than 12 ms to plan plans in the background (the status bar says "Updating stitches…" and the last plan stays on screen meanwhile; when you drop a moved object its stitches move with it until the new plan lands). Dragging points or objects, and typing, preview without re-planning until you let go. The stitches live on the GPU: each color block's segments are uploaded once and drawn by a shader (thread shading and needle points included), so panning, zooming, dragging and the stitch player cost nothing per stitch on the CPU, whether the design has a thousand stitches or half a million. The Objects list lays out only the rows in view. An object whose stitches hit an internal error is left out with a warning in Issues rather than taking the plan down. For development: TL_PROFILE=1 prints each frame's sections to stderr, TL_NO_GPU=1 draws the stitches with the painter instead, and cargo test --release --features gui --bin zigzag-studio perf_bench -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1 times typing and dragging on a traced logo ( examples/bench-grid.svg is a 213,000-stitch design for the studio itself). Follows the system's light or dark appearance ( ZIGZAG_THEME=light|dark overrides) and uses the San Francisco system font on a Mac. Pick a stitch type per object: big buttons, the task bar, right-click, or F/S/R/C/X (Blanket and Manual from the Stitch panel). The preview re-plans live. Layout, the Illustrator way: drag to move (Shift: 45° steps; Option: drag a copy). Handles resize freely (Shift keeps proportions, Option resizes from the center, drag past the far side to flip); just outside a corner rotates (Shift: 45°). Smart guides snap edges and centers to other objects and the hoop (View › Smart Guides, ⌘U). ⌘D is Transform Again: Option-drag a copy, then ⌘D for more at the same spacing. Hold Space to pan with any tool (a tap plays the stitch-out). The Transform panel has Illustrator's reference point: X/Y show the chosen point and W/H resize around it. Also rotate, flip, center in hoop, fit to hoop (artwork bigger than the hoop is scaled down to fit when you open or place it; Undo restores full size), ⌘C/⌘V, arrows nudge 0.5 mm (Shift 5 mm). Edits are saved as SVG transforms. Groups work like Illustrator: a click or drag takes the whole group; double-click goes into it (the rest dims and a breadcrumb shows where you are), double-click again to go deeper; Esc or double-click on empty canvas comes back out. ⌘-click picks one object without going in. Layers (Illustrator's "Layer 1", Inkscape layers, Figma frames) aren't groups. Copy, paste and duplicate keep groups. Type (T), as in VectorCraft and Illustrator: click where the text should go and type straight onto the canvas (Enter for a new line, Esc or a click elsewhere when done); click text, or between its letters, to edit it with the caret where you clicked (or double-click it with the Selection tool, which picks text anywhere in its box and shows it as a box, not its letters' points; delete every letter and finish, and the text is removed) (←/→, ↑/↓, Home/End and ⌘←/→ move it; Backspace and Delete remove either side; Shift with any of those, a drag, a double-click for a word, a triple-click or ⌘A for the lot selects text, which typing replaces and ⌘C/⌘X/⌘V copy, cut and paste); click a selected path to put text on it. The Lettering panel is a compact Character panel (hat text isn't long copy): font (with search), bold/italic, letter height, tracking, pair kerning (pick the pair, or Option+←/→ while typing kerns the pair at the caret), horizontal and vertical scale, case (as typed, UPPER, lower, Title), alignment and leading for two-line text, baseline (straight, arc over, arc under, or on a path with offset and flip), and the stitch type. The Type menu has Type on a Path, Change Case, Align and Create Outlines (⇧⌘O). Text is a shape like any other: Direct Selection, Round Corners, Simplify, Pathfinder and Clean Up all work on it (it quietly becomes plain paths at the first point-level edit, one undo step), and it saves as real SVG text until then. Pen (P): draw filled shapes or lines with corners and curves, or place manual stitches one by one. Snaps to the grid when it's showing, else to smart guides. Shapes (M, L, \): rectangles (with rounded corners), ellipses, polygons, stars and lines. Measure , mm grid , needle points , First/Last , Group colors . Open machine files (PES, PEC, DST, EXP, JEF) to view, resize and re-export them, and images to trace. Settings per type: fill angle (with a drag-to-set angle tool , A ), spacing, length, pull, underlay. Satin options: column vs border, stitch (satin, S-stitch, zig-zag), threads across the column, width, underlay passes, short stitches. Contour and ripple: rings or spiral. Cross-stitch: cell size. Tartan: the stripes (color and width each, mirrored), angle, row spacing. Run options: single or triple. Lean in the Stitch panel, for satins: how far the stitches lean from square across the column (a few degrees keeps them from sinking between a knit's rows; more shows a slant, like a leaf's veins). Sewing row in the Stitch panel: Start and End (click the outline; green and red markers you can drag), Trim and Stop after the object. Edit › Copy / Paste Stitch Settings carries one object's type and settings to others (each keeps its thread and start/end); Edit › Select Same Stitch Type; Object › Path › Reverse Direction sews a path from its other end. Test swatches (Object › Test Swatches…): copies of the selection in a grid, one setting (spacing, length, pull compensation, satin width, fill angle) stepped from a value to another, each lettered with its value, to stitch out and compare on the real fabric. View › Density Map tints where stitches pile up (yellow from 2.5 per mm², red at 4), and View › Sewing Order numbers the objects on the canvas. Machine in the Document panel: choose the machine a design is for (Brother's 4×4, 5×7 and PR machines, the Skitch, Janome's 550E, Husqvarna Viking's Jade 35, Melco's Summit, ZSK's Sprint 8, any commercial machine that reads DST, or one of your own) and its hoops lead the Hoop menu, Export offers the file it reads first, and new documents start set up for it. What the machine asks of the stitches (a shortest stitch, its own locks) shows under the row. The gear beside it, and Machine Settings… in the menu, open Settings. A machine is a name for ordinary settings, saved into the design, so a file opens the same anywhere. Settings (ZigZag › Settings…, ⌘, ; at the foot of Edit on Windows and Linux): what's set once for this computer. Machines: ZigZag's and yours; + makes one from the document's hoop, Duplicate copies one (ZigZag's own can't be changed, but a copy can); each has its name, hoops (and the one new documents start in), the file it reads, a shortest stitch for machines that drop short ones, and its lock stitches (back and forth, a triangle or none, with their length and number). With a shortest stitch, nothing in the plan or the file is shorter: fill rows closer together than that are sewn every second row and then the rows between (the same needle points, longer turns), other short stitches are merged into their neighbours, and locks are never shorter than it. General: units, light or dark, and whether stitches are drawn on the GPU. Agent: which agent the Agent panel runs, and the server other agents connect to (on or off, and its port; from the next launch). Narrow satin in the Document panel: satins narrower than this (1 mm unless you say) get the too-narrow warning. Set it to what sews cleanly on your fabric. Fabric preset, hoop, Remove overlaps and Cap order in the Document panel. The hoop menu has the standard sizes from 1×2.5 in (20 × 60 mm) to 9.5×14 in (240 × 360 mm), the Skitch's two and Janome's A and B; Custom takes any width and height, for magnetic and other frames. Preview on your hat's color. Issues list (status bar): problems link to the object. Satins show their rails on the canvas. Sewing order: Earlier/Later. Stitch player (Space). Undo/redo everything. Save (Ctrl/⌘ S) writes settings into the SVG; Export PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3/PEC/PEN or a worksheet (HTML: picture, size, time, every color stop with the nearest Brother and Janome thread); Send to Skitch . Measuring and units. Measure (I) works like VectorCraft's: drag between two points to read the distance, angle, width and height. The ends snap to points, edges and the hoop (or to the grid when it's on), Shift keeps the line to 45°, and the reading stays until the next drag (Escape clears it). View › Units, or the unit menu in the status bar, shows sizes, positions, distances and the grid in millimeters, centimeters, inches, points or pixels (SVG pixels, 1/96 in, as files are read); it's remembered between launches. Any length field also takes a typed unit or a sum ( 1/4 in , 25.4mm , 10+5 ). The grid (⌘') follows the unit, inches in halves down to 1/32, and labels its major lines along the canvas's top and left edges from the hoop's center. Stitch settings (spacing, density, pull compensation) stay in millimeters. Picks up where you left off. Quit (or crash) and reopen: the same files come back, every tab with any unsaved changes, the zoom and the selection, and the same tab in front. Changes are kept as you work ( session.json and one recovery file per tab, recovery.svg , recovery-2.svg …, in ZigZag's settings folder ( ~/Library/Application Support/ZigZag ), each written whole or not at all), never written into your file until you save. Opening the app with a file skips this. If the app went down while bringing a document back, the next launch keeps it aside as recovery-crashed.svg instead of trying again (and an unreadable one as recovery-unreadable.svg ), and says so in the status bar. A job on the Skitch comes back too: the design last sent is kept ( sent.json ), the Skitch window reopens if it was open and reconnects, and once the machine reports that design its progress shows on it again (the machine keeps the design and where the needle is; Stop ends the job on both). Agents (MCP) The studio runs an MCP server on http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp (Streamable HTTP, localhost only, Origin-checked). Agents edit the live document you're looking at (the tab in front), and every call is one undo step. MCP in the status bar (bottom right, next to the Skitch) shows whether agents can reach the studio: a gray dot while it waits, green once a client has connected, blue and pulsing while calls come in, red if the server couldn't start. Click it for the address, the commands to connect Claude Code and Claude Desktop (with Copy buttons), the clients that have connected, the recent tool calls (failed ones in red, with the error on hover) and the tools on offer. Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http zigzag http://127.0.0.1:7878/mcp Claude Desktop / stdio clients ( claude_desktop_config.json ): { "mcpServers" : { "zigzag" : { "command" : " /path/to/zigzag-mcp " } } } zigzag-mcp forwards to the running studio. Use --port N if you changed it. With "args": ["--headless"] it works without the app open: the same tools on a document no one is watching ( zigzag-studio --mcp-stdio ), kept only when the agent saves or exports it. Tools: get_design , add_svg (place/scale artwork in mm), set_object , delete_object , move_object transform_objects (size, scale, rotate, mirror, move), duplicate_objects add_text , edit_text , list_fonts set_document (machine, shortest stitch, lock stitches, how narrow a satin may be before it's warned about, fabric, hoop as a standard or any WIDTHxHEIGHT in mm, overlaps, cap order, preview color), list_machines , group_colors render_preview (returns a PNG of the stitches), check_design , get_svg , select export with objects: true also writes FILE.objects.json : which object each stitch, jump and trim in the machine file is for, so a checker can name the shape behind a fault open_file (SVG, machine file or image, in a tab of its own), list_documents , switch_document , new_document , undo , save , export (machine formats or html worksheet; without a format, the one the path ends in, or else the one the document's machine reads), send_to_skitch , machine_status Any tool that changes the design takes terse: true for a short answer (ok, the names of objects added, and the design problems that are new) instead of the whole object; on batch it covers every step. trace_image (PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP or TIFF logo → shapes, colors snapped to a thread chart), round_corners , simplify (VectorCraft's 0–100 levels, or Auto), clean_up batch : several calls in one, all or nothing and one undo step; later steps can use earlier results ( "$0.added.0.name" ) Arguments a tool doesn't take are refused with the ones it does (a misspelt widht_mm isn't silently ignored), and each tool says whether it only reads. Try asking: "Draw a 50 mm round badge with mountains and a sun for my thin cotton cap, check it, and show me the preview." CLI zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.pes -o logo.jef -o preview.png -o sheet.html [--fabric thin-cap] [--hat] zigzag convert old.dst -o old.pes # machine files convert too zigzag convert logo.png -o logo.pes # PNG, JPEG, WebP… logos are traced first zigzag info logo.svg # stats + checks zigzag fabrics # list presets zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.exp --machine melco-summit # that machine's hoop and shortest stitch zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.dst --min-stitch 0.4 --lock triangle:0.5:3 zigzag machines # list machines zigzag convert logo.svg -o logo.exp --objects # and logo.exp.objects.json: which object each stitch is for zigzag skitch info | status # needs --features ble zigzag skitch send logo.svg --trace Illustrator workflow Export with File → Export → Export As → SVG (Styling: Presentation Attributes, Object IDs: Layer Names). Outline text, or it falls back to system fonts. Opening the ZigZag-saved SVG back in Illustrator keeps the settings in the layer names. Name layers or objects to set their stitching. Illustrator's _x3D_ -style escapes are decoded, and group settings apply to everything inside the group. Token Meaning fill satin run skip stitch type a=45 fill angle (degrees) s=0.3 row / zigzag spacing (mm) l=3 max stitch length (mm) pc=0.2 pull compensation (mm per side) w=3 satin width (mm) border satin along a filled shape's outline instead of across it u=0 underlay off ul=center+contour+zigzag satin underlay passes ( ul=none ) ss=0 short stitches off r=3 running passes (3 = bean) contour blanket applique manual the other stitch types split=7 satin auto-split length (mm); split=0 off t=e8a33c thread color override o=2 sewing order stroke.… applies only to the stroke of an object that also has a fill, e.g. stroke.run Example layer names: logo fill a=45 s=0.35 , title satin , outline stroke.satin stroke.w=1.5 . Skitch over Bluetooth The Skitch window (the toolbar's Send button or File › Send to Skitch…) runs the whole job, like a slicer's device page follows a print: the design on the left, what to do on the right, and the steps across the top (Connect · Home · Send · Trial · Sew · Done). Connect and pair. It scans for the Skitch. The first time, hold the Skitch's Bluetooth button until it beeps, then Connect (or Try Again); if the computer asks to pair, accept. On a Mac the Skitch never appears in System Settings › Bluetooth (it's a Bluetooth LE device): it pairs when ZigZag connects. Allow ZigZag to use Bluetooth if macOS asks (Privacy & Security › Bluetooth). Close Artspira first: the Skitch talks to one app at a time. Home. A machine just turned on asks to be homed (frame off, Accept, frame back on); the window shows the steps and moves on when it's done. Send: the hoop with the design where it will sew: As Placed (where it sits in the studio's hoop, so you can put it high on a cap) or Centered ; the threads to have ready, in sewing order, by Brother Embroidery name and number; a "before you sew" checklist; Send Design. Trial run (Brother's name for it; on by default after sending): press Accept on the machine and the needle goes around the design's outline without sewing, so you can check it clears the frame's magnets, seams and the brim. Trial Again whenever you rehoop. Sew: Start, then press Start on the machine. The picture shows what's sewn, faded where it hasn't been yet, with the needle and the thread on now; under it, a timeline of the threads with the needle's place. The side shows progress, time left, the thread on now and the next one, and at each thread change exactly which thread to put on. The canvas and the status bar follow along too. Start / Pause / Stop. Start (or Resume, or Sew Again) readies the machine; Pause is the Skitch's own Start/Stop button (it can't be paused over Bluetooth); Stop ends the job, taking the design off the machine. While paused, drag along the timeline or step the needle by 1, 10 or 100 stitches or back to the thread's start, then Resume. Errors say what they are and what to do (thread breaks, bobbin, needle plate, frame). After a thread break the needle goes back over the gap (6 stitches for the top thread, 2 for the bobbin, as Artspira does). Minimize it (–) to keep working while it stitches: the canvas is your design again, and the machine's icon at the right of the status bar shows what it's doing and how far, with a small bar (click it to bring the window back). The window comes back by itself when the machine needs you: a thread change, an error, or the end. The ••• menu also links to Brother's Skitch how-to videos (threading, the bobbin, the frame, a thread break, tension, cleaning). The window's ••• menu can connect to a simulated machine , which does each step on the machine by itself, to try it all without a Skitch. Agents can send_to_skitch and follow along with machine_status . The protocol was reverse-engineered (see NOTICE), so avoid firmware updates. Working out undocumented commands Thread tension isn't a Bluetooth setting on the Skitch: it's the tension dial on the machine. Speed is fixed (about 400 stitches a minute). The machine does report a block of settings, and Artspira has a settings screen, so two tools are here for working out what else it can do: Settings bytes (in the Skitch window, under the machine's details): reads the settings block the machine reports. Read it, disconnect, change one setting in Artspira, close Artspira, reconnect and read again: the bytes that changed are marked. Every read is kept in skitch-settings.log beside the panel layout. On the command line: zigzag skitch settings --label "what changed" --log settings.log . zigzag capture FILE lists the Skitch conversation in a Bluetooth recording of Artspira, by command name, with changed settings bytes in [brackets] ( --all for the upload and polling too, --raw for every ATT operation). It reads both: iPhone: install Apple's Bluetooth logging profile on the phone (developer.apple.com › Bug Reporting › Profiles and Logs), restart it, plug it into the Mac, and in PacketLogger (Apple's Additional Tools for Xcode ) choose File › New iOS Trace; save the trace ( .pklg ). Android: Developer options › Enable Bluetooth HCI snoop log, then adb bugreport and take btsnoop_hci.log from it. Writing settings stays out of ZigZag until a layout is known and a write of the machine's own settings, unchanged, reads back the same. Ink/Stitch parity Checked against Ink/Stitch 's features and tool docs: Ink/Stitch ZigZag Running, bean, manual stitch; satin column (two rails with rungs), E-stitch; tatami, contour, circular (spiral) fill ✓ Ripple, meander, cross-stitch and tartan fills; S-stitch, zigzag and multicolor satin ✓ Params per object with fabric-aware defaults; start/end commands; trim and stop commands ✓ (Stitch panel's Sewing row) Auto-route (travel inside fills, underpath along the outline, under what's sewn on top), Jump to Stroke ✓ (document's Connect bar) Simulator, stitch plan preview, density map, stacking-order labels ✓ Lettering (system fonts, arcs, text on a path, multi-line, case, scale), thread palettes, Match All, thread kits ✓ (Brother and Janome charts) Duplicate params, select by type, flip satin direction, test swatches, cleanup, troubleshoot (Issues) ✓ Import stitch files and edit at stitch level; PES/DST/EXP/JEF/VP3/PEC ✓ Gradient fill, guided fill; redwork, cutwork; pre-digitized fonts; 60+ thread brands; PDF print not yet Hatch parity Checked against Wilcom Hatch's core feature set: Hatch ZigZag Tatami, satin, run/triple run, contour fill, blanket, appliqué, manual stitches ✓ Auto underlay, pull compensation, auto spacing, satin auto-split, short stitches ✓ Fabric settings that set densities and compensation ✓ (4 presets) Lettering with TrueType fonts, straight, arc and path baselines, typed on the canvas ✓ (system fonts) Select, move, resize, rotate, mirror, duplicate, copy/paste, align to hoop ✓ Digitize shapes and manual stitches by hand ✓ (pen tool) Remove overlaps, color sequencing, re-order objects ✓ Stitch player, show needle points, grid, measure ✓ Open and save PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3 ✓ (VP3 write only) Production worksheet ✓ (HTML) Auto-digitize bitmaps ✓ (Image Trace: flat logos, posterized photos, centre lines) Built-in embroidery fonts, monogramming, multi-hooping, motif/pattern fills, 3D foam not yet Status Verified: 136 library tests, 153 editor/MCP tests (UI interactions via egui_kittest, a full agent workflow, a real HTTP JSON-RPC session, atomic batches, the Skitch flow against a simulated machine), with and without Bluetooth built in, plus the 222 tests of the vendored Image Trace. Every writer (PES, DST, EXP, JEF, VP3) reads back through pyembroidery with identical stitch positions; our readers read pyembroidery-written files. PEN output checked against hand-computed sequences. Studio run on Mesa OpenGL and driven by an agent over MCP. Tested on a real Brother Skitch (PP1). Screenshots and videos Start the studio with ZIGZAG_CAPTURE=<folder> and ⌃⌥⌘S saves the window as a full-resolution PNG; ⌃⌥⌘R starts and stops recording it. packaging/media/encode.sh <folder>/take-001 demo turns a recording into demo.mp4 and demo.gif (needs ffmpeg). Credits See NOTICE , and THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md for the licenses of the libraries ZigZag is built from (regenerate it with packaging/licenses/generate.sh after changing dependencies). PES/PEC/DST layouts and the Brother palette are from pyembroidery (MIT). Image Trace is vendored from VectorCraft (MIT OR Apache-2.0), whose curve fitting, live corners, snap targets and colour difference were also ported (see vendor/README.md ). Tatami, satin and short-stitch approaches follow Ink/Stitch . About Free, open-source embroidery software for Mac and Windows. Turn SVG artwork into machine embroidery, edit stitches visually, and create designs with AI agents via MCP. zigzag.diy/ Topics brother-skitch embroidery embroidery-digitizing embroidery-software machine-embroidery macos mcp model-context-protocol rust svg vector-editor windows Resources Readme Apache-2.0 license Activity Stars 619 stars Watchers 5 watching Forks 29 forks Report repository Releases Packages Contributors Languages Footer © 2026 GitHub, Inc. title: Brave Search API now accepts agentic payments via the x402 protocol
body_text: The Brave Search API now accepts agentic payments via the x402 protocol | Brave Yes Dismiss Browser Downloads Desktop Android iOS Features Shields adblocker VPN Privacy features Premium services Brave Origin Browser AI More features Brave vs. other browsers Search Try Brave Search Ask Brave Search features Web Discovery Project Brave vs. other search engines Search API Get started Get API key API features Use cases Sign up Log in Resources Developer docs How-to guides Tools & integrations MCP Server Latest API news Brave Ads Overview Browser Ads Search Ads Resources Help center Ads manager Get Brave Search the Web a]:no-underline [&>a]:text-text-primary"> All blog posts AI news & features B2B & advertiser news BAT, creators, & Brave Rewards Brave Search news Browser performance Company news Developers & community New products & features Policy & legislation Privacy updates Research Web3, crypto, & NFTs WebStandards@Brave All topics AI news & features B2B & advertiser news BAT, creators, & Brave Rewards Brave Search news Browser performance Company news Developers & community New products & features Policy & legislation Privacy updates Research Web3, crypto, & NFTs WebStandards@Brave Blog > Brave Search news The Brave Search API now accepts agentic payments via the x402 protocol Published Nov 12, 2026 Share on X (formerly Twitter) Share on Reddit Share on Telegram Share on LinkedIn Brave Search news The Brave Search API , our developer tool for building applications with data from the Web, is adding support for instant, pay-as-you-go, agentic payments enabled by the open x402 payment protocol. Developers and autonomous AI agents that specifically require agentic search can now programmatically query Brave’s independent search index, ground agent responses, and settle requests in real time, which eliminates the need for traditional API key management. Integrating x402 with the Brave Search API makes it easier for an agentic harness to leverage Brave Search API via a CLI wallet, as Brave runs its own facilitator accepting USDC on the Base blockchain, with acceptance on other networks and with other stablecoins incoming soon. This allows a Brave Search API user the ability to pay for LLM Context (agentic grounding) or general web search on-demand, without first creating an account and selecting a plan. Instead, simply transfer USDC stablecoin to your agent’s wallet via the Base network and it’s ready to access the same high-quality search results powered by Brave’s search engine. How does it work? Brave Search API endpoints behind x402 require payment on every request rather than authentication. A request sent without payment receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response that states the price of that search and the payment details needed to pay it. The agent signs a USDC payment for that amount and retries the request with the signed payment attached. Once the payment is verified, the search runs and results are returned with a receipt of the transaction that occurred on the Base blockchain. Get started today Pricing follows Brave’s published API rates: LLM Context, an API designed specifically for providing search context for agents, will cost $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Additionally, web (search for humans), news, image, video, and local endpoints will also be available for $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Gas fees for transacting on the Base blockchain will be covered for a limited time. Since each request carries its own payment, a Brave Search API account is no longer needed to use the service. The easiest path to query via x402 is to install Purl Wallet, a Stripe-developed CLI wallet for your agent. Set up your wallet, top it off using Base-native USDC, and start querying today. Ready to build pay-as-you-go search into your apps or AI agents? Check out our Brave Search x402 Proxy Documentation and explore: https://api-dashboard.search.brave.com/documentation/guides/agent-payments Share on X (formerly Twitter) Share on Reddit Share on Telegram Share on LinkedIn Previous: How Googleâs anti-scraping moveâ¦ Related articles How Googleâs anti-scraping move became our problem (and how we solved it in a user-first way) Nov 11, 2026 Google's GOTO redirects pushed scrapers toward Brave Search. Our answer is a URL cloaking scheme built on partially oblivious pseudorandom functions, so bots get more expensive and we still never learn which result you clicked. title: IceWM
body_text: IceWM | Window Manager IceWM Window Manager IceWM is a window manager for the X Window System. The goal of IceWM is speed, simplicity, and not getting in the user’s way. It comes with a taskbar with pager, global and per-window keybindings and a dynamic menu system. Application windows can be managed by keyboard and mouse. Windows can be iconified to the taskbar, to the tray, to the desktop or be made hidden. They are controllable by a quick switch window (Alt+Tab) and in a window list. A handful of configurable focus models are menu-selectable. Setups with multiple monitors are supported by RandR and Xinerama. IceWM is very configurable, themeable and well documented. It includes an optional external background wallpaper manager with transparency support, a simple session manager and a system tray. IceWM is available on popular Linux distributions like Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, OpenSUSE, Gentoo, Slackware, CentOS, antiX, NixOS and on most *BSDs. Software IceWM was created by Marko Maček in 1997 using C++. It is now maintained at Github . Releases The latest released version is 4.1.0 (2026-08-06). Features Easy to use, simple and fast Standards compliant → Fully usable with keyboard Alt+Tab window switching Efficient resource usage Task bar (optional) Multiple workspaces Fully documented → A large number of themes → Usable with GNOME and KDE environments Regenerates menus when configuration changes Support for sound effects → Multiple focus modes Manual placement of windows option Autoraising of windows option Tooltips Configurable keybindings → Supports DockApps in a container Tabbed windows Screenshots The IceWM Screenshots Collection Themes IceWM is themeable . The visual appearance of icewm can be changed by a theme, which is a collection of settings and small images. Over 450 themes can be downloaded from box-look.org . Extra is a collection of 91 highlights. See icewm -i list . Translations IceWM is translated into three dozen languages. To improve the translation for your language at Weblate, first register an account either here or there , then update . Documentation IceWM man pages IceWM Manual Themes Howto IceWM FAQ Bug Tracking Report your icewm bugs on Github . Only report it once and give relevant details. Install the latest release as follows $ wget https://github.com/ice-wm/icewm/releases/download/4.1.0/icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz $ tar -x --lzip -vpf icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz $ cd icewm-4.1.0 $ ./configure --prefix = /usr $ make $ sudo make install Install from unreleased development source code Gettext must be installed. $ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm $ cd icewm $ ./autogen.sh $ ./configure --prefix = /usr $ make $ sudo make install If you have cmake, an alternative is: $ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm $ cd icewm $ ./rebuild.sh -r --prefix = /usr $ cd build $ sudo make install Install package dependencies To install all package dependencies in one go use the following script. $ wget https://ice-wm.org/scripts/os-depends.sh $ sudo bash -x ./os-depends.sh Verify package dependencies by: $ pkg-config --modversion x11 xext xcomposite xcursor xdamage xfixes xres xrender xrandr xinerama xft fontconfig sm ice sndfile alsa ao gio-2.0 gio-unix-2.0 gdk-pixbuf-xlib-2.0 imlib2 librsvg-2.0 xpm libpng libjpeg # or simpler: $ ./rebuild.sh -d More installation and configuration IceWM from scratch . title: Why Zig over C for Systems Programming
body_text: Why Zig Over C for Systems Programming · Mihalis Tsoukalos | Μιχαλης Τσουκαλος Mihalis Tsoukalos | Μιχαλης Τσουκαλος About CVEN CVGR Blog Contact Why Zig Over C for Systems Programming After I wrote Why Zig Over Rust for Systems Programming , the obvious next question was C. The Rust question was about safety and how much ceremony I was willing to accept for it. The C question is different, because Zig and C want the same things. Both are small languages without a Garbage Collector and both stay close to what the machine does. So this post is not about leaving C for something completely different. It is about the parts of C that cost me time and how Zig deals with them. All the code was compiled on a Mac with Zig 0.17 and clang. What C gets right Link to heading C is the language of UNIX. The kernels, the C libraries and most of the system libraries that every other language calls in the end are written in C and the man pages describe them with C prototypes and C examples. A C program from the 1990s still compiles today and there is a C compiler for almost every CPU that was ever made. The language is small enough that one book, The C Programming Language by Kernighan and Ritchie, covers all of it. Zig itself does not try to replace any of that. It talks to C libraries directly and it uses the C ABI when it needs to. I am not writing this post because I think C is bad; C is my favorite programming language! I am writing it because I do not want to write new code in C any more. Cleanup without goto Link to heading The C code that I like the least is a function that acquires several resources and has to release them in reverse order when something fails halfway. The usual answer, which is also the one the Linux kernel uses, is goto : struct user * user_new ( const char * name, size_t n_groups) { struct user * u = malloc ( sizeof * u); if (u == NULL) goto fail; u -> name = strdup (name); if (u -> name == NULL) goto fail_user; u -> groups = calloc (n_groups, sizeof * u -> groups); if (u -> groups == NULL) goto fail_name; return u; fail_name: free (u -> name); fail_user: free (u); fail: return NULL; } It works, but the cleanup is far away from the allocation and the order of the labels has to match the order of the allocations by hand. The same function in Zig looks like this: fn newUser (allocator: std.mem.Allocator, name: [] const u8 , n_groups: usize ) !* User { const u = try allocator. create (User); errdefer allocator. destroy (u); u.name = try allocator. dupe ( u8 , name); errdefer allocator. free (u.name); u.groups = try allocator. alloc ( u32 , n_groups); return u; } Each errdefer sits right below the allocation it undoes and runs only if the function returns an error. Zig runs them in reverse order, so there are no labels to keep in order. What I like even more is that I can test every failure path. The std.testing.FailingAllocator type fails on the first, second or third allocation, depending on the value of fail_index . The testing allocator below it reports any memory that is not freed: test "newUser does not leak when an allocation fails" { for ( 0 .. 3 ) | i | { var failing = std.testing.FailingAllocator. init (std.testing.allocator, .{ .fail_index = i }); try std.testing. expectError ( error .OutOfMemory, newUser (failing. allocator (), "mihalis" , 4 )); } } $ zig test user.zig 1/1 user.test.newUser does not leak when an allocation fails...OK All 1 tests passed. Testing the same three paths in the C version needs a wrapper around malloc() or an external tool. A slice knows its length Link to heading In C an array that goes to a function becomes a pointer and the length travels separately, if at all. The following C function has an off-by-one error, <= instead of < : int sum ( const int * a, size_t n) { int total = 0 ; for ( size_t i = 0 ; i <= n; i ++ ) total += a[i]; return total; } With an array of {1, 2, 3} it prints sum = 7 on my Mac and exits with 0. The extra 1 came from whatever was in memory after the array. Neither clang with -Wall -Wextra nor the program itself complains. In Zig a slice carries its length, so the same mistake stops the program in the debug and safe modes: fn sum (a: [] const i32 ) i32 { var total: i32 = 0 ; for ( 0 .. a.len + 1 ) | i | total += a[i]; return total; } $ zig run sum.zig thread 1278459 panic: index out of bounds: index 3, len 3 sum.zig:5:38: 0x1023c5b4b in sum ( sum ) for ( 0..a.len + 1 ) |i| total += a [ i ] ; ^ In real Zig code you would write for (a) |x| and the mistake cannot happen at all. Strings work the same way. A Zig string is a slice of bytes with a length, so there is no strlen() call that walks the memory looking for a 0 byte and no buffer that is one byte short because somebody forgot the terminator. Errors you cannot ignore Link to heading In C a function reports an error by returning -1 or NULL and setting errno , or by returning an error code, or in some other way that the man page describes. Nothing forces you to check. A lot of C code calls close() and fclose() without looking at the return value and the compiler is fine with it. In Zig an error is part of the return type and the compiler refuses to compile a call whose error you ignore. You have to use try , catch or if . The failure path is in the source code, right next to the call, which is also what I liked about Go. comptime instead of the preprocessor Link to heading The C preprocessor works with text and knows nothing about C. The classic #define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b)) evaluates one of its arguments twice and a big C project usually has a lot of #ifdef lines for every Operating System it supports. In Zig, code that runs at compile time is ordinary Zig code. Instead of #ifdef __linux__ I write if (builtin.os.tag == .linux) and the compiler drops the branch that does not apply. Generic data structures are functions that take a type and return a type. The compiler checks all of it like the rest of the program. I wrote about this in Zig comptime . Fewer undefined surprises Link to heading In C the overflow of a signed integer is undefined behavior. The following C program adds 1 to INT_MAX : int add ( int a, int b) { return a + b; } int main ( void ) { printf ( "%d \n " , add (INT_MAX, 1 )); return 0 ; } Compiled with clang it prints -2147483648 and exits with 0, but the C standard allows the compiler to do anything, including removing code that it decides can never run. In Zig the overflow of any integer, signed or unsigned, is checked in the debug and safe modes and the program stops with panic: integer overflow and the line where it happened. When I want wrapping, I write +% and when I want the result to stop at the maximum value, I write +| . Zig is also a C compiler Link to heading The zig cc command is a C compiler that you can use instead of gcc or clang . It also cross compiles out of the box. On my Mac, zig cc -target x86_64-linux-musl -o sum sum.c creates a static Linux executable without installing anything else. In the debug mode zig cc also turns on the undefined behavior sanitizer, so the add() program above compiled with zig cc stops with panic: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int' . A build.zig file can compile C files next to Zig files, so you can move a C project to Zig one file at a time and keep using the same build. If your Zig code needs C header files, Zig 0.17 removed @cImport() and you use zig translate-c instead. I wrote about that in @cImport() Is gone in Zig 0.17 . The honest tradeoff Link to heading Zig is not C with all the problems solved. It does not stop you from using memory after you free it or from keeping a pointer to a stack variable that no longer exists. In the fast and small modes most safety checks are turned off and you are back to undefined behavior, just as in C. C is also stable in a way that Zig is not yet. When Zig 0.17 came out, I had to change 35 of the 152 Zig files of my book, while C code from decades ago still compiles. C has more tools, more books, more people who know it and compilers for chips that Zig does not support. If you write code for a microcontroller that only has a vendor C compiler, the choice is made for you. Conclusion Link to heading C is not going away and I still read a lot of it, because the UNIX source code and most system libraries are written in C and their man pages document them with C prototypes. But for new code I choose Zig. It lets me write the same kind of code as C, close to the machine and with no runtime, while the compiler and the debug mode catch many of the mistakes that C lets through without a word. Happy coding in Zig! Want to learn Zig? Look at my book Systems Programming with Zig . © 2020 - 2026 Mihalis Tsoukalos · Powered by Hugo & Coder .

Â· 3 min read Share Copy link Share on X Share on Bluesky Share on LinkedIn Share Today, weâre rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency. Selecting Orchestrator (Carbon) from the model selector in Google Antigravity. Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems. For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static âmodel routerâ that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves. Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks. Pairing Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon with the Antigravity SDK for automated open-source issue triage and code generation. Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argonâs 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flashâs 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier. Using Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Google Antigravity to upgrade dependencies, refactor shared utilities, and generate accessible image alt text. Getting started Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out as Orchestrator (Carbon) and Orchestrator (Argon) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and as Orchestrator (Argon) for paid Google AI Pro subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business . title: Dwarf planet candidate appears which takes roughly 280 years to orbit our sun
body_text: Astronomers Found a Mysterious Object Orbiting Far Beyond Pluto. It Could Be a New Dwarf Planet Hidden in Our Solar System Skip to main content Search Shop Newsletters Renew Give a Gift Subscribe Membership i Subscribe Give a Gift Renew Sections Smart News History Science Innovation Arts & Culture Travel At the Smithsonian More from Smithsonian magazine Newsletters Photo Contest Podcast Videos Our Partners Smithsonian Store Smithsonian Journeys Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine and get a FREE tote. Astronomers Found a Mysterious Object Orbiting Far Beyond Pluto. It Could Be a New Dwarf Planet Hidden in Our Solar System The dwarf planet candidate, called ED138, appeared in telescope images and takes roughly 280 years to orbit the sun. Astronomers need to determine its size to properly classify it Carlyn Kranking | Associate Web Editor, Science November 12, 2026 Share Copy link Email SMS Facebook X Reddit LinkedIn Bluesky Print Add as preferred source The new dwarf planet candidate, called 2026 ED138, orbits on a plane tiled nearly 25 degrees compared to our solar system's main planets, suggesting it was disturbed by gravitational interactions with Neptune. NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor Image Processing: M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Orbit data provided by the IAU Minor Planet Center (MPCorb catalog), funded by NASA PDCO and the Tamkin Foundation. Gaia DR2: ESA/Gaia/DPAC Matthew Holman , a senior astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, was sifting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile when something odd caught his eye. Running a custom-made computer program, he and his colleague Kevin Napier had already spotted more than 2,000 little bright dots in the telescope data, corresponding to newly discovered small objects in the distant solar system. But this one was different: It seemed to be big. Holman managed his expectations. After all, astronomers in the business of finding distant objects are used to disappointment. “We all have ‘found Mars’ … in terms of a false positive,” Holman tells Smithsonian magazine. They find a bright object that seems really big, then, with a closer look, learn that it’s nothing very remarkable after all. “We’re all really cautious when you see something that looks like it’s large.” Still, this object grabbed Holman’s attention, so he tried to verify it with Napier and Rubin solar system lead scientist Mario Jurić . They found the celestial body in previous photos of the sky throughout the past decade, which helped them zero in on its orbital path—and the more historical data they found, the more confident they became. “We know that it’s real,” Holman says. “Every time you look at the predicted location, there it is.” They even found it in photographic plates from 1937, stored in the Harvard plate stacks , he says. The object, called 2026 ED138 , is 46 times farther from the sun than Earth is, and it takes 281.1 years to complete an orbit. Now, the central question is whether it’s big enough to be classified as a new dwarf planet, which would put it among the rare ranks of only five other objects in our solar system. “This is incredibly exciting,” Paul Byrne , a planetary scientist at the Washington University in St. Louis who was not involved in the discovery, tells National Geographic ’s Robin George Andrews. “It heralds a new era of solar system and planetary science.” 2026 ED138 3D orbit Watch on Dwarf planets are smaller planets that orbit a star and have a nearly round shape, which happens naturally with objects above a certain size, as their gravitational force pulls evenly on all sides . But dwarf planets are not large enough for their gravity to clear their orbital paths of similar-size debris—the eight planets of our solar system, meanwhile, have achieved that feat. (Pluto’s designation was changed from planet to dwarf planet in 2006 for this reason—its orbit is littered with icy Kuiper Belt objects.) Quick fact: Dynamic dwarf planet Ceres, a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, may contain salty water that can percolate onto the surface in some regions. ED138 is likely big enough to be round and, therefore, a dwarf planet—estimates for its size currently range from 370 miles to 930 miles across. But astronomers will have to confirm that measurement, and from the object’s brightness alone, that’s impossible. A highly reflective, smaller object, perhaps covered in gleaming ice caps, might appear just as bright as a less reflective, duller body that’s much larger. Astronomers have two ways to get the required data. They could observe the world in infrared light, which reveals the thermal energy that it emits after being warmed by the sun. “From that you can figure out how big it is, because we know approximately what temperature it should have,” Holman says. Alternatively, astronomers could watch the dwarf planet candidate pass in front of a star. If they know how much light comes from that star and how fast ED138 is moving, they can calculate the body’s size based on how long it obscures the light. Holman says people are working on making those observations with telescopes such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The dwarf planet candidate isn’t extremely easy to see at the moment, he adds, but “in the next few months it will be, and people will try.” The Vera C. Rubin Observatory captured the dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 in these images between March and June this year. NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA Image Processing: M. Jurić (UW), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Right now, astronomers recognize five dwarf planets: Pluto , Eris , Makemake and Haumea in the distant Kuiper Belt, and Ceres in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Experts have long suspected that there could be more of these objects, but many of them could have highly elliptical orbits that keep them too far away for us to see most of the time. What we observe is potentially the “tip of the iceberg of a few that are in the close part of their orbit,” Holman says. “There must be a lot that we just haven’t yet detected.” The discovery also hints at a relatively unexplored area of our solar system—the region that’s in front of the dense, starry core of the Milky Way from our perspective. It’s harder to pick out objects against all the background light in that zone, and ED138 has been traveling through it for the past 25 to 30 years, Holman notes. “There’s a swath on the sky where we really don’t have a good idea of what is there,” he adds. What’s more, ED138 is in the southern hemisphere’s sky, and a lot of astronomical observations have focused on the northern hemisphere. But Rubin is poised to help change that: The new telescope, which has the world’s largest digital camera and captured its first images last year, is one of several observatories operating out of Chile’s Atacama Desert. “Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth and precision,” Jurić says in a statement . “I was surprised that it found such an object so early,” Megan Schwamb , a planetary scientist at Queen’s University Belfast in Northern Ireland and a member of the Rubin solar system operations team, tells CNN ’s Jacopo Prisco. “This was not on my bingo card for this year.” Understanding more about how and where ED138 formed could reveal new details about the early days of the solar system. And its existence offers a clear reminder that surprising objects remain to be found on the fringes of our planetary neighborhood. “Is there a Mars- or Earth-size or bigger object out there?” Holman says. “That’s not ruled out.” You Might Also Like Astronomers Discover a Possible Dwarf Planet Far Beyond Neptune, Where There Should Have Only Been Empty Space May 29, 2025 Meet Farout, the Solar System's Most Distant Minor Planet December 18, 2018 Astronomers Discover 'Ammonite,' a Mysterious Distant Object That Could Shed Light on Our Solar System's History July 22, 2025 Say Hello to Our Solar System’s Newest Dwarf Planet October 13, 2016 Astronomers Propose New Criteria to Classify Planets, but Pluto Still Doesn't Make the Cut July 19, 2024 Carlyn Kranking is Smithsonian magazine's associate web editor for science. Our software engineering interviews are changing a little
body_text: Jane Street Blog - Our software engineering interviews are changing (a little) Home All Posts Machine Learning Authors Index Jane Street Subscribe to email updates Subscribe to Email Updates Featured Reads Read more Using ASCII waveforms to test hardware designs Read more Finding memory leaks with Memtrace Tags async book c camlp4 code-review comments compiler core hackerschool hg incremental internship interviewing machine-learning ocaml parallel-programming performance ppx real-world-ocaml registers speed ui Get the RSS feed Jane Street Open Source Join Our Team Our software engineering interviews are changing (a little) Nov 02, 2026 | 3 min read Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn By: Matthew Saffer Over the last few years, LLMs have changed how software gets built and that’s no different for us at Jane Street. Most of our engineers now use them every day not only for writing code, but also for reading, debugging, and reviewing code, and plenty of things that aren’t code at all. We’ve talked about this recently in a podcast on how we use AI in our development , and in a post on formal methods that touches on how agentic coding is reshaping the way we work. Our coding interviews haven’t changed, though. The questions we ask software engineers today are the same style of question we’ve been asking for years: sit down with an interviewer or two, program through a problem together, and talk as you go. That style has served us well and the key goals remain the same: we want to see how you solve problems, structure your work, communicate, and collaborate in the pursuit of excellent software development. But the shape of the job has evolved, and we think our interviews should evolve, too. As generating code has become arguably cheaper than ever, other parts of the job have come to matter even more: taste about what to build, choosing abstractions that last, and making sure what got built is actually correct, among other things. So this summer we started trialing some new kinds of interviews in our onsites for campus candidates. Broadly, they involve less code-writing, and lean more higher-level, focusing on software design, on verifying the quality, structure, and intention of code, and on using LLMs to produce code. Most rounds will continue to be traditional coding interviews, conducted without LLM assistance. We know this sounds vague, but that’s intentional: the formats are still evolving, and we’d rather not describe something in detail today that looks different in six months. A few things worth knowing: Not every onsite includes these new rounds yet, and when you come on-site we’ll give you a heads-up about what to expect. The rest of our process is unchanged. If you’ve read our earlier posts about interviewing here , they’re still accurate. While we find LLMs incredibly valuable as part of our daily work, we also recognize that not everyone has deep experience working with them. You shouldn’t feel like you need to have a highly worked out methodology for working with agents in order to do well in our process. In the end, we’re looking for people with great instincts for building software, and we don’t feel like we need an LLM to evaluate that. Different folks have integrated LLMs into their workflows in different ways and to different degrees, and we don’t expect you to have a particular setup or to use them for everything. What we care about is that you think clearly about the tools you use: what they’re good at, where they fall short, and when to reach for something else. As has been the case for some time, our more experienced candidates’ interviews will continue to be more varied, featuring a range of interview styles, from producing software to designing systems and discussing prior work. As always, we’ll keep iterating, and we’ll write more when there’s more to say. If you’re interested in working with us, apply on our website !
