Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X In this article Gemini 4 Hydrogen is available Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads Scaling developer and enterprise workflows Adaptable speed and intelligence across thinking levels Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search Designed for safe, dependable execution for scale Available to everyone today Last updated November 13, 2026 Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows. While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon , excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio , the Gemini API, Gemini for business , the Gemini app , Google Search , and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity . Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity . Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs. Scaling developer and enterprise workflows Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows: Iterative repository coding and debugging: Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash. Open-ended agentic execution: On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on Agent Arena , arena.ai’s live benchmark. For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), ties for #1 on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and leads its class on AutomationBench-AA . Multimodal knowledge work: Hydrogen pairs native 1 million-token input with up to 1 million output tokens to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and recorded video into polished, cited reports and structured deliverables. It outperforms other models on the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows. Web development : On tasks where speed matters to developers, like live UI prototyping, design-to-code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional, feature-complete layouts in fewer prompts. Using Hydrogen for on-the-fly 3D coding, Geminisland lets anyone add to a shared voxel island from a single prompt to generate custom structures live on the map that players can walk around and explore in first person. Try the live app . Paired with our new Gemini front end design skill in Google Antigravity, Hydrogen built an e-commerce storefront in one shot complete with a WebGL2 topographic shader, pinned four-stage scrollytelling, a thermal split-slider, a 3D wireframe spec card, and a live finish configurator. Try the live app and the Gemini front end design skill . In Google Antigravity, Hydrogen turned Google Sheets into an animated pixel canvas by shrinking thousands of cells combining Python, native =LET(...) formulas, and conditional formatting to paint and animate full-motion scenes directly inside a live spreadsheet. Starting from a YouTube keynote video and a design template in Google Antigravity, Hydrogen generated a multi-slide presentation directly in Google Slides, then ran an autonomous audit-and-fix loop to catch overlapping text and clean up every slide layout. With Gemini in Google Sheets, Hydrogen can help teams rapidly turn financial data into interactive models that dynamically adjust based on various forecasting scenarios, generating outputs over 30% faster than previous models in Sheets canvas. Adaptable speed and intelligence across four thinking levels We built Gemini 4 Hydrogen for real-world usability. Hydrogen’s four thinking levels — low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier — offer a wide range of options across quality, latency, and cost, scaling in a smooth, predictable progression so you only wait and pay for the reasoning depth a task requires. Across thinking levels, Hydrogen matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class while often finishing tasks faster and using fewer output tokens. Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search For consumers, Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes it easier to get things done, staying on track and following instructions more closely across multi-turn conversations. In the Gemini app, Hydrogen makes your everyday assistant even more helpful — it’s better at following your guidance, calling the right tools, and getting you to a reliable output with less back-and-forth. Ready-to-go writing, research, and everyday work: Hydrogen sticks closely to your tone, format, and specific rules, so email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try. When you are comparing products or synthesizing dense material, it pulls together clear tables and visual breakdowns without dropping key details. Connects the dots and gets more tasks done: Hydrogen breaks down your goal step-by-step, pulling relevant context from your uploads, Google apps like Gmail and Google Drive, and Connected Apps like Airtable and Dropbox. When you start a task in Gemini, it also more frequently calls the right tools and skills for the job, helping save you time as you check things off your to-do list. Everyday prototyping and iteration: For exploring and testing ideas, Hydrogen generates clean, working layouts in fewer prompts, making it easy to prototype and refine interactive projects quickly, like synthesizing real-time global lightning strike data into an interactive 3D globe. Moving fast from idea to working prototype, Hydrogen built an interactive 3D globe and Web Audio music engine driven by real-time lightning strikes and mapped every bolt around the world into visual ripples and live ambient music. When tasked to create a WebGL2 water and glass visualizer, Hydrogen built it from pure math and SDF textures — simulating real-time light refraction, reflection, dispersion, and absorption. Using a custom skill for video assembly and adhering to a creative brief, Gemini 4 Hydrogen created an archival sizzle reel about the element ‘Hydrogen’, sourcing public-domain footage and cutting it into one continuous edit with clean narration. Hydrogen is significantly upgrading Search , delivering more helpful, intuitive responses for all users globally. Better understands your true intent: With Hydrogen, you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for. More visual responses: You’ll get highly adaptive, visual, and easy-to-scan responses that are uniquely relevant to your needs, at the speed you expect from Search. Wider range of relevant links: With Hydrogen’s advanced reasoning, we’re also upgrading our query fan-out technique in Search, connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before, helping you find sites you previously might not have discovered. Designed for safe, dependable execution at scale Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings improvements from our latest Gemini 4 safety and security stack to our broadest audience yet, combining built-in training with real-time surface safeguards to help mitigate both misalignment and misuse. Beyond foundational protections, we focused on two areas that matter most for a faster model that’s for everyday work: Safe, aligned, and secure agentic workflows: While 3.8 Flash has strong alignment and safeguards, Hydrogen is a leap ahead. It reduces overreach in agentic tasks by up to 81% and under-service by up to 79%, and cuts misaligned actions and task shortcutting across tool-use and coding evaluations by 12x. When faced with impossible or blocked tasks, it is up to 2x less likely to bypass permission boundaries and achieves a 94% honesty rate on our internal agent honesty evaluation. Building on our commitment to reasoning transparency , Hydrogen also preserves 99.9% chain-of-thought legibility with zero deceptive reasoning edits across more than 200,000 audited turns. Against indirect prompt injection attacks, Hydrogen is more than 2.3x more resilient on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark, while significantly improving robustness across tool use, computer use, and coding agents. Helpful, reliable everyday interactions: Across our product surfaces, we tuned Hydrogen to make everyday conversations more reliable and safe. Our updated safeguards are also much more precise at distinguishing between real biosecurity risks and legitimate medical or scientific questions — keeping false refusals on HealthBench Pro under 0.4%. For more details see the Gemini 4 Hydrogen model card . Gemini 4 Hydrogen, available to everyone today Starting today, Hydrogen is rolling out globally across our developer, enterprise, and consumer surfaces: For developers: Build with the Gemini API in AI Studio and Android Studio , try it in AI Studio and if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity . For enterprises: Deploy it in Gemini for business via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, and in Gemini in Google Sheets for eligible business subscriptions. For everyone: Start using it in the Gemini app model drop down 1 and in Google Search for all users, and in Gemini in Google Sheets starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. As the SVP of Google DeepMind, he leads the development of Google DeepMind’s state-of-the art generative AI models and their integration into Google’s products at scale. Prior to his current role, he was VP of Research at Google DeepMind, where he founded the deep learning team and his team pioneered major research breakthroughs such as DQN (Deep Q-Network) and WaveNet. title: Tim Peters has died
body_text: In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 - Core Development - Discussions on Python.org = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> Discussions on Python.org In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 Core Development guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:36am 1 I am immensely sad to announce that Tim Peters has died earlier this year on July 15. It’s hard to overestimate Tim’s influence on Python. He’s probably best known for writing the Zen of Python ( PEP 20 ), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that. Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float , because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing. Tim quickly became a major phenomenon on the Python mailing list (including later incarnations and spinoffs), where he earned the nickname “Timbot” by his innumerable, careful and patient answers to user questions. These he filled with mild humor (always marked by <wink> or <0.5 wink> ) and often referred to as “channeling Guido”. At the same time Tim participated in numerous in-depth design discussions, saving me or others from embarrassing design mistakes or solving deep problems, guided by his vast mathematical knowledge and compiler-building experience. In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. In 2002, Tim gave us Timsort : a new sorting algorithm he designed for Python lists, which was later adopted by Java and Android. Python-would-not-be-what-it-is-today-without-Tim-ly y’rs, –Guido 224 Likes guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:41am 2 Feel free to respond with your own Tim anecdotes. I could not cover everything he did. 12 Likes Rosuav (Chris Angelico) November 11, 2026, 6:04am 3 Very sad news. I have had the privilege and pleasure of discussing MANY topics with Tim, and his input into technical discussions has always been something I value very highly. He never treated you like an idiot, never dismissed your concerns out of hand, always answered and explained. I exchanged emails with him many times, but geography meant that sadly, we never met in person. 18 Likes hugovk (Hugo van Kemenade) November 11, 2026, 6:13am 4 Guido van Rossum: In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. From the start to the end. His last post concluded: Which is all a long-winded say of saying the real world is more complicated than our clean abstractions hope for . 49 Likes mcdonc (Chris McDonough) November 11, 2026, 6:41am 5 I wrote this some time ago about Tim: “”" I worked with Tim and the rest of Python Labs for a couple of years in the early 2000s. Tim was a hugely positive influence on me throughout my Python career. Before I had ever spoken to Tim, he was already legendary. He had worked for Cray Research writing compilers for supercomputers, and for Dragon Systems, writing speech-to-text software at a time when such a task was considered largely impossible. He took up Python on a lark in its very early days, becoming something like Python’s second real user after Guido. Guido came to rely on Tim heavily. Tim will demur about this, but as far as I can tell, Tim and Guido were largely partners in the design evolution of very early Python, and before most important features made it in to Python, you could be sure that they had been examined from every angle, shaken, stirred, and thunk about very hard by both of them. Tim often played the role of gatekeeper and polisher. You have Tim to thank at least partially if you were a refugee from Java or Microsoft languages, which made excuses for their sprawling verbosity, complexity, and poor readability. Python, at the time, made none of those and had none of that (it now does). Tim was crucial in ensuring it stayed that way during his most active years. He will claim differently, but, by my observation, it is no accident that Python ballooned in complexity after his exit as day-to-day core developer. Perhaps this was more due to the resignation of Guido as BDFL and the new Steering Council model, which was also coincident, but not having Tim around didn’t help either. It was pure joy to read Tim’s Usenet and mail list posts, which were full of humor and good nature and measured positivity and not a little winking darkness. They somehow resonated with me on my journey from becoming a new programmer to a not-so-new programmer and they lit a path to becoming one on which you could be dramatically competent without becoming cryptic and insufferable. He was intensely knowledgeable, and unfailingly precise when arguing for or against some design change. But he was always gentle and patient and matter-of-fact, preferring to use humor and warmth rather than bile and authority as the currency in which he dealt. Tim penned “the Zen of Python” (“beautiful is better than ugly…”) which can be seen via “import this” to this day. You can see a bit of his wonderful humor and style in the prelude to his introduction of the poem . His enthusiasm was infectious, and in the days when he was most involved, most everyone could be witnessed spouting Tim-isms (winks and “'lys” and whatnot). When I did get the chance to work with Tim, he was just as influential. He had absolutely no pretensions. If I hadn’t already known him to be a computer savant, I would have assumed he was a biker or mechanic due to his long grey locks, full mustache and and working-class fashion sense. I would later find out that he had indeed worked at Harley-Davidson. I think he’s originally from Wisconsin, but an East- or West-Coaster not fluent in Midwest tongues could be excused for believing his disarming accent is Chicagoan. He seemed just like a regular-looking neighborhood punch-the-clock guy, not unlike all the mechanics and deliverymen and cooks and dishwashers and event staff I’d worked around as a kid and in my 20s. I often failed, of course, because I’m not Tim, but I was at least a twentieth a Tim, and at the time, I think my co-contributors would have agreed that the projects I led were fun and worthwhile to work on. It is in this way that Tim’s influence is likely most obvious to people today, because I’m not the only one who channeled him; any Python project started between 1995 and 2010 has a bit of Tim culture in it. “”" In sadness, . title: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer
body_text: Edge0-145B: Open-Source On-Device AI with 145B Parameters - edge0 Models Docs Solutions Research Blog Company Connect Introducing Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer November 12, 2026 · 19 min read · Edge0 releases Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B , together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer. On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity. This release addresses those constraints in four ways: The constraint What Edge0-145B makes possible Large models are difficult to run on personal hardware. A 145B model runs locally on a compatible laptop, with reported peak memory of 29GB and decoding above 80 tokens/s. Small on-device models can fall short on demanding tasks. Coding, reasoning, and instruction-following results are competitive with specific frontier cloud models, as the comparisons below show. A useful assistant needs to finish work, not just answer questions. The model plans, writes and runs code, debugs errors, and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs, and PCB designs. Cloud workflows bring recurring fees, sensitive-data restrictions, and network dependence. Local inference incurs no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees; data can stay on the computer, and core capabilities keep working offline. Hardware and electricity still cost money. We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products. Get the model weights , explore the inference framework , or try the Edge0 App . How We Make 100B+ Parameter AI Run on a Personal Computer Edge0-145B Laptop Performance: Memory, Speed, and Power Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks. Requirement Reported Edge0-145B result What it enables Memory 29GB peak memory Runs on a compatible personal laptop, such as a MacBook Pro, without a server. Prompt processing 1,100+ tokens/s prefill Processes long prompts, including dozens of pages of code, before generation begins. Generation 80+ tokens/s decode Generates faster than a person reads. Power Approximately 120W typical power Sustains operation without throttling in the reported setup. Long tasks 128K–256K context Maintains essentially the same speed on long inputs, supporting extended work. Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware. On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards. Why On-Device Models Have Stayed Small Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026. Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, while Google's Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions. Even a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB of memory. Larger models faced a memory wall. Model weights occupy storage and must be read during generation, competing for limited memory and bandwidth with the operating system and other apps. Even an aggressively compressed 35B model could need approximately 20GB of memory, far more than a phone could make available. Compute, bandwidth, and power created competing constraints. Larger models offered more capability, but strained memory capacity, generation speed, and battery life. Making models smaller helped them fit, often at the cost of capability. Privacy alone could not close that gap. Apple Intelligence protected user data, but Apple acknowledged that its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge. The prevailing assumption was that on-device intelligence could not match the cloud. Under the Hood of Edge0: Four Layers of Model and Inference Design We designed Edge0-145B and its inference engine together to reduce the memory and data movement that make large models difficult to run locally. The design spans architecture, training, loading, and scheduling. Architecture: share large matrices across sparse experts. Sharing matrices substantially reduces the weights that must be stored and moved while keeping the expert count unchanged. Each group of 64 experts shares two large matrices, while each expert retains a small set of parameters that captures its differences. Previously, every expert stored a complete set of matrices. Of the model's 145B total parameters, only approximately 10B participate in computation on each inference step. Training: build for local execution from day one. We train the model in its on-device architecture from the outset, with deployment constraints built into its design. This avoids treating local deployment as a compression or pruning step after training a cloud model. Loading: pipeline GPU memory, system memory, and SSD access. Reading and computation overlap across three storage tiers, avoiding serial waits. Frequently used “hot experts” remain in GPU memory. An expert library of approximately 40GB sits in system memory, with experts brought into GPU memory as needed. Approximately 48GB of vocabulary data resides on the SSD and is read on demand. Scheduling: use the CPU and GPU together. The GPU computes cached experts while the CPU handles the remaining work in parallel. Speculative decoding verifies multiple candidate tokens at once, spreading the cost of reading weights across more output tokens. These choices support the reported 80+ tokens/s decode rate. Model and inference-engine design work together to make 100B+ parameter inference practical on personal computers. Source: internal testing. Together, these changes let parameter counts grow from tens of billions to more than a hundred billion without proportional increases in memory use, power consumption, and latency. What Edge0 Can Do: Anything From Chat to Complex Work on Your Computer Edge0-145B can carry a complex task through to a usable result. Its coding and reasoning capabilities support local workflows that combine planning, tool use, execution, debugging, and visual checks. The benchmarks establish its capabilities; the demonstrations show how it puts them to work. Coding and reasoning that rival frontier cloud models Edge0-145B is competitive with specific frontier cloud models across coding, reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following: Coding: It scores 64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1 , ahead of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next at 58.7 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 54.4. Reasoning and knowledge: It scores 90.4 on GPQA-Diamond , close to DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 90.8 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 91.3. Instruction following: It scores 80.6 on IFBench , ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 at 79.2 and Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) at 62.5. Its 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 also exceeds Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 83.3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731's 82.7, and Claude's 78.2. On AA-LCR, Edge0-145B scores 79.3 to Claude's 78.0. These comparisons apply to the named models and evaluations. Model DeepSWE 1.1 Terminal-Bench 2.1 HLE GPQA-Diamond IFBench AA-LCR Edge0-145B 64.6 86.52 35.4 90.4 80.6 79.3 Edge0-120B 53.6 81.3 31.0 87.4 79.3 81.0 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 58.7 83.3 35.9 91.7 81.3 79.1 Qwen3.8-27B 42.2 73.0 30.8 89.2 79.5 82.0 DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 54.4 82.7 33.8 90.8 79.2 79.7 Flint 40B — 54.9 — — 89.2 — Muse Glimmer — 51.7 22.0 83.5 77.0 83.3 Gemma 4 — 43.4 22.7 85.7 76.0 62.0 Claude-Opus-4.6 \(Max\) — 78.2 40.0 91.3 62.5 78.0 Scores are percentages; higher is better. A dash means no public score is available, rather than a score of zero. Edge0, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Claude results come from Edge0's internal evaluations. Claude-Opus-4.6 has no public DeepSWE 1.1 score. For Flint, Muse Glimmer, and Gemma 4, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and IFBench results come from the Recursive Flint evaluation; HLE, GPQA, and AA-LCR results come from Artificial Analysis. The largest gains over Qwen3.8-27B, a mainstream on-device model baseline, are in agent and coding work: 18.5% on Terminal-Bench and 53.1% on DeepSWE . The relative gains on HLE, GPQA, and IFBench are 14.9%, 1.3%, and 1.4%, respectively. DeepSWE 1.1 and Terminal-Bench 2.1 evaluate agent and coding work. HLE, GPQA-Diamond, and IFBench cover reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following. The complete evaluation setup, hardware environment, and reproduction instructions are being released with our technical report. Competitive capability with a smaller memory footprint Edge0-145B combines a 72.8 mean score across six benchmarks with 29GB measured peak memory . Qwen3.8-Flash-Next averages 71.7, with an estimated 70GB footprint for standard 4-bit deployment. That puts Edge0-145B at about 40% of the estimated baseline memory while delivering comparable or higher capability, enabling local use on a 48GB laptop. Model Mean across six benchmarks Memory footprint \(measured or estimated\) Edge0-145B 72.8 29GB Edge0-120B 68.9 29GB Qwen3.8-27B 66.1 Approximately 18GB* Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 71.7 Approximately 70GB* DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 70.1 Approximately 87GB* The means cover DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, HLE, GPQA-Diamond, IFBench, and AA-LCR. Edge0 memory figures are measured internal peaks. Asterisked baseline figures are estimates for standard 4-bit deployment and remain to be measured. Claude is excluded because it is cloud-only and has no DeepSWE score. [Figure: Quality versus peak memory, with 48GB laptop and 64GB workstation capacities marked. Lower memory and higher scores are better; the chart's vertical axis does not start at zero.] Local agents that plan, code, run, and check their work A single natural-language request can start an entire local workflow. Edge0-145B breaks down the requirements, plans the steps, writes code, and calls tools to run it. When something fails, it debugs and repairs the code. It then takes screenshots to inspect the result and keeps iterating until the work is complete. These projects often take dozens of rounds of planning, execution, and review. Local inference means those additional conversations, code revisions, and visual analyses incur no corresponding cloud-model token or API charges. Code and data can stay on the computer, and core model capabilities work offline. Video production: generating Tesla's Roadster explainer within an hour Edge0-145B produced an explainer about how Roadster could fly, handling technical research, scriptwriting, asset generation, and editing. We asked it to make the principles understandable to a general audience. The model ran locally without cloud-model calls or cloud token consumption, avoiding network round trips for inference. The video was generated within an hour. Producing comparable work manually would have taken a director and scriptwriter, a 3D modeler, an editor, and a physics expert a month. An AI video workflow could previously cost more than hundreds of dollars; local inference eliminates the corresponding cloud-model token and API fees. 3D modeling: a Manhattan city scene in Blender Edge0-145B built a 3D scene of Manhattan within an hour. Working in Blender from text and reference images, it constructed the scene, adjusted materials and lighting, and iterated on the rendered output. The workflow brings visual inspection, code generation, and revision together inside Blender. The model works with objects, spatial relationships, and the creative goal, going beyond the pixels in a reference image. It inspects the result, writes code, and makes changes without handing those steps back to a person. The entire process stays local. Creating a Manhattan-scale city scene manually would typically cost approximately $12,000-18,000 and take at least a month. A leading cloud model would still incur more than $150 in cloud token charges. Edge0-145B completes the local inference without those cloud-model token fees. Game development: playable games and a medieval city Edge0-145B can create playable games locally. We also used its 3D modeling capabilities to build an original medieval capital for a fantasy RPG and render a 20-second fly-through at game-trailer quality. The model planned the city independently and built it from scratch in Blender: city walls, more than a thousand old-town homes, a plaza fountain, a Gothic twin-tower facade, a rib-vaulted nave, and stained-glass windows. The fixed camera path made errors visible. Geometry clipping, occlusion, or incorrect proportions would appear along the route, so the model inspected the renders and corrected its work as it built. The workflow ran entirely locally. A leading cloud model required hundreds of tool calls and hundreds of millions of tokens for a single completion, using the same prompt, reference images, and camera route. Edge0-145B delivered it on a laptop without cloud-model token or API fees for local inference. An art team would typically spend weeks and thousands of dollars producing a city scene to this standard. Hardware control: code that flies a real drone Edge0-145B wrote the program for a real drone from one instruction: “Write a drone program that navigates through obstacles and finds a red backpack.” It generated the flight-control and visual-recognition programs locally. The drone then took off indoors, navigated through a dense row of obstacle poles, searched autonomously, and located the red backpack beside a wall. The task required no human-written code and no cloud call. Hardware developers can describe the behavior they want and have the model turn it into a program for a real device, without moving repeatedly between an editor, documentation, and debugging tools. PCB design: from KiCad layout to an assembly animation Edge0-145B took a PCB design from component placement through an assembly visualization. We asked it to design a board for itself. It started from scratch in KiCad, placed components, routed a two-layer board, and imported the design into Unreal Engine 5. It then set up cameras and lighting and rendered an animation of PCB fabrication and assembly. A single computer delivered work that previously required a hardware engineer and a 3D designer to hand tasks back and forth over several days. Schematics and board layouts can stay on the team's own hardware, supporting trade-secret protection and data-handling requirements without uploading the designs to a cloud model. Why Edge0: A Full Stack for On-Device AI Useful on-device AI requires model development, inference engineering, and hardware adaptation to work together. Our progress rests on three capabilities: developing complementary models quickly, optimizing the full stack, and carrying lessons from each deployment into the next. Our September release of Edge0-35B showed what that approach could deliver on a phone. Its launch post passed 1.2 million views on its first day without paid promotion in overseas communities. Researchers and technical experts at OpenAI, NVIDIA, Qualcomm, and other companies shared it, and the model reached No. 1 on Hugging Face's overall Trending chart. We released the model weights and unified inference framework together, giving companies and researchers a standard approach they could reproduce. The release helped move the discussion of on-device AI from a few billion parameters to the 35B tier. Four Model Families for On-Device AI Over the past year, we released 200 models across four families. Each handles a different part of the work, from listening and speaking to fast decisions, memory, and complex agent tasks. Model family Role Models and capabilities Edge0 Complex agent tasks and vibe coding 145B and 120B models for laptops; 35B and 8B models for phones. The laptop models support vibe coding, while the phone models support agent tasks. Audio8 Listening and speaking ASR-Infinite and 3B, 0.6B, and 0.1B ASR models for speech recognition; 0.6B and 0.1B TTS models for speech synthesis; and a 0.1B Chat model for end-to-end voice interaction. Decision0 Fast decisions 0.6B and 3B models covering text, speech, and vision, with multimodal decisions in approximately 40 milliseconds. Embedding0 Memory A 0.6B multimodal embedding model for text, speech, images, video, and files, supporting local long-term memory and retrieval-augmented generation \(RAG\). The portfolio spans tens of millions to more than a hundred billion parameters. Both Edge0 and Audio8 have reached No. 1 on Hugging Face's Trending chart. Models and Inference Systems Designed Together We develop the model and the inference framework together, building hardware constraints into training and optimizing the engine for different chips. This connects model capability with the software and hardware needed to use it locally. That work requires expertise in model development, inference frameworks, and low-level hardware adaptation. The combination is difficult for a company focused only on model development to reproduce. Hardware Optimizations That Carry into Each Deployment Each deployment gives us reusable optimizations for the next chip, model, or product. This matters because on-device hardware is fragmented: NPU architectures differ, as does support for numerical formats such as INT4, INT8, and FP4. A general-purpose model cannot automatically make full use of every chip. We adapt to individual platforms. Our portfolio now covers 95% of mainstream chip platforms, including Qualcomm, BES, Rockchip, Allwinner, D-Robotics, and NVIDIA, across headphones, glasses, phones, PCs, and robots. This is portfolio-wide coverage; model requirements vary, and it does not mean every device can run Edge0-145B. That deployment work now spans more than 5 million production devices. Our open-source models passed 15 million downloads within three months. By October 2026, we had more than 110,000 customer organizations. The portfolio figures come from company papers and internal testing. They describe the broader Edge0 portfolio; the 145B performance results in this article apply specifically to Edge0-145B. For Edge0-145B, day-one support covers macOS, Windows, and Linux, including Apple M-series chips and NVIDIA platforms such as RTX Spark, RTX 4090, and RTX 5090. The release includes one-click deployment tools and hardware guides. The Future of On-Device AI and the Cloud More complex work can stay on the device as local models approach cloud-level capability. Privacy, cost control, and offline access have long favored local execution; the remaining question was whether an on-device model could do the work. Edge0-145B expands the range of tasks for which it can. Why More AI Work Can Stay Local Local execution addresses four practical obstacles to adopting cloud-only AI: Control cloud-model costs. Local inference adds no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees as usage grows. Keep sensitive data local. Code, documents, and business records can stay on the hardware, giving teams control over data handling. Sustain a responsive experience. Model and inference-engine design address response speed, power use, system responsiveness, and continuous operation together. Keep core capabilities available offline. Local tasks continue when connectivity drops; features that depend on online information or services still need a connection. From Cloud First to More Complex Work On-Device We see the division of work between devices and the cloud shifting through three stages. Before September 2026: cloud first, with on-device support. Apple Intelligence reflected this stage: it protected privacy, but handled a limited range of tasks locally while more demanding work relied on cloud capabilities. After Edge0-35B's September 10 release: everyday tasks locally, complex tasks in the cloud. Local models could take on frequent requests that needed immediate responses. For one leading headphone manufacturer, our hybrid solution now handles 92% of AI usage on-device and 8% in the cloud. Everyday conversation accounts for most use cases on consumer wearables. With Edge0-145B: toward on-device first, with cloud support. Vibe coding and other complex tasks can now run on a personal computer, giving teams more scope to choose local execution. This extends the range of work that can stay on the device while preserving the cloud for tasks and hardware that need it. The diagram shows the shift from cloud-first AI to everyday local tasks and then more complex local work. Its colored areas are schematic, not measured usage shares. Where Cloud AI Still Fits Hardware constraints still determine which model fits. Compute capacity, heat, and battery life matter: Edge0-35B runs on phones, while Edge0-145B runs on suitably equipped laptops. A very low-compute device cannot currently run a 145B model locally. It needs a smaller model suited to its hardware or cloud access to a model of that size. Cross-device long-term memory and searches requiring highly current information still require cloud services. Local and cloud models can work together; the appropriate split depends on the task, the hardware, and the information it needs. The aim is to make local execution a practical choice for demanding work, with a capable model that can keep working close to the person using it. That is the next step toward our goal of enabling intelligence at zero distance for everybody. Get Started with Edge0 Download the models to run locally, evaluate or fine-tune them, and build them into your own products: Model weights: Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B on Hugging Face. Inference framework and deployment guides: Edge0 on GitHub . Try it without environment setup: Download the Edge0 App . Its core model capabilities work offline, without an account or usage quota. Community: Join us on Discord . For hardware or product integrations, reach the Edge0 team through GitHub or contact@autoark.ai . FAQ What is Edge0-145B? Edge0-145B is an open-source AI model with 145 billion parameters, designed to run on personal computers. It offers capabilities like coding and reasoning, comparable to cloud models, but operates locally. How does Edge0-145B handle large models on personal hardware? Edge0-145B can run on a compatible laptop with 29GB peak memory and generates over 80 tokens per second. It uses shared matrices and efficient memory management to handle large models locally. What are the benefits of using Edge0-145B locally? Using Edge0-145B locally eliminates cloud-model fees, keeps data on your device, and maintains functionality offline. It supports complex tasks like coding and 3D modeling without relying on cloud infrastructure. Can Edge0-145B perform complex tasks? Yes, Edge0-145B can handle complex tasks such as coding, 3D modeling, and game development. It plans, executes, and iterates on tasks locally, making it suitable for demanding workflows. How does Edge0-145B compare to cloud models? Edge0-145B is competitive with specific cloud models in coding, reasoning, and instruction-following benchmarks. It offers similar capabilities while running locally, avoiding cloud-related costs and delays. What hardware is required to run Edge0-145B? Edge0-145B requires a compatible laptop with at least 29GB of memory and supports platforms like macOS, Windows, and Linux, including Apple M-series chips and NVIDIA RTX platforms. TV boxes, old phones and tablets, single-board computers and routers all have a CPU, some RAM and flash storage that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing finds the biggest model each of them can really run, then pushes it further with custom kernels, careful memory use and weights streamed from flash. Every number in this repo was measured on the device itself. Three devices so far 📺 Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen) 📱 iPad Air (2013) 📲 OnePlus Nord CE 2 (2022) Chip Amlogic S7D, 4× Cortex-A55 Apple A7, 2 cores MediaTek Dimensity 900, 2× Cortex-A78 + 6× A55 RAM 1.9 GB (about 1 GB usable) 1 GB (about 700 MB usable) 7.4 GB (about 3 GB free) OS Android 14, no root iOS 12.5.7, jailbroken Android 13, no root Everyday model Qwen3.5-2B at 7.7 tok/s Bonsai-1.7B (1-bit) at 24-26 tok/s Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at 4.9-5.7 tok/s Biggest model Ling-mini-2.0, 16B, at 5.1 tok/s Ling-mini-2.0, 16B, at 2.6-4.5 tok/s Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B at 2.6-3.1 tok/s Full results docs/tv-box.md ipad-air/README.md docs/phone.md The TV box and the iPad run 8B and 16B mixture-of-experts models on about 1 GB of RAM, and the phone runs 35B and 80B ones with about 3 GB free. They all keep only part of each model in memory and read the rest from flash as it's needed. The chart below compares the two 1 GB devices size class by size class; the phone plays in a bigger league, and its results are in docs/phone.md . More devices (single-board computers, routers, more phones) are coming. The techniques aren't tied to one box: the 1-bit kernel needs only basic NEON, and the flash streaming works on any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM. Got a small device? Run a model on it and submit your numbers : we'll add them to the results. How it works All of it is a patch on llama.cpp . The main ideas: Kernels built for the chip. A 1-bit lookup-table kernel, repacked 2-bit and ternary formats for the Cortex-A55, and versions of them for the A7, which has no dot-product instructions. Less RAM per model. Most of a small model's vocabulary is rarely used, so we drop those output rows. On the TV, a "headless" mode also stops the launcher and Google services while a model runs. Experts paged from flash. A mixture-of-experts model only uses a few experts per token. We keep the popular ones in RAM, read the others from flash on demand and prefetch the next layer's. This is how 8B and 16B models run on 1 GB, and 35B and 80B models on a phone. Streaming for dense models bigger than RAM, at the flash's full speed. docs/how-it-works.md has every technique with its measured gain. Try it The quickest start is a ready-made model file from Hugging Face. The TV box and iPad files need the patched llama.cpp (stock llama.cpp can't load their pruned heads); the phone files load anywhere, but their speeds need the patch's expert pager. TV box or another ARMv8.2 Android device: docs/tv-box-setup.md Jailbroken iPad on iOS 12: ipad-air/README.md Android phone with 8 GB of RAM: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (12.3 GB) and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B (27.6 GB, two files), set up as in docs/phone.md . body_text: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy - 9to5Mac Skip to main content Toggle main menu 9to5Mac Logo Go to the 9to5Mac home page Switch site 9to5Toys 9to5Google Logo 9to5Google Electrek Drone DJ Logo DroneDJ Space Explored About Privacy Toggle social menu Toggle dark mode Search for: Submit Toggle search form Forums Store Podcasts Apple@Work Happy Hour 9to5Mac Daily Overtime iPhone iPhone Mac Mac MacBook Pro MacBook Air iMac Mac mini Mac Studio Mac Pro iPad iPad Pro iPad Air iPad mini iPad iPadOS Watch Apple Watch Apple Watch Ultra Apple Health Apple Watch SE Vision Vision Pro visionOS Music and TV Apple Music AirPods HomePod Apple TV Guides Reviews How Tos AAPL Apple Store Apple Arcade Apple Card Apple Silicon Apple One Apple Fitness+ CarPlay Siri HomeKit Toggle dark mode AI Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy Ryan Christoffel  | Nov 10 2026 - 11:15 am PT 0 Comments Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs. New ‘Harbor’ app revealed at Apple: ‘turns your Mac into a private AI inference server’ The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more. It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server. Here’s Perris’s post on X with the details: Apple is working on a new app called Harbor Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool… pic.twitter.com/UYJBQeX4Nf — Aaron (@aaronp613) November 10, 2026 As the post notes, here’s what the app does: Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone. And here are the feature highlights: Setup in minutes, not hours : “Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you’re running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.” Download and run models directly : “Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.” Cluster for scale : “Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer’s capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.” Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead. Are you interested in using Harbor on your Mac? Let us know in the comments. title: Nvidia employees petition to bring back Jensen Huang
body_text: ‘Bring Back THE Boss’: Nvidia Employees Petition for Jensen Huang’s Return | WIRED Skip to main content READ FREE IN THE APP DOWNLOAD NOW » Menu WIRED SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Menu WIRED Account Account Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews Chevron More Expand The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams WIRED Store Search Search Paresh Dave Zoë Schiffer Business Nov 12, 2026 8:17 PM ‘Bring Back THE Boss’: Nvidia Employees Petition for Jensen Huang’s Return An internal post urging the board to consider employee sentiment about Nvidia’s former CEO has drawn more than 1,600 comments, the majority in full support of reinstalling him. Photograph: JOEL SAGET/Getty Images Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation , according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED. An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter. “We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another. One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.” The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment. Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset . The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email. Got a Tip? Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at peard33.24. Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips. It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned . In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation. One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED. Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.” Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.” Comments Back to top Join the discussion Comments Back to top Triangle You Might Also Like In your inbox: Inside WIRED’s newsroom with Katie Drummond They war-gamed dimming the sun —it went worse than you think The Big Interview: Nathan Fielder tells us everything Live tracker: Elon Musk’s America PAC is spending big on the midterms Introducing the app: More ways to make the most of WIRED Paresh Dave is a senior writer for WIRED, covering the inner workings of Big Tech companies. He writes about how apps and gadgets are built and about their impacts while giving voice to the stories of the underappreciated and disadvantaged . He was previously a reporter for Reuters and the Los Angeles Times, ... Read More Senior Writer Zoë Schiffer is a contributing editor and previously oversaw coverage of business and Silicon Valley at WIRED. Prior to that, she was the managing editor of Platformer and a senior reporter at The Verge. ... Read More Contributing Editor Topics NVIDIA Jensen Huang chips Silicon Valley Semiconductors WIRED is obsessed with what comes next. Through rigorous investigations and game-changing reporting, we tell stories that don’t just reflect the moment—they help create it.
