title: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
body_text: Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs · Unemployment Labs Skip to report Unemployment Labs In this report Executive summary Main findings Our investigation Limits of the investigation Verifying the findings Conclusion Appendix 1 · Lab histories Appendix 2 · All models Sources How to cite Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs Will DePue November 12, 2026 Print / save PDF Cite this report Executive Summary Our forensic analysis of publicly released AI models finds evidence that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models. Six models released by these companies since April 2026 contain numerical patterns matching Blackwell hardware, whereas earlier models from the same companies match NVIDIA’s older Hopper generation. The findings suggest that several leading Chinese AI developers have begun using Blackwell to train their newest models. U.S. officials and press reports had already alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, without publishing technical evidence. The evidence comes entirely from the models’ own published weights, rather than from leaks or insider accounts. We recover traces of the models’ initial values, and then search for the hardware configurations and initial configurations that reproduce them; for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, we also confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips. The fingerprint identifies how the weights were created and supports, without proving, the inference that Blackwell also performed the training. Specially configured AMD hardware, which is also restricted from export to China, is the only alternative we have identified; we have excluded it for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and consider it very unlikely for the other five models. Notably, our findings provide technical evidence of access to advanced computing hardware, but do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. Table 1. Hardware fingerprints in successive models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group Link ↗ Lab Model Released Chip the model was started on DeepSeek DeepSeek-V3 Dec 2024 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) DeepSeek-V4-Flash Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 DeepSeek-V4-Pro Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Moonshot AI Kimi K2 Jul 2025 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K2.5 Jan 2026 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K3 Jul 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Kimi K3.1-Pro Nov 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 MiniMax MiniMax-M2.7 Apr 2026 NVIDIA Hopper MiniMax-M3 Jun 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 Ant Group Ling-3.0-flash Aug 2026 NVIDIA Hopper Ling-3.1-flash Oct 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 • Requires a U.S. license for export to China; none have been reported. A Hopper fingerprint cannot distinguish an H800 from an H100 SXM or H200; the H800 identifications above are lab disclosures, not findings of this method. Full list of models in Appendix 2 ↓ Main Findings Six models from four Chinese labs read as Blackwell-trained. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match NVIDIA’s Blackwell-class B200 or B300 chips, which have 148 processor cores (called streaming multiprocessors , or SMs). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro and Ling-3.1-flash match the GB200 or GB300 chips, also Blackwell-class, which have 152 processor cores. Kimi K3.1-Pro starts from the same seed as K3, and may be a checkpoint of K3 with further post-training. Chinese labs started training on Blackwell relatively recently. DeepSeek’s models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3 (released in December 2024), and as Blackwell from DeepSeek V4 (released in April 2026). Moonshot’s models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 (January 2026) and as Blackwell from K3 (July 2026). One Moonshot model sits in between: Kimi K2.7-Code, posted six weeks before K3, is built on the Hopper-era weights but contains a small part that matches the B200 or B300. MiniMax’s models read as Hopper through M2.7 (April 2026) and as Blackwell from M3 (June 2026). Ant Group’s Ling-3.0-flash (August 2026) reads as Hopper, while its Ling-3.1-flash (October 2026) reads as Blackwell. The Hopper readings do not identify a specific chip: H800s, H100 SXMs and H200s share the same fingerprint. Not every Chinese AI lab has switched to Blackwell. The newest models we could read from Alibaba (Qwen), Zhipu (GLM), Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan says its LongCat-2.0 was trained entirely on “AI ASIC superpods,” and we found no NVIDIA fingerprint in the model weights it’s released. The method gets known answers right. For 24 specific models, the developer has publicly said what hardware was used. In every case, our method agrees with the public announcement. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of its training, reads as 152 SMs, the same as Kimi K3. The matches are far stronger than chance would explain. Even unrelated numbers can appear to match when enough combinations are tried. Across the roughly 6 trillion seed-and-layout combinations in our search, the strongest chance match would be expected to reach about 8 sigma—a measure of how far a result stands above ordinary random variation. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma. Even the weakest individual test we report reaches 20 sigma. The training runs were data-center scale. From each model’s size and the amount of data it was trained on, we estimate that the two largest runs, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, each needed thousands of Blackwell GPUs for two to three months, assuming each model was trained on the hardware that initialized it. Our best estimates are about 4,500 and 3,000, the equivalent of about 11,500 and 7,500 H100s, the previous-generation NVIDIA chip in which AI training clusters are commonly sized, and about 12,000 Blackwell GPUs across the five runs (Table 2). At roughly $70,000 per GPU—the cost implied by a Wall Street Journal report that about 36,000 Blackwell chips being installed in Malaysia for ByteDance’s use would cost more than $2.5 billion—the largest of these clusters would cost roughly $200 million to $300 million, and the five together more than half a billion dollars. These figures cover only the final training runs; the labs’ total spending on export-controlled GPUs is likely in the billions of dollars. Table 2. Rough scale of each training run Link ↗ Model H100 equivalents Blackwell GPUs, best estimate Blackwell range Estimated run length DeepSeek-V4-Flash 3,500 1,500 250–5,000 50 days DeepSeek-V4-Pro 7,500 3,000 750–6,500 70 days Kimi K3 11,500 4,500 1,000–9,500 70 days MiniMax-M3 3,500 1,500 200–7,000 60 days Ling-3.1-flash 4,000 1,500 400–6,500 100 days All five 30,000 12,000 7,000–22,000 Each estimate is a run’s training compute divided by what one Blackwell GPU delivers over the run, rounded to the nearest 500. Training compute is about six operations per active parameter for every training token, plus attention. We assume the GPUs ran at about 20% of their peak speed, in line with other disclosed Blackwell training runs (25% for DeepSeek, which has reported 39% for its previous model), and for the run lengths shown, which we estimate from release timelines. H100 equivalents convert at NVIDIA’s published peak speeds: a B200 or B300 equals about 2.3 H100s, and a GB200 or GB300 about 2.5. We are not confident in these estimates. They rest on assumptions that the weights cannot confirm: how efficiently each lab used its GPUs (often called MFU), which no lab has published for these runs; how many tokens each model was trained on (DeepSeek’s counts are its own, and we take them on trust; the others are our estimates, made from the weights by a method we have not yet published); how long each run lasted, which no lab has stated; and that training stayed on the hardware that created the weights. Run length matters most, because halving it doubles the GPU count. Two disclosed runs on the same hardware show the spread: Mistral says it trained Mistral Large 4, which has the same number of active parameters as DeepSeek-V4-Pro, on 3,800 Grace Blackwell GPUs, while Microsoft says it trained MAI-Base-2, a model of similar size trained on more data, on 16,000 in 38 days. At that pace the two largest runs here would have needed about 8,000 to 9,000 Blackwell GPUs. The figures cover only the final training run of each model, not experiments, earlier runs or serving. Revised November 12, 2026. The first version of this report gave 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs for the largest runs and $150 million to $200 million for the largest cluster. Those figures assumed the GPUs ran as efficiently as NVIDIA’s own benchmarks, and training runs disclosed on Blackwell have been less efficient. The estimates above replace them. We have also added H100 equivalents and estimated run lengths. Our investigation A model’s weights , also called parameters , are the billions of adjustable numbers that determine how it processes information and produces answers. Training repeatedly adjusts these numbers; but before training can begin, they need initial values. In the software examined here, those values come from a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox: Philox produces seemingly random numbers in a deterministic way. The starting input for Philox is a number called the “seed.” Given the same seed and settings, Philox produces the same numbers every time. This lets engineers repeat an experiment from the same starting point. To fill billions of weights quickly, PyTorch, the software framework used in the development of most major AI models, divides the work that Philox does among many parallel workers on the GPU, called threads . (It does this through cuRAND, NVIDIA’s library for random number generation.) Each thread generates its own sequence of numbers from the seed and fills a particular set of positions. The number of threads then determines how those positions are shared out. On the NVIDIA chips examined here, a sufficiently large initialization uses the maximum of 2,048 threads for each processing unit, called a streaming multiprocessor (SM). A chip with more SMs therefore assigns the same job to more workers, changing where their numbers go. Figure 1 illustrates how this works on a simplified GPU with six SMs and eight threads per SM, giving 48 threads in total. Imagine the weights as a long row of empty boxes, wrapped into a grid to fit on the page. The first thread fills the first box, the second fills the second box, and so on through all 48 threads. The first thread’s next number then goes into box 49, its next into box 97, and so forth. The black outlines follow this one thread through the grid: the first thread fills every 48th position. The colors identify which processing unit supplies each set of values, while the brightness in the right-hand panel represents the value itself. Figure 1. How a GPU fills the weights. This simplified example uses six processing units and eight threads per unit, for 48 threads in total. The outlined cells belong to thread 0, which fills every 48th position. Real chips use many more threads, but the placement rule is the same. Link ↗ Now keep the seed fixed, but use a GPU with five SMs instead of six. In our simplified example, that means 40 threads rather than 48. The first thread generates exactly the same sequence, but now puts its numbers in boxes 1, 41, 81, and so on, rather than boxes 1, 49, 97. Figure 2 follows these numbers as their positions change. Across the grid, only 6 percent of the values match the original arrangement. The seed is right, but the worker count is wrong. That is what makes the arrangement of model weights a clue to the chip used to create it. Figure 2. The same seed on a different GPU. With five processing units and 40 threads in this toy example, thread 0 generates the same sequence but fills every 40th position instead of every 48th. Only 6% of the displayed matrix matches the original arrangement. Link ↗ Reproducing the weights therefore requires two things to be right at once. The seed must generate the right numbers, and the thread count must put them in the right places. A correct seed with the wrong thread count mostly gives the right numbers in the wrong positions; a correct thread count with the wrong seed gives different numbers. Figure 3 shows why only the correct combination recreates the original arrangement. Figure 3. Both the seed and the layout must match. The original matrix is reproduced only when the seed and thread count are both correct. Changing either one destroys most of the match. The simplified chips represent a Blackwell B300 and a Hopper H100. Faded cells differ from the published weights. The numbered cells show where thread 0’s numbers land, and the strip beneath each panel shows the numbers themselves. Link ↗ On real chips, the thread counts are much larger, but the principle is the same. In the NVIDIA configurations examined here, the Hopper H100 SXM, H200 and H800 have 132 SMs and use 270,336 threads; the Blackwell B200/B300 have 148 SMs and use 303,104 threads; and the Blackwell GB200/GB300 have 152 SMs and use 311,296 threads. Recovering the thread count therefore tells us which of these hardware groups matches the starting arrangement, although it cannot distinguish chips within a group. A Hopper match, for example, cannot tell an H800 from an H100 or H200. The question is whether enough of that arrangement survives training for us to recover it. Some weights, such as those reserved for words or symbols never encountered during training, can remain untouched and retain their starting values almost exactly. We can compare these preserved values directly with the starting values generated by a candidate seed and thread count. Figure 4 shows such a comparison: DeepSeek-V3’s preserved weights match the Hopper arrangement, while DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s match the Blackwell arrangement. Figure 4. Preserved starting values reveal the layout. Each dot compares a published weight with the value regenerated from the seed. A diagonal line means the values match. DeepSeek-V3 matches the Hopper layout, while V4-Flash matches the Blackwell layout. The panels show 4,096 values from four preserved rows per model. Link ↗ Even weights that training has changed can retain a faint trace of their starting values. Each final weight is its starting value plus all the adjustments made during training. If those adjustments do not completely cancel or overwhelm the starting differences, some of those differences survive. For example, two weights that begin at 0.2 and 0.8 and each increase by about 0.1 will still be ordered the same way afterward. Real adjustments vary much more, so one weight tells us little. But across hundreds of thousands of weights, we can test whether higher starting values still tend to correspond to higher final values. Figure 5 shows this weak but measurable relationship. It is a finding in these weights, not a property guaranteed to survive every training run. Figure 5. Trained weights retain a weaker trace. The left and middle panels average 745,472 weights per layer across 42 layers of DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Under the Blackwell layout, higher starting values still predict slightly higher final values (r = 0.066, 57 sigma); under Hopper, the relationship disappears. The right panel shows the weaker evidence from individual layers. Link ↗ These surviving traces let us work backward. Suppose, in an invented example using Figure 1’s layout, seed 7 makes the first thread produce 0.2, −0.5 and 0.8. With 48 threads, those values go into positions 1, 49 and 97; with 40 threads, they go into positions 1, 41 and 81. If the published weights preserve the first pattern, we can try candidate seeds and thread counts until we recreate it. In the actual investigation, we compare thousands of values in their corresponding positions. Untouched weights can match exactly; trained weights may show only the weaker resemblance described above. In either case, we look for the combination that best reproduces the surviving pattern. We then test that combination on weights we kept out of the search. Having chosen a seed and thread count using one set of weights, we use them to predict the starting values of a different set, without changing either setting to improve the fit. A match on these previously unused weights is stronger evidence than a match confined to the weights that helped us choose the combination. Figure 6 shows the comparisons: DeepSeek-V3 matches the initialization layout of Hopper H100 SXM, H200 or H800 chips; DeepSeek-V4-Flash matches Blackwell B200/B300; and Kimi K3 matches Blackwell GB200/GB300. Figure 6. Comparing candidate layouts. Each model has one clear peak: DeepSeek-V3 at 132 SMs, V4-Flash at 148, and Kimi K3 at 152. The other tested layouts score near zero. Link ↗ In our investigations, we found patterns strongly suggestive of initialization on Blackwell chips in six models from four Chinese companies: DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro from DeepSeek, Kimi K3 and Kimi K3.1-Pro from Moonshot AI, MiniMax-M3 from MiniMax, and Ling-3.1-flash from Ant Group. V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match the 148-SM layout; the other four match the 152-SM layout. These are fingerprints of the starting weights, which support, but do not by themselves prove, the use of Blackwell chips for training AI models. Limits of our investigation Notably, the forensic method we used to identify the hardware on which these models were initialized only works for certain models. It needs published weights, so closed models cannot be checked. It also needs a recognizable, hardware-dependent pattern from the software that generated the starting weights. PyTorch on the GPUs examined here leaves such a pattern; Baidu’s PaddlePaddle framework, which was used to train Baidu’s ERNIE-5.5 model, does not. We were able to recover the seed for ERNIE-5.5 (2760), but could not identify which hardware was used to initialize it. Likewise, weights initialized on an ordinary processor rather than a GPU leave no GPU fingerprint; several of Alibaba’s Qwen3 models were initialized this way, and thus leave no trace of which GPUs were used to train them. We also found no fingerprint in Meituan’s LongCat-2.0, which the company says was trained on “AI ASIC superpods,” or in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, despite an exhaustive search. The method identifies the hardware that generated the starting weights, not every chip that later helped train the model. When a training run creates its weights on the same GPUs that will train it, the fingerprint points to both. But a lab could generate the weights on one system and move them to another, or continue training an existing model on new hardware. The weights alone cannot rule out those possibilities. A mixed cluster introduces the same limitation. If NVIDIA chips generated some weights and Huawei chips later helped train them, the NVIDIA pattern could survive without revealing Huawei’s participation. Different NVIDIA generations could leave different patterns in the parts they initialized, if those traces survived. In Kimi K3, at least 64 separately seeded processes each left the same 152-SM layout. A Blackwell-compatible pattern therefore supports its use at initialization, subject to the AMD alternative below; it does not establish that the entire training run used Blackwell. A Hopper pattern likewise does not rule out later training on Blackwell. The weights also cannot reveal who owned the chips or where they were located. Blackwell systems can be rented from data centers outside China. The evidence concerns access to the hardware; by itself, it does not establish that chips were smuggled into China or that an export-control violation occurred. Could a different chip produce one of these Blackwell-compatible patterns? Among the NVIDIA configurations tested here, the older chips cannot: software can use fewer of a chip’s processing units, but cannot give it more than it physically has. Under the standard PyTorch behavior examined here, they cannot produce the 148- or 152-SM layouts. The China-market Blackwell graphics cards use a different number of threads per SM and do not produce either total. AMD presents a different possibility. An MI300X normally uses 304 processing units, but it can be divided into two groups of 152 or configured to use only 148. Its random-number software can also generate the same underlying sequences as NVIDIA’s. Such configurations would be very unusual, but we confirmed on a physical MI300X that, limited to 152 or 148 of its units, it reproduces the layouts we associate with Blackwell, so the layout alone does not settle the question. To distinguish them, we looked for small numerical differences in the values themselves. AMD and NVIDIA perform one calculation in the number-generating process slightly differently. On a physical MI300X, DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s preserved weights point to NVIDIA: in the 377 values where the two vendors’ results differ, the published weight matches NVIDIA’s in 363 and AMD’s in none. The same test could not settle the other five models, but we consider the AMD explanation very unlikely for them. In its normal configuration, an MI300X produces neither layout; a lab would have had to configure an entire cluster to use the same number of processing units as a Blackwell chip. Other public evidence also points to Blackwell: U.S. officials and press reports have alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, and Ant Group’s public code includes benchmark results generated on a GB300. Verifying our findings To reproduce the result that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, we ran unmodified PyTorch on a Hopper-class NVIDIA H100 and a Blackwell-class NVIDIA B300. We had identified DeepSeek’s seed number as 953049583, and found that it was used in the initialization of both DeepSeek-V3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Using that seed, the H100 reproduced the preserved starting values in DeepSeek-V3, but not V4-Flash; the B300 reproduced the preserved values in V4-Flash, but not V3. On the B300, unmodified PyTorch reproduced 461 of the 469 selected rows in DeepSeek-V4-Flash with correlations above 0.99, including 445 entire rows that matched bit for bit. Eight selected rows were partly changed by training. On the H100, it reproduced all 57,344 preserved values in DeepSeek-V3 bit for bit. Neither chip reproduced the other model’s preserved rows. Changing the seed by one reproduced no matching rows on either machine. On a rented GB200, unmodified PyTorch likewise reproduced all 13 of Kimi K3’s preserved rows using Moonshot’s seed, 20256586; changing the seed by one reproduced none. The code and the preserved weights needed to repeat these checks are public ; the same comparison also runs without a GPU. Our forensic method also gets the right answer when the answer is already known. There are 24 cases where a developer has publicly named the hardware behind a specific model; our forensic method agrees with every one. Meta’s Llama 3.1 models, trained on H100s, read as 132; eight of EleutherAI’s Pythia models, trained on A100s, read as 108. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of training, reads as 152, the same as Kimi K3. DeepSeek and Moonshot have reported H800 use for earlier models. Our Hopper readings are consistent with those disclosures, but would also be consistent with H100 SXM or H200 hardware; they do not independently verify H800 use. When we compare the published weights with the numbers generated by a candidate seed and chip layout, some resemblance is inevitable even if the candidate is wrong. How much resemblance counts as evidence depends on how many weights we compare: agreement across a handful of numbers could easily be accidental, while agreement across thousands is much harder to explain by chance. Our statistical model accounts for the number of weights compared and measures how far the observed match exceeds the resemblance expected by chance. We express that distance in standard deviations, or sigma . A higher score means stronger evidence against an accidental match, provided the statistical model correctly describes the random variation in the data. We must also account for how many candidates we tried. Searching roughly six trillion combinations of seed and layout gives us trillions of opportunities to find a lucky match. Under a normal-distribution model, a positive match of five sigma or more occurs by chance about once in 3.5 million comparisons. That would be striking in a single test, but unsurprising somewhere in a search as large as ours. We therefore use approximately eight sigma as our benchmark for assessing accidental matches across the full search. Our findings exceed that benchmark by a wide margin. We first select a seed and layout using one set of weights, and then test that same combination on a separate set that played no part in choosing it. This checks whether the apparent fingerprint extends beyond the numbers that led us to it. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma; even the weakest individual test reported reaches 20 sigma. Under our statistical model, these results are far too strong to attribute to accidental resemblance. They establish evidence of a shared initialization pattern; identifying precisely which computing hardware produced that pattern, and whether it also performed the training, requires the separate arguments discussed above. Conclusion Based on our forensic investigation, we believe that we have strong evidence that six Chinese AI models were initialized on export-controlled NVIDIA hardware, and that for DeepSeek-V4-Flash the evidence is conclusive ; we believe that this initialization also strongly suggests that they trained on the same export-controlled hardware. While this leaves unanswered other questions—such as the circumstances through which the companies that developed these models acquired export-controlled NVIDIA systems—we believe that this fact deserves urgent attention from the public. DeepSeek-V2 and V2-Lite share one “H800 cluster” sentence, MoE-16B says “A100 or H800,” and Coder says “A100 and H800.” MiniMax’s MiniMax-01 paper describes a cluster of H800s, and Ant Group’s Ling 2.0 report says its training ran on “Hopper GPUs.” These are consistent with our readings but are not independent tests. V2-Lite reuses MoE-16B’s initialization: their preserved rows are byte-identical. ² License required. The B200, B300, GB200 and GB300 have needed a U.S. export license for China since before they shipped, and none have been reported. The AMD MI300X is also controlled. ³ Compliant variant existed. The A100/H100 class was controlled from October 2022, but the A800 and H800, which have the same SM counts, could be exported until October 2023. ⁴ Unresolved Hopper hardware. These models were first published from December 2024 onward and show a 132-SM fingerprint compatible with H800, H100 SXM or H200 hardware. DeepSeek and Moonshot have reported H800 use for some models, but the fingerprint cannot distinguish these chips. A model’s release date does not establish when or where its hardware was acquired, and this reading alone does not establish export-control compliance. ⁵ 148 part. See the note on Kimi K2.7-Code under the results table. † Reported by one analysis pass and not yet independently re-run. In every other row added for this brief, the first model named was re-run independently; models listed as sharing its initialization were not. These flags describe the hardware class under the U.S. export rules of October 2022 and October 2023. They are not a finding that any law was broken. No GPU signature recovered. A blank says nothing about a model’s hardware. We recovered no signature from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (after an exhaustive search), Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Qwen3-0.6B and 1.7B, gpt-oss-120b and Grok-1. Qwen3-235B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.5-9B were initialized on the CPU, which leaves no GPU layout. Baidu’s ERNIE-5.5 uses PaddlePaddle, whose generator carries no chip layout (we recovered its seed, 2760); ERNIE-4.5 gave no result. Meituan’s LongCat-2.0 gave no result. Its model card says training ran “entirely on AI ASIC superpods,” and a since-deleted fine-tuning configuration sets device_arch to 910 with NPU and HCCL options, which we read as Huawei Ascend 910. Intern-S2 is built on Alibaba’s Qwen3.5-397B and carries its initialization. DBRX and Llama-4-Scout could not be downloaded. Code. The code and preserved rows needed to reproduce the results for DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Kimi K3, MiniMax-M3 and Ling-3.1-flash are at github.com/macrogrants/checkpoint-forensics . The check runs on a laptop in a few seconds, and a second script repeats it with unmodified PyTorch on a GPU. Contact: Will DePue, will@unemploymentlabs.com. Sources The Information, Dec. 10, 2025, on DeepSeek and Blackwell ( via Bloomberg ). Reuters, Feb. 23, 2026, “China’s DeepSeek trained AI model on Nvidia’s best chip despite US ban, official says” (syndicated copy). Michael Kratsios, White House OSTP director, July 22, 2026, on Moonshot AI ( via Bloomberg ). The Wall Street Journal, March 2026, on Blackwell chips in Malaysia for ByteDance’s use ( via Reuters ). DeepSeek engineer’s GitHub comment, June 12, 2025: DeepGEMM pull request 112 . Ant Group’s GB300 benchmark results, March 31, 2026: cuLA, BENCHMARK_GB300.md . U.S. export licensing rule: 15 CFR 742.6 . Disclosed hardware: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report ; Kimi K2 paper ; Nemotron-3 Ultra Technical Report . Training runs used for comparison: Mistral Large 4 model card ; Microsoft AI, Oct. 15, 2026, “Frontier Pre-training at Microsoft AI” ; DeepSeek, “Insights into DeepSeek-V3” . Code to reproduce the results: github.com/macrogrants/checkpoint-forensics . PyTorch code that sets the thread layout: DistributionTemplates.h . Model weights: DeepSeek-V3 , V4-Flash , V4-Pro , Kimi K3 , K3.1-Pro , MiniMax-M3 , Ling-3.1-flash . Overview The Foundation Models framework is a native Swift API for integrating any large language model into your app — including direct access to the Apple Foundation Models on-device and in Private Cloud Compute. Powerful capabilities like guided generation, tool calling, image understanding, and Dynamic Profiles are built in, so you have what you need to build unique experiences. What’s new in the Foundation Models framework Meet the Foundation Models framework Foundation Models framework Human Interface Guidelines for Generative AI Image understanding Multimodal prompts let you pass images alongside text so your app can reason about visual content. This opens up new categories of experiences you can build with image understanding — it's as simple as attaching an image to your prompt. The Vision framework is also integrated directly, giving your model purpose-built tools like OCR for precise text extraction and barcode readers for quick code scanning — all on-device. What’s new in image understanding Model support The Foundation Models framework gives you direct access to the on-device foundation model at the core of Apple Intelligence so you can build experiences that are smart, private, and work without internet connectivity. On-device models are highly useful for many tasks, yet sometimes you need a larger model for a more complex workflow. The Foundation Models framework now extends to server models — like Claude, Gemini, and more — all through the same Swift API, with full support for features like tool calling and guided generation. Any model provider can create a Swift package conforming to the Language Model protocol , a fundamental component of the framework that allows you to pick the right language model for your app. Supported third-party models Core AI Language Models MLX Language Models Claude Gemini Private Cloud Compute For those just getting started, developers who are enrolled in the App Store Small Business Program and have fewer than two million first-time App Store downloads can access the Apple Foundation Models running on Private Cloud Compute with no cloud API cost.* This delivers frontier-level intelligence with unparalleled privacy protections, ensuring that your users' data is not stored or accessible to Apple or anyone else. Learn more about Private Cloud Compute Build with the new Apple Foundation Model on Private Cloud Compute Bring an LLM provider to the Foundation Models framework Dynamic Profiles Dynamic Profiles are new declarative APIs for continuously updating your session's model, tools, and instructions on the fly. Rather than creating a session with a fixed configuration, you define profiles — each with its own model, temperature, reasoning level, and toolset — and swap between them within a single continuous session. The session transcript is shared across every profile switch, so your app gets more contextual intelligence with less prompting. Dynamic Profiles are designed to be adaptable building blocks: use them to build AI agents, skills, or any other high-level abstraction your app needs. Build agentic app experiences with the Foundation Models framework Debug and profile agentic app experiences with Instruments LLM search using Core Spotlight Evaluations framework The Evaluations framework gives you the ability to test your prompts and validate that your intelligence-powered features work correctly across dynamic conditions, going beyond what unit tests alone can catch. Whether you're iterating on instructions, switching models, or tuning a Dynamic Profile, Evaluations gives you confidence that your app's behavior holds up before you ship. Meet the Evaluations framework Improve your prompts by hill-climbing with Evaluations Create robust evaluations for agentic apps CLI The new fm command line tool in macOS 27 lets you streamline scripting, automate model workflows, and accelerate your development without writing a line of app code. You can prototype quickly, giving you a fast path from idea to implementation. Build AI-powered scripts with the fm CLI and Python SDK Open source To help you get started with adopting emerging AI patterns, the Foundation Models framework utilities package adds experimental abstractions on top of the framework — including custom skills, context management helpers, and a Chat Completions client that connects to a hosted model of your choice. The Foundation Models SDK for Python extends the framework into the Python ecosystem, letting you integrate with popular tooling and evaluation packages in Python. Foundation Models framework utilities package Foundation Models SDK for Python Requirements The Acceptable Use Requirements for the Foundation Models framework outline prohibited uses of Apple Foundation Models. Additionally, pursuant to Article 53(1)(b) of the AI Act, we make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems who intend to integrate AFM 3 Cloud into their AI systems. Acceptable Use Requirements for the Foundation Models framework AFM 3 Cloud Model Documentation Form Developer Footer *Certain Apple Intelligence features that rely on server-side models are subject to daily usage limits, including but not limited to Siri AI, Intelligent Photo Editing Tools, Image Playground, AFM 3 Cloud models in Shortcuts, and Developer apps using Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute. Daily limits may vary by feature, request complexity, system demand, system policies, and other factors. Expanded access to such features will be available for a fee in the future. Use of these features is subject to the Apple Intelligence Terms and Conditions. Learn more at apple.com/apple-intelligence . You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI). You don’t need an AWS account. Your requests go to the emulator, not to AWS. So you work with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. The emulator is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint. It has no graphical interface. After you start the emulator, you set environment variables to point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at its endpoint. Then you run your code as usual. In embedded mode, you pass the emulator’s HTTP client to your SDK instead. AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Don’t use it for production workloads or to test security. See Security in AWS Emulator . Documentation: AWS Emulator User Guide Quick start With an AI coding agent Install the aws-emulator skill, then ask your agent to set up the emulator. This needs the AWS CLI version 2.35.0 or later. See Getting started with an AI coding agent . aws agent-toolkit add-skill --skill-name aws-emulator --region us-east-1 Server mode (CLI and any SDK) Linux: install the RPM or Debian package and run aws-emulator . See Getting started on Linux . Windows / macOS: run the emulator in a container built from a short Dockerfile. See Getting started with Docker . Point your SDK at a running emulator by setting environment variables. See Pointing your AWS SDK at AWS Emulator . Embedded mode (Rust tests) Add the emulator as a dev-dependency and run it in-process, one isolated instance per test. There is no endpoint URL, certificate, or environment variable to set. Your test wires the emulator's HTTP client straight into the SDK client. See Getting started with embedded mode , and Building from source below for its build cost. Known issues To see how closely each service matches AWS, check the fidelity scores published with each release on the releases page . To check whether your own project is expected to work, see Checking whether your project works with AWS Emulator . Individual gaps are tracked in the repository's issues/ directory. APIs and behaviors that don't work yet are under issues/things-that-do-not-work/ , and ones that have since been fixed move to issues/things-that-now-work/ . Building from source You need this if you are modifying the emulator, running it from a checkout, or using embedded mode. Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so the prerequisites and build-cost guidance below apply to it too. Most other users install a prebuilt package instead (see Quick start ). Building from source is supported on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64) ; on Windows and macOS, use the Docker path above. Prerequisites A Rust toolchain with Cargo (install via rustup ). A C compiler, such as GCC or clang. Some dependencies build C code. At least 100 GB of free disk for target/ . The workspace has one crate per AWS service, so a debug build of everything is large, and it grows as services are added. A multi-core machine. A cold full build compiles every service crate, so the first build takes a while; fewer cores take proportionally longer. After that, rebuilding after a change to one service is much faster. Build and run cargo build -p aws-emulator-router cargo run -p aws-emulator-router The emulator serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 (self-signed certificate). Embedded mode build cost Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so your project's first cargo test builds the emulator's service crates alongside your own code. Budget a first build and target/ on the same order as building from source above, then fast incremental builds. Recommendation: reuse one CARGO_TARGET_DIR across projects, cache target/ (or use sccache) in CI, and pin the emulator to a release commit so it isn't rebuilt on every change. Repository layout . ├── Cargo.toml # workspace: one member per service, plus the core crates ├── services/ │ └── service-<name>/ # ONE CRATE PER SERVICE │ ├── smithy-model/ # <name>.json — the Smithy model that drives the wire protocol │ ├── build.rs # generates the service declaration from the model │ ├── src/ │ │ ├── service.rs # request routing and refusal overrides │ │ ├── state.rs # this service's in-memory state │ │ └── ops/ # one file per operation │ └── tests/ ├── core/ │ ├── router/ # the emulator binary: mounts every service on one endpoint │ └── embedded/ # the in-process (embedded mode) facade ├── vendor/ # framework crates — do not edit (replaced on update) └── issues/ # tracked fidelity issues Telemetry AWS Emulator is configured to collect and report usage data to AWS, to gain insight into how AWS Emulator is used. Telemetry is on by default. AWS Emulator collects telemetry data with strict data minimization in mind, preventing identification or attribution to specific users, accounts, or organizations. Its records never include what’s in your requests or responses, your code, your credentials, or personal data. We don’t share telemetry with third parties. For details on what is collected and how the data is handled, see Telemetry in AWS Emulator . To turn telemetry off, use one of the following options. Use a command-line option Start the emulator with the --telemetry option (short form -t ) set to off . This setting applies only to that emulator process. aws-emulator --telemetry off In a container, add --telemetry off after the image name in the docker run command. Use an environment variable Set EMULATOR_TELEMETRY to off before you start the emulator. This setting applies to every emulator that you start from that shell. EMULATOR_TELEMETRY accepts on , true , or 1 to turn telemetry on, and off , false , or 0 to turn it off. Values aren’t case sensitive. Any other value turns telemetry off, and the startup notice shows a warning. export EMULATOR_TELEMETRY=off aws-emulator Use a configuration file To turn telemetry off for every run on a machine, add these lines to the emulator settings file, config.toml . The file is ~/.aws/emulator/config.toml on Linux and macOS, and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\emulator\config.toml on Windows. To use a different file, set the EMULATOR_CONFIG environment variable to its path. [ telemetry ] enabled = false Use the embedded configuration API In embedded mode, turn off telemetry in the options that you pass when you create the emulator. use aws_emulator_embedded :: { AwsEmulatorEmbedded , EmbeddedOptions , Telemetry } ; fn main ( ) { let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded :: new ( EmbeddedOptions :: default ( ) . telemetry ( Telemetry :: Off ) ) ; let _http_client = emulator . http_client ( ) ; } You might build a tool that includes the emulator, such as a test framework that other people run. If you do, tell your users about telemetry and give them a way to turn it off. You can also ship your tool with telemetry off. Reporting issues and contributing Report bugs and fidelity gaps in GitHub Issues . The most useful report names the service, the operation, your SDK and version, the request you sent, and how the response differed from real AWS. This repository does not take PRs. title: Abandoned Quake 4 expansion finished by modders and now playable
body_text: openq4 0.14.1 windows x64 file - ModDB Hello guest register or sign in   or with: openq4 0.14.1 windows x64 file HOME Today Week Month Year games popular latest indies publishing add game mods popular latest add mod addons popular latest upload files popular latest upload RTX Remix Games Compatibility Remix Mods Remix Files PBR Assets News Tutorials Statistics videos images audio articles reviews headlines blogs post article engines popular latest add engine developers popular latest add dev groups popular latest add group forums jobs post job openQ4 Quake 4 mod | Released Sep 18, 2026 summary articles reviews files videos images openQ4 is a free, open-source engine and game-code replacement for Quake 4. Play the original campaign and multiplayer on today's Windows, Linux and Steam Deck, with widescreen support, smooth high-refresh motion and optional visual upgrades. Add file Report openq4 0.14.1 windows x64 Location Games : Quake 4 : Mods : openQ4 : Files Filename openq4-0.14.1-windows-x64.zip Category Full Version Uploader themuffinman86 Added Nov 11th, 2026 Size 648.86mb (680,374,349 bytes) Downloads 268 (3 today) MD5 Hash 665488382e34a7d9b3dcd33d355dff04 Embed Button Embed Widget 648.86mb Download Now Description openQ4 0.14.1, the Awakening Edition: play the recovered Quake 4 expansion beside the original campaign, with stable shadow mapping, a new interface, Vulkan on Windows, smarter bots and an experimental Android app. The Quake 4 expansion that never shipped is now playable. openQ4 0.14.1, the Awakening Edition , is out now, and it is the biggest update since 0.13.2. It brings a second campaign, stable shadow mapping, a rebuilt interface, Vulkan on Windows, smarter bots and an experimental Android app, then spends the extra weeks polishing all of it toward production quality. 0.14.0 was withdrawn soon after release, so for most of you this is the first look at everything below. 0.14.1 replaces it, with every 0.14 feature refined, fixed and optimized. It is a big step on the road to 1.0. The Awakening, at last Raven Software and Ritual Entertainment built an expansion for Quake 4 that was never released. Justin Marshall recovered and published it, and openQ4 now plays it beside the original campaign: pick Single Player &gt; Campaign and choose Quake 4 or The Awakening. All 13 maps on openQ4's own code. The expansion's monsters, weapons and vehicles are rebuilt in openQ4's engine and game code. openQ4 never loads the alpha's game DLL. Finished where the alpha wasn't. Where the alpha's own code or content stopped something working as designed, openQ4 fixes it: the Valkaryne finale, the beach's death-ray turret, the Pain Lord's weak spot and Retches that could never move are the biggest examples. New toys. A chaingun turret with heat and its own HUD, and vehicle HUDs in both the new and classic interfaces. Two campaigns, kept apart. Each keeps its own saves and settings, and returning to Quake 4, Arena or multiplayer removes the expansion's overrides. openQ4 ships none of the expansion's content; you supply the files. The Awakening guide shows how. Looks better, runs faster Shadow mapping you can leave on. The Quality and Ultra presets cast soft, stable shadow maps on OpenGL and Vulkan, with sharp contact shadows that soften with distance. They are cached while lights and casters stay still, so they cost less every frame and no longer shimmer as you walk. The flashlight casts shadows on every preset that draws them. Vulkan on Windows is now supported and the automatic choice for new installs. It was tested across every stock single-player map and 20 multiplayer maps, picks your GPU in Settings, recovers from driver resets, and falls back to OpenGL in the same launch if it has to. Presets re-tiered by frame rate. Ultra now plays smoothly instead of asking for everything at once; the old everything-on Ultra lives on as Maximum . New Low and Enhanced tiers fill the gaps, and Minimum and Low Power suit weak or battery-powered hardware. Smarter Auto-Detect reads your active GPU, memory, resolution and CPU, and fresh installs use it automatically. No more restarts. V-Sync, MSAA, texture quality, window and fullscreen changes and most presets apply to the running game. Quicker loading. Maps load faster, sounds decode in the background, declarations parse a fifth faster and start-up is over a second quicker. Cleaner motion. Temporal AA rebuilds full detail below native resolution and holds still when nothing moves, motion blur looks the same at any frame rate, and cutscenes, cameras, ragdolls and spectating stay smooth on high-refresh screens. A whole new interface The Remastered HUD with Minimal, Competitive and Classic layouts, controller button prompts, and Reduced Motion and Reduced Flashing options. Rebuilt menus and tabbed settings, including a Display page that keeps or reverts a change on a countdown, plus New Game and Chapters pages for the campaigns. Vector weapon wheels and scopes for Marine and Strogg, with live ammo. Animated crosshairs. Each weapon's original crosshair assembles, kicks, charges and reloads with the weapon. Built for every screen: controllers, touch, portrait and tall layouts, and text up to 200%. Arena regains its ceremony: the match-start camera move and "Fight!", opponent introductions and a real pause menu. Prefer the original look? The classic screens and HUD are one setting away: seta ui_retained 0 . Multiplayer, bots and demos Your inputs reach the server on time again, and prediction and lag compensation no longer correct the same delay twice. Bots that take orders. They plan safer routes, hear the fight, time item respawns and follow commands such as everyone follow me . They also stop knocking team-mates off walkways, swim to underwater routes and escape napalm and grenades. Talk to your team: quick chat on D-pad Down or V, push-to-talk voice chat with per-player mute, and objective markers for flags, assault points and DeadZone zones. Demos you can navigate. Multi-view demos gain kill, capture and round markers, Auto-Track and near-instant seeking, and you can record a whole campaign, level transitions included, as one demo. Hosting works as set: Create Server options take effect, the Admin page accepts remote-console passwords, dedicated servers change maps faster, and networking is hardened throughout. Sound and languages Room reverb for every map, as the original game had with EAX hardware: closed doors muffle, hangars boom and radio chatter stays dry. Truer audio: sound variety, stereo width, radio levels and distance falloff now match the original game, and unplugging your headphones no longer cuts the music. Dialogue subtitles with size, backing and speaker names, plus a separate Dialogue Volume. Six new languages: German, Brazilian Portuguese, Czech, Hungarian, Turkish and Ukrainian menus and game text. New frontiers (experimental) Android: a signed ARM64 APK with touch controls, portrait play and a touch layout editor, built on Emile Belanger's port and OpenGL ES renderer. VR: head-tracked stereo through OpenXR, with motion-controller aiming, room-scale movement and comfort options, now on Vulkan too. Level editor: edit brushes, patches and entities in 2D and 3D views, then build and play the map in one click. For modders and mappers: physically based materials with reflection probes, recompiled maps that keep their AI cover positions, and clip brushes that block what they were built to block. Sturdier under the hood Three code audits and static analysis fixed crash, memory-safety and save-restore defects throughout the engine and game code. Saves are now written in a portable format and reported only once they are safely on disk, and openQ4's own data ships as separate packs so future patches can be small downloads. Before you install You need your own copy of Quake 4 from Steam or GOG. openQ4 finds it on its own. Install into a fresh folder. 0.14.1 repacks openQ4's own data, so don't copy it over an older openQ4. Your settings, bindings and saves carry over. Reapply your preset in Settings &gt; System to get the re-tiered values. New saves use a format older builds can't read, so back up your saves if you might go back. Multiplayer needs matching openQ4 0.14.1 clients and servers. Retail Quake 4 and mods built for its original game DLLs are not compatible. Mappers: recompile maps that use vehicle, fly, shot or item clip brushes. Experimental means experimental: VR has not yet been qualified on headset hardware, Android has been qualified on one phone so far, and The Awakening is built from unfinished alpha content, with full playthrough qualification still in progress. Your reports help. Download Grab it from the openQ4 downloads here on ModDB, or get any package from the GitHub release page : Windows x64, as an installer or a zip Linux x64, as an AppImage or an archive (also used on Steam Deck) macOS on Apple Silicon (preview); signed builds are also offered by Mac Source Ports Linux ARM64 (preview), Windows ARM64 and Android ARM64 (experimental) The full release notes list everything new since 0.13.2, with upgrade notes and known limitations. The road to 1.0 0.14.1 is a deliberate push toward 1.0: fewer new experiments and more polish on what already exists. The same engine work now underpins the rebased openPREY and openD3 projects, which share fixes with openQ4 in both directions. Thank you to Emile Belanger for the Android port, Justin Marshall for recovering and publishing The Awakening, Schnapple of Mac Source Ports for the signed macOS builds, akacross for tireless playtesting and pull requests, and everyone who reported issues after 0.14.0. Trigger phrases: 'teach me', 'tutor me', 'quiz me', 'drill me', 'help me master'. Not for one-off 'explain X' or 'what is X' questions. Socratic Tutor Act as a personal tutor that takes the user from their current level to genuine mastery of a topic using the maieutic (Socratic) method: teach primarily by asking questions that force the user to reason, predict, and explain — not by lecturing. Guard: confirm intent before starting This skill is for an ongoing teaching session, not for answering questions. If the user asked a one-off question ("explain X", "what is X", "how do I use X"), answer it normally and do not start the tutoring loop. If intent is ambiguous, ask one short question ("Want a quick answer, or should I actually teach you this properly?") before launching the diagnostic. A false start costs the user an unwanted quiz; a confirmation costs one word. Session start Break the topic into 4-10 concrete subskills (fewer for narrow topics). For broad topics, make a two-level tree and pick the first branch to work on. Tell the user that you will start by asking a few questions, one at a time, to see what they already know. Run a short diagnostic: 3-5 probing questions spanning easy to hard, to place the user's starting level per subskill. Do not teach anything until the diagnostic is done. Show the initial skill map (format below) and propose where to start. Let the user override. Skill map Track each subskill at levels 0-5: 0 unaware . 1 heard of it . 2 can follow along . 3 can do with help 4 can do independently . 5 can teach it / handle edge cases Render the map as ASCII after every level change, and whenever the user asks for progress: Topic: <topic> overall: ######.... 58% ----------------------------------------------------------------- subskill A [########..] 4/5 * independent subskill B [######....] 3/5 <- current focus subskill C [##........] 1/5 ----------------------------------------------------------------- Use solid/light block characters (U+2588 / U+2591) for the bars when rendering. Teaching loop (repeat per subskill) Ask ONE question at a time. End the message immediately after the question and wait for the answer; do not add hints, example answers, or teaching content after it. Prefer questions that make the user: predict an outcome, explain why, find the flaw in a plausible-but-wrong claim, apply an idea to a new case, or connect two ideas. When the user is wrong, do not give the answer. Ask a narrower question that exposes the contradiction in their reasoning. Only explain directly after 2-3 failed attempts, and then immediately re-test the same idea from a different angle. When the user is right, occasionally play devil's advocate ("are you sure? what about X?") — they should be able to defend correct answers under pressure. Give short explanations (a few sentences) only to introduce genuinely new material the user could not derive, then return to questioning. Where tools are available and relevant, set practical exercises (e.g. "write a query that...", "predict what this code prints") and check the user's actual output rather than their description of it. Evaluation rules — be strict Levels are earned, not given. Raise a level only on demonstrated performance across 2+ independent checks, at least one of them unprompted recall (not immediately after the user was told the answer). A vague or partially-correct answer is not correct. Probe until you know whether the user actually understands. Do not attribute to the user any insight they did not actually express. Interleave spaced review: periodically re-test earlier subskills without warning. If the user fails a review, lower the level and revisit. Level 5 requires the user to handle an edge case or adversarial question AND explain the concept clearly enough that you would trust them to teach it. Do not flatter. "Not quite — why would X happen if Y were true?" beats "Great try!". Mastery and completion The course ends only when every subskill is at the target level (default 4/5; 5/5 if the user asked for full mastery). Then run a final mixed assessment covering everything, with at least one question per subskill and one integrative problem. If the user passes, show the final map and a summary of their weakest areas. If not, back to the loop. Commands the user can use anytime "show progress" — render the skill map "harder" / "easier" — adjust difficulty "just tell me" — override Socratic mode for the current question only "save state" — emit a compact block (topic, skill map with levels, notes on misconceptions and what has been covered) that can be pasted into a new session to resume "resume from:" — followed by a saved state block; restore it and continue where it left off Footer © 2026 GitHub, Inc.
